DIY cervical checks will be offered to around four million women via kits sent through the post.
Women who have failed to attend cervical screening appointments will be able to order self-testing kits from the NHS, under plans to boost uptake and help eliminate cervical cancer.
The kits test for high-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), a common virus passed through sexual contact and causes almost all cases of cervical cancer.
Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game-changer – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.”
Eligible women aged between 30 and 65 who have not attended screening appointments will be sent invitations from Tuesday through the NHS app, text message, email or letter.
They will then be able to order a kit through the NHS app or online.
The kits contain a swab which can be used to collect a sample from the vagina. The kit can then be posted free-of-charge to NHS laboratories.
If high-risk HPV is found, women will be invited to book a follow-up cervical screening appointment at their GP surgery or sexual health clinic, where a nurse or doctor will take a sample from the cervix to check for cell changes.
Around 13 high-risk types of HPV are known to cause cervical cancer, while the infection itself usually causes no symptoms.
Screening ‘saves thousands of lives annually’
The phased rollout forms part of the NHS’s target to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.
Latest NHS England figures show 68.8 per cent of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80 per cent target.
The health service estimates this means around four million women are not up to date.
Dr Mann said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two-thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS.
“There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test.
“So, if you’re invited to take part, please order a test – it’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.”
Health officials said attending cervical screening appointments with a clinician was still the best way to reduce the chance of cervical cancer.
Vaccinated women still urged to get checked
They said self-testing, which will be by invitation only, was being offered as an extra choice for those who have not taken up previous invitations.
The scheme is being rolled out in phases across England as part of the NHS cervical screening programme, starting with women aged between 30 and 65 who have previously failed to attend.
Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening by the NHS every five years, or more frequently if HPV is detected.
Anyone who has been invited for cervical screening can still book an appointment at any time, even if the invitation was sent months or years ago.
Experts said women who have been vaccinated against HPV should still attend cervical screening appointments because the vaccine does not protect against all types of the virus.
summary: NHS England is launching a phased rollout of DIY cervical screening kits for around four million women who have missed their regular appointments. Eligible women aged 30 to 65 can order the home test kits through the NHS app or online to check for high-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV). The initiative aims to boost screening uptake and support the goal of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040.
key_points: DIY self-testing kits for HPV will be offered to approximately four million women in England who have not attended regular cervical screening appointments.
Eligible women aged 30 to 65 can receive invitations via the NHS app, text, email, or letter and order kits online to use at home.
The kits involve a simple vaginal swab that is mailed to NHS laboratories free of charge.
If high-risk HPV is detected, women will be invited for a follow-up appointment with a clinician for further checks.
The scheme is part of the NHS target to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040 and address low screening attendance rates.

title: Autism and ADHD care complaints more than triple in five years in England
author: Sarah Marsh
content:
Complaints about autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder services in England have more than tripled in five years, official figures show, with the NHS ombudsman warning of years-long waits and patients paying thousands of pounds for private care.
One woman was removed from an ADHD medication waiting list without warning after almost four years, leaving her without the support she needed for about six months. Another patient was given an autism assessment lasting just 50 minutes that failed to follow guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, while a man referred to an ADHD service that was not yet operational ended up paying almost £4,000 for private treatment.
Complaints rose from 410 in 2021-22 to 1,257 in 2025-26, an increase of more than 200%, as referrals and the number of people waiting for assessment, treatment and support also increased.
Demand for ADHD and autism assessment and support services has surged dramatically across England, with open NHS referrals reaching roughly 562,000. More than 60% of adults and children face waiting lists exceeding a year, while prescribing data shows historic multi-year increases.
The parliamentary and health service ombudsman, Paula Sussex, said ADHD and autism services were “under significant pressure, with demand outstripping capacity”, adding: “While commissioning cannot solve these supply constraints, the way services are designed, commissioned and delivered can compound the pressure people experience and make it harder to make the best use of available resources.”
She said: “Right now, the system is too complex and inconsistent, leaving too many patients falling through the gaps.”
A report, called Improving ADHD and Autism Services: Commissioning With Confidence, shares the ombudsman’s findings based on 3,000 complaints. It found recurring issues, including uncertainty around patients’ right to choose a provider. Under right to choose, patients in England can choose from eligible NHS-funded providers for certain services, including some independent providers. However, the ombudsman found uncertainty around how this right applied, with patients sometimes being told wrongly that they could not exercise it.
Other problems included inconsistent recognition of diagnoses across NHS and independent providers, and lengthy waits for assessment and treatment.
In one case, Rich, 48, asked to be referred to Psychiatry UK for his ADHD treatment. NHS South East London integrated care board denied Rich’s request and wrongly insisted he be referred to a local ADHD service, which was still being developed and had no opening date. The ombudsman found his NHS treatment was delayed by five months. Rich felt he had no choice but to pay for private care, amounting to almost £4,000.
In another investigation, South London and Maudsley NHS foundation trust removed a woman from the ADHD medication titration (the process of adjusting medication to find the right balance) waiting list without warning or valid reason, leaving her without specialist monitoring support for about six months. This delay may have affected her symptoms and her ability to carry out everyday activities, causing frustration and distress.
Sussex said: “People should not have to fight their way through a confusing system to get ADHD and autism care.”
The ombudsman’s office itself has a six-month waiting time because of the rise in complaints it is receiving.
A government spokesperson said: “Last December, we asked clinical psychologist Professor Peter Fonagy to lead an independent review, examining the prevalence of - and support for - ADHD, autism, and mental health conditions. Professor Fonagy’s final report will be published later this summer, and will inform our new national approach in this area.”
summary: Official figures show that complaints regarding autism and ADHD services in England have more than tripled over five years, surging from 410 in 2021-22 to 1,257 in 2025-26. The parliamentary and health service ombudsman highlighted that over 60% of adults and children face waiting lists exceeding a year amid roughly 562,000 open NHS referrals. A new ombudsman report identifies recurring issues such as lengthy waits, inconsistent diagnoses, and confusion over patients' right to choose providers, which has driven some individuals to pay thousands for private care.
key_points: Complaints about autism and ADHD services in England increased by more than 200% over five years.
Open NHS referrals for ADHD and autism have reached approximately 562,000, with over 60% of patients waiting more than a year.
The parliamentary and health service ombudsman published a report citing issues like long waits, inconsistent diagnoses, and confusion surrounding the right to choose providers.
Some patients faced severe delays, such as being removed from waiting lists without warning or being forced to pay thousands of pounds for private treatment.
A government-backed independent review led by Professor Peter Fonagy is set to inform a new national approach when its final report is published.

title: 'Game changer' study seeks answers for heavy periods and endometriosis
author: Matthew Hill
content:
![Professor Gemma Sharp, an epidemiologist at the University of Exeter is holding up a specialist sanitary pad and pipette and looking at the camera in a lab. She has short brown hair in a bob and is wearing a brown and white pinstripe blouse.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/917/cpsprodpb/be51/live/3f4d91a0-85e1-11f1-9837-c51febdbeb82.png)
Professor Gemma Sharp, from the University of Exeter, hopes the study will be "a real game changer" for menstrual health research
- Published
A major new research project aiming to transform care for women with heavy periods is to create the world's largest menstrual fluid biobank.
The CycleTrack study hopes to improve understanding of heavy menstrual bleeding and related conditions such as endometriosis and fibroids, helping speed up diagnosis and treatment for millions of women.
Led by researchers from the universities of Bristol and Exeter, it will collect real-time health data and menstrual fluid samples from thousands of women across the UK.
Professor Gemma Sharp said the study was going to be "a real game changer" for menstrual health research and could cut waiting times for effective treatment.
More from Bristol
As part of the study, researchers are working with women who have personal experience of heavy periods.
Maria Lewis, 34, from Weston-super-Mare, has lived with heavy menstrual bleeding since she first started menstruating and was diagnosed with endometriosis last year.
She has taken part in the Children of the 90s, external study since childhood and was keen to support the latest research.
Describing the impact of her condition, she said: "It's horrific. I'm in pain every day."
Although she cannot take part in the menstrual fluid collection because she takes hormonal contraception to manage her symptoms and no longer menstruates, she believes the research could help improve understanding of conditions affecting women.
She said: "Absolutely, it needs more of a platform and a louder voice."
![Maria Lewis from Weston-super-Mare. She has wavy brown hair in a bob and is wearing bright pink glasses and a white v neck top.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/993/cpsprodpb/2f14/live/4dd26300-9d64-11f1-a07c-85afe5c51b6f.png)
Maria Lewis, who suffers from heavy periods, says she is in pain on a daily basis
Heavy menstrual bleeding, sometimes known as HMB, affects up to half of women worldwide and can have a significant impact on physical, emotional and social wellbeing.
Symptoms can include periods lasting more than seven days, the need to change sanitary protection every one to two hours, passing large blood clots and signs of iron deficiency such as fatigue and dizziness.
Researchers say menstrual health remains poorly understood despite being a key indicator of overall health, partly because of a lack of high-quality data.
Recent studies have suggested heavy periods can affect many aspects of daily life, external, including educational attainment and school attendance.
Tracking symptoms in real time
The study will recruit participants from two long-running birth cohort studies: Children of the 90s in south-west England and Born in Bradford in West Yorkshire.
Thousands of volunteers will use a specialist app and detailed questionnaires to record symptoms, sleep, mood, energy levels and overall wellbeing.
Participants will also provide menstrual fluid samples over three menstrual cycles using specially designed period pads.
By linking those samples with long-term health information and genetic data already held by the cohort studies, researchers hope to uncover biological signals associated with heavy menstrual bleeding.
They believe the findings could lead to earlier diagnosis, more personalised treatment plans and new methods of identifying health risks linked to heavy periods, including iron deficiency.
The project is being led by Sharp, an epidemiologist at the University of Exeter who specialises in women's health research.
She said: "HMB is excessive menstrual blood loss that interferes with your physical, social, emotional and/or quality of life.
"It can occur with or without underlying pathology such as fibroids, hormonal issues.
"Common symptoms can often include: bleeding lasting longer than seven days, needing to change protection every one to two hours, passing large clots, signs of iron deficiency anaemia (e.g. fatigue, dizziness)."
The study is part of a wider international programme known as The Missed Vital Sign,, external led by Wellcome Leap, which aims to dramatically reduce the time women wait for effective treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Professor Sharp said CycleTrack would be the largest bank of dried menstrual fluid samples in the world.
She added: "We'll be able to understand what causes different conditions, like endometriosis, fibroids, the impact of those conditions on other areas of life, and then hopefully new ways to predict, prevent, and treat those symptoms as well."
Gaps in understanding
Researchers say the work could help address long-standing gaps in understanding menstrual health and improve support for millions of women.
Although periods are experienced by around half the population during their lifetime, campaigners and health experts have often argued menstrual health has not received the same level of research attention as many other areas of medicine.
The CycleTrack, external team hopes the large volume of data generated by the study will provide new insights into how heavy periods affect everyday life, work, education and general health.
The information could also help shape future guidance for schools and employers on supporting people affected by heavy menstrual bleeding.
Scientists say many women face delays in diagnosis and treatment, while some may not realise symptoms such as extreme tiredness or dizziness can be linked to blood loss and iron deficiency.
By analysing biological samples alongside day-to-day symptom information, the team hopes to identify markers that could eventually help clinicians recognise problems sooner and tailor treatment more effectively.
Sample collection is due to begin this month, with researchers expecting data from thousands of participants to contribute to what they describe as a step change in understanding menstrual health.
All the data will have been collected by end of November 2027. Preliminary findings will follow by early 2028.
Currently only Children of the 90s and Born in Bradford participants can take part, but the research team has a waiting list, external if people are interested in taking part in future studies (funding dependent).
summary: Researchers from the universities of Bristol and Exeter have launched the CycleTrack study, a major project aiming to create the world's largest menstrual fluid biobank to improve care for heavy periods, endometriosis, and fibroids. The study will collect real-time health data and menstrual fluid samples from thousands of UK women recruited from existing birth cohort studies. Scientists hope this research will speed up diagnoses, reduce waiting times for effective treatments, and address historical gaps in menstrual health understanding.
key_points: The CycleTrack study will create the world's largest bank of dried menstrual fluid samples.
Thousands of UK volunteers from the Children of the 90s and Born in Bradford cohort studies will track symptoms and provide samples.
Researchers aim to improve understanding of heavy menstrual bleeding, endometriosis, and fibroids to speed up diagnosis and personalize treatments.
Heavy menstrual bleeding affects up to half of women worldwide and can severely impact physical, emotional, and social wellbeing.

title: Fears over patient care at Nant y Glyn mental health unit in Colwyn Bay
author: Dafydd Evans; Anaba Khan
content:
![Ryan Shields and his mother Aly Shields standing together looking towards the camera. His mother is wearing a pink bandana on her blonde hair and has brownish glasses. Ryan is wearing greyish jacket and a blue beanie. He also has a long, light brown beard.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1040/cpsprodpb/efb8/live/447394a0-9fad-11f1-bff6-57f1422ebb0b.jpg)
Ryan Shields and his mother Aly say there has been a lack of continuity in his care
- Published
Mental health patients are being "left in limbo" because of high staff turnover and delayed care at a north Wales unit, it has been claimed.
One patient said it was "truly heartbreaking" that he was unable to make progress despite years of treatment at the Nant y Glyn community mental health centre in Colwyn Bay, Conwy.
The unit has been the subject of complaints for a number of years according to Clywd MS Darren Millar who says he has raised the matter again with inspectors.
Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board (BCUHB), which runs the centre, said it took concerns raised by families "extremely seriously".
![The outside view of Nant y Glyn community mental health unit.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/987/cpsprodpb/4a92/live/d2f0e530-9fac-11f1-bff6-57f1422ebb0b.jpg)
The community health unit at Nant y Glyn covers the county of Conwy
Ryan Shields has been receiving community mental health treatment since he was 19 and has been going to Nant y Glyn for most of that time, but says he has not seen improvement in his condition.
"The despair is truly heartbreaking for me. It doesn't feel like it's ever going to get better," said the 27-year-old.
He said the unit had suffered from delayed appointments, poor communication and low staff retention.
"There's lots of care co-ordinators that have come, they're ready and there's positive change in your life and you think 'this is great, this person is a star, they're amazing'," he said.
"And then over the months you just see them getting whittled down until there's not much there any more. Then they go, and once they go, the patient is left in limbo."
![Ryan Shields is wearing a green beanie and a grey jacket. He has a long, light brown beard.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1056/cpsprodpb/0df1/live/9e905640-a060-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Shields says care co-ordinators have been "whittled down" at the unit over the years
The situation has had a "devastating" impact on Ryan and his family, according to his mother Aly.
"Support without treatment means the patient ends up in a constant loop of illness rather than recovery. He hasn't been able to have a life," she said.
"I've watched staff go from being bright and vibrant coming into their roles to suddenly changing. It's almost like a cloud comes down on them.
"Obviously I'm not privy to their experience within Nant y Glyn, but my observation is that these people just change. It's not good for them and not good for patients."
In 2024, Health Inspectorate Wales (HIW) found the unit at Nant y Glyn to be "well led".
There were reported issues with contacting the centre via telephone, but service users were "satisfied" with the care, it said.
"There was evidence of cohesive team working and staff, in general, told us that they were happy in their roles," the report added.
But Geoff Ryall-Harvey, from patient representative body Llais, said staffing issues at the unit were "consistent" and seemed "very difficult to resolve".
![Darren Millar MS is looking towards the camera wearing a grey suit with a sky blue shirt as well as a green spotted tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b6dd/live/e58d88e0-9fae-11f1-bff6-57f1422ebb0b.jpg)
Welsh Conservative leader in the Senedd Darren Millar says he is aware of the concerns around the unit
Darren Millar, MS for Clwyd, said the health board had been "unable" to get on top of the situation.
"I've been aware of concerns. Whenever a concern is raised with me I always demand action," he said.
"I'm afraid it's got to a situation where even after HIW inspections fairly recently the situation is still unacceptably poor and that's why we need more urgent intervention now."
Teresa Owen, BCUHB's executive director of allied health professionals and health science, said: "We take the issues raised by patients and their families extremely seriously.
"As a health board our number one priority is providing the correct care at the correct time and we fully understand the value of continuity of care, for patients accessing our mental health services.
"The health board remains committed to fostering a culture in which staff feel able to raise concerns safely."
HIW said it was aware of concerns regarding Nant y Glyn but would not comment on individual cases.
"We will continue to monitor the service through our assurance activities and will take any appropriate action required to help ensure patients receive safe and effective care," said a spokesperson.
A Welsh government recently announced "ministerially directed intervention" on the health board.
If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.
summary: Concerns have been raised regarding patient care at the Nant y Glyn community mental health unit in Colwyn Bay due to high staff turnover and delayed appointments. Patients and their families claim the lack of continuity leaves individuals in limbo and hinders recovery, despite previous inspection findings that the unit was well-led. Local MS Darren Millar has escalated these ongoing issues to inspectors, while the Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board stated it takes such feedback extremely seriously.
key_points: Patients at Nant y Glyn community mental health centre are reportedly left in limbo due to high staff turnover and delayed care.
A 27-year-old patient, Ryan Shields, and his mother stated that constant changes in care co-ordinators prevent long-term recovery.
Clwyd MS Darren Millar has raised concerns with inspectors, stating that the situation remains unacceptably poor.
Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board emphasized that it takes family concerns seriously and values continuity of care.
Health Inspectorate Wales previously rated the unit as well-led in 2024, but monitoring of the service continues amid ongoing complaints.

title: First cases of bluetongue confirmed at two Cumbrian farms
author: Sophie Swain
content:
The first cases of bluetongue have been confirmed in Cumbria with infected animals identified at farms in the Carlisle and Millom areas.
Bluetongue is a notifiable viral disease spread mainly by biting midges. It does not infect people and does not pose a food-safety risk, but it can have serious welfare and financial consequences for affected livestock farms through illness, deaths, reduced productivity and restrictions on moving or trading animals.
Symptoms farmers should watch for
The current strain, bluetongue serotype 3 (BTV-3), can affect sheep, cattle and other ruminants including goats and deer, as well as camelids such as llamas and alpacas.
Signs can vary between animals, but farmers are being urged to look out for:
- Nasal discharge and crusting around the nose or muzzle
- Redness and swelling of the lips, nose, mouth or face
- Excessive drooling
- Mouth sores or ulcers
- Fever
- Lameness, stiffness or swelling around the hooves
- Reluctance to stand, walk or move
- A fall in milk production in cattle
- Diarrhoea in cattle
   (Image: Animal & Plant Health Agency)
Sheep can become particularly severely unwell. In more serious cases, swelling and impaired blood flow in the mouth can cause the tongue to appear blue — the symptom from which the disease takes its name
What happens to affected animals?
There is no treatment that removes the bluetongue virus itself. A vet may provide supportive care, such as pain relief, anti-inflammatory medication, fluids and soft feed, while closely monitoring an animal’s condition.
The impact can range from mild illness to severe disease. Sheep may suffer high death rates during outbreaks, while infected cattle can experience reduced milk yields, diarrhoea and fertility problems. Bluetongue has also been linked to abortions in cattle, temporary infertility in bulls and health problems in newborn calves. Animals which are unable to eat, remain unable to stand, or are in severe distress may need to be humanely euthanised on veterinary-welfare grounds.
Reporting suspected cases
Livestock keepers who suspect bluetongue must report it immediately. In England, the Animal and Plant Health Agency can be contacted on 03000 200 301.
Because bluetongue is notifiable, confirmation can lead to disease-control measures including surveillance, testing and restrictions on the movement of susceptible livestock. These restrictions are intended to limit spread, but can disrupt farm sales, breeding plans, transport and trade.
National picture
The Cumbria cases come as BTV-3 continues to spread across Great Britain. National figures reported on August 24 put the total for the 2026-27 bluetongue season at 593 confirmed premises: 556 in England, 29 in Wales and eight in Scotland. A “case” means a premises where at least one animal has tested positive.
Farmers are advised to contact their vet promptly if they notice suspicious signs and to seek advice on vaccination and measures to reduce animals’ exposure to midges.
summary: The first cases of bluetongue virus serotype 3 (BTV-3) have been confirmed at two farms in the Carlisle and Millom areas of Cumbria. While the notifiable disease does not affect humans or food safety, it causes significant welfare and financial impacts on livestock through illness, reduced productivity, and movement restrictions. Farmers are urged to monitor sheep, cattle, and other ruminants for symptoms and to report suspected cases immediately.
key_points: Bluetongue is a viral disease spread by biting midges that affects sheep, cattle, goats, deer, and camelids.
Symptoms include nasal discharge, facial swelling, excessive drooling, fever, lameness, and reduced milk production.
There is no direct treatment for the virus, and severe cases can result in high death rates or necessitate humane euthanasia.
Suspected cases in England must be reported immediately to the Animal and Plant Health Agency.
As of August 24, a total of 593 premises across Great Britain have confirmed cases for the 2026-27 season.

title: Dad's 'guilt' after passing on genetic cancer risk
author: Victoria Hicks; Becky Measures
content:
![Harjit Singh Nijjer is smiling. He is standing in the park with trees behind him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/5231/live/8b7732b0-9280-11f1-9985-cdf6a137096d.jpg)
Harjit said it was really important for families to talk about hereditary health issues
- Published
"It's not what you want to do as a parent. It's the last thing you want to do."
Harjit Singh Nijjer said when he discovered he had inherited a genetic condition he immediately began to worry about potentially passing it on to his son.
Harjit, of Market Harborough in Leicestershire, was 48 when he was diagnosed with bowel cancer in 2015.
After undergoing surgery and chemotherapy, he found out he had inherited Lynch syndrome - a condition that increases the risk of certain cancers, including bowel, ovarian and pancreatic.
"It's the guilt you carry," the 59-year-old said. "Things you'd want to pass on to your children - good looks, intelligence - but not something like this."
Harjit, a nurse, said his eldest son, William, had tested positive for Lynch syndrome, which affects an estimated one in 400 people in England.
Harjit and William have backed BBC Radio Derby's 'It Starts With You' campaign, which aims to get people talking about hereditary cancer risks.
The campaign is led by radio presenter Becky Measures, who had a preventative double mastectomy in 2006.
She was 24 at the time and became the youngest woman in Britain to undergo the procedure, following in the footsteps of her mum Wendy Watson.
The mother and daughter both carried the same BRCA1 gene mutation, meaning they had a significantly increased risk of developing breast cancer and ovarian cancer.
![Harjit Singh Nijjer sits on a bench in the park in the sunshine with his son William. Harjit is wearing beige shorts and brown sandals and a green and white striped shirt. He is bald. William is wearing grey shorts and trainers with a black t-shirt. He is sitting with his hands on his knees and has short black hair and a short beard.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/87e2/live/946c7d90-8ffa-11f1-b2a2-11d8521bf2f1.png)
Harjit was diagnosed with Lynch syndrome, a genetic condition his son William has inherited
William, 26, said he wanted to find out if he had inherited the disease so he could "take control of the situation".
"Unfortunately, I tested positive for Lynch, but that's become a powerful tool for me," he added.
"I'm now able to plan preventative measures, like taking aspirin.
"I'm on the colonoscopy programme, so bi-annually I have a colonoscopy to make sure there's no polyps in my bowel. It's been really useful for me."
Harjit, who said he was now in remission, is encouraging others to understand their family's health history and talk about any hereditary cancer risks.
Around 1,100 bowel cancers are caused by Lynch syndrome each year in England, according to the NHS.
While it does not directly cause cancer, it does lead to genetic mutations which run in families and can make the disease more likely at a younger age.
According to the NHS, people diagnosed with Lynch syndrome usually have a family history of bowel cancer and other Lynch syndrome-related cancers.
![A man in his 20s is smiling. He has black hair and a black beard and is wearing a black t-shirt. He is standing in a park.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/743/cpsprodpb/e564/live/bc9fd070-9011-11f1-aabc-c3c7aa714117.png)
William said finding out he had inherited Lynch syndrome gave him the power to take preventative action
Harjit said he was a young boy when his father died at the age of 62, in 1972.
He did not know of any cancer risk within his family and said not as much was known about Lynch syndrome then.
"It might explain why my father died much younger," he added.
"Family never talked about it. I'm sure culture played a part in it - but no, nothing.
"Had they, things could have changed."
Harjit said his mum sat with him when he received his own diagnosis of Lynch syndrome.
He said: "As much as my mum has pioneered everything, she broke down. She didn't want to have given this to me.
"However, you've got to understand from our perspective, it can't be helped.
"The knowledge now is what's so important."
![A man with grey hair and a grey beard and wearing a blue sweatshirt is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/452/cpsprodpb/135f/live/3c492bd0-9285-11f1-9985-cdf6a137096d.jpg)
Professor Julian Barwell said vaccines are being developed to protect against tumours developing in people diagnosed with Lynch syndrome
According to the NHS, Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition.
Each child and sibling of an affected individual has a 50% chance of inheriting the condition.
The NHS can carry out genetic tests to investigate whether Lynch syndrome runs in someone's family.
Lynch syndrome affects around 175,000 people, but only 5% are aware they are living with it.
Professor Julian Barwell, consultant in clinical genetics at the University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust, said: "It's important for people to be able to have conversations about cancer running in their families.
"There are so many things that we can do now to help support and protect families and keep them together for longer.
"But it starts with you having that conversation and taking that first step."
Barwell, who is also an Honorary Professor in genomic medicine at the University of Leicester, added: "There are groups looking to develop vaccines against Lynch syndrome tumours.
"We are hopeful within the next generation, we will be able to offer vaccines to people with Lynch syndrome, to reduce the risk of them actually developing a tumour in the first place."
William said if people can have "those open and honest conversations you can actually make a difference to your future by doing so".
Harjit added: "It's really, really important that we should talk. We are here because we have Lynch syndrome and we want to make a difference.
"If it changes the lives of one person - saves a family - then I think that's key at the end of the day, so [we are] happy to share our story."
Listen to BBC Radio Leicester on Sounds and follow BBC Leicester on Facebook, external, on X, external, or on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to eastmidsnews@bbc.co.uk, external or via WhatsApp, external on 0808 100 2210.
summary: Harjit Singh Nijjer, diagnosed with bowel cancer in 2015, discovered he had inherited Lynch syndrome, a genetic condition that increases the risk of certain cancers. He experienced parental guilt after passing the condition to his son, William, who subsequently tested positive for the syndrome at age 26. Both father and son are now supporting a campaign to encourage families to openly discuss hereditary cancer risks and take preventative health measures.
key_points: Harjit Singh Nijjer was diagnosed with bowel cancer at age 48 and later found to have Lynch syndrome.
His 26-year-old son, William, also tested positive for Lynch syndrome, allowing him to take preventative measures such as taking aspirin and undergoing bi-annual colonoscopies.
Lynch syndrome is an inherited condition affecting an estimated one in 400 people in England, though only 5% of those affected are aware of it.
Harjit and William are backing BBC Radio Derby's 'It Starts With You' campaign to promote open conversations about hereditary cancer risks.

title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
author: Michelle Roberts
content:
![Two young men sit outside vaping. They are chatting, while looking at a mobile phone.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/55d4/live/9aa98d10-a08a-11f1-8116-c5aabe4388a9.jpg)
- Published
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.
The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.
They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.
And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.
Long-term risks not yet clear
Experts say vaping, although not entirely risk-free, is far safer than smoking.
In the UK, there are now more over-16s using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, figures show. Around 5.3 million people or 10% of adults say they smoke, while around 5.4 million use vapes daily or occasionally.
The review, external of the most recent and best quality evidence to date applies to regulated vapes that are checked for quality and compliant with strict safety laws.
It doesn't look at unregulated ones that can contain illicit substances, like spice or THC.
One of the report authors, Dr Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, cautioned: "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals.
"Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body."
The review found no evidence of any increased risk of serious harm from using e-cigarettes to quit.
The long-term risks of vaping are not yet clear though, and the NHS says children and non-smokers should never vape.
Doctors say vaping could lead to health harms in children and should be made "less attractive" to them.
![An ash tray containing lots of cigarette butts](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/bb00/live/c7831c00-a08c-11f1-9234-011c63dfa263.jpg)
Smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million a year
Around two in three people who smoke long-term will die from a tobacco-related illness, says the charity Action on Smoking and Health.
According to the World Health Organization, smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million people a year.
Quitting smoking reduces your risk of serious illnesses like heart disease, lung cancer, and stroke.
Almost every local NHS stop smoking service provides vapes or other support to help people quit.
You can search online, external for your local service with your postcode.
summary: A major review by the Cochrane team of 80 trials involving nearly 30,000 people found that nicotine e-cigarettes offer smokers the best chance of quitting, outperforming traditional aids like patches, gum, and non-nicotine vapes. While vaping is considered far safer than smoking and carries no evidence of increased risk of serious harm in these trials, its long-term risks remain unclear. Experts emphasize that these findings apply only to regulated, approved vapes rather than illicit or unlicensed devices.
key_points: Nicotine e-cigarettes increased quit success rates by about 60% compared to traditional aids like patches and gum.
The review evaluated 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 participants.
Experts caution that findings only apply to regulated, quality-checked vapes, warning against dangerous unregulated devices.
The long-term risks of vaping are not yet clear, and children and non-smokers should never vape.

title: I ate blueberries every day for a week—and there was one big change I felt
author: Julie Stewart
content:
It’s rare to try a new healthy habit and enjoy it so much that you make it part of your routine going forward. But that’s what happened when I started eating a serving of blueberries every day for a week. It turns out blueberries might be the perfect health food because they’re delicious, versatile, and packed with research-backed benefits.
Blueberry health benefits
“Blueberries have long been associated with supporting health,” says Anne VanBeber, a professor of nutritional sciences. Research suggests that eating berries and other anthocyanin-rich foods may support cardiovascular and metabolic health. There is also promising but still early evidence for possible benefits to vascular function, cognition, gut microbes and exercise recovery. However, blueberries should not be described as proven to prevent heart disease, diabetes, cognitive decline or high blood pressure.
A serving of blueberries—about 150g, or roughly one cup—provides fibre, vitamin C, vitamin K and manganese. It contains approximately 3.5–4g of fibre, equivalent to around 12–13% of the UK adult fibre target of 30g per day. This is higher than the US example of 25g per day for women aged 19–50. Adding blueberries to porridge, yoghurt or cereal can therefore make a useful contribution to daily fibre intake, although fibre should come from a variety of foods, including wholegrains, pulses, vegetables, nuts and seeds.
Blueberries also contain anthocyanins—red, purple and blue plant pigments with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory studies. Human research suggests they may modestly support blood-vessel function and some markers of cardiometabolic health, but it has not established that blueberries directly prevent heart attacks, high blood pressure or cognitive decline. Their fibre and polyphenols may also interact with gut bacteria, although claims about improved immunity and gut health remain preliminary.
Blueberries may also be useful around exercise. A small randomised study found that a blueberry smoothie consumed before and after strenuous exercise was associated with faster recovery of muscle strength, but the study involved only 10 women, so stronger evidence is needed before making firm claims about exercise recovery.
In the UK, 80g of fresh or frozen fruit counts as one portion towards the NHS 5-a-day recommendation, so 150g of blueberries is roughly two portions. Whole blueberries are also suitable for people with diabetes: Diabetes UK advises that whole fruit can form part of a healthy diet, while juice and smoothies are easier to consume quickly and contain less intact fibre.
What happened when I ate blueberries every day
I often began with breakfast, using blueberries to boost my nutrient intake before the day got away from me. I’d pile a cup of freshly washed blueberries on top of cold cereal (Cheerios or Nature’s Path Organic Mesa Sunrise) or hot cereal like oats. Sometimes I ate fresh blueberries with plain or lightly sweetened yogurt at lunchtime.
On other days, I relied on frozen blueberries, a convenient alternative to fresh berries that work great in between grocery runs. “It’s nice to have a bag of wild blueberries in the freezer because then they are readily available to add to a lot of dishes,” says VanBeber.
Frozen berries also tend to be cheaper than fresh ones. At my favourite supermarket, a 300g container of blueberries (about two servings) cost about £3.30, but about 10 servings of frozen wild blueberries cost about £8.35. On top of convenience and price, that particular frozen option comes with another benefit: Wild blueberries are smaller and contain more anthocyanins per serving than regular blueberries, says VanBeber.
Sometimes during the week I added frozen blueberries to a smoothie with other fruits and vegetables, seeds, and protein powder. Or I gently thawed them and ate them with protein-rich cottage cheese.
Fresh or frozen, I find the flavour of blueberries delightful—a sweetness that might have curbed my desire for sweet snacks later in the day. (Surprisingly, I found myself wanting less chocolate than usual.)
Plus, there's a nice versatility that comes with blueberries. Some healthy foods require a lot of prep work or taste just OK, but washing or thawing berries was quick and simple, and eating them was a joy. What's more, the blueberries paired well with foods I eat on the reg so adding them to my diet never really felt like a chore, although I did make one extra grocery run during the week to stock up on more berries. Since I’m not the only blueberry fan in my household, I had to monitor our supply and make sure I didn’t deplete our fresh and frozen stashes of blueberries before replacing them.
Overall, this experiment was a success. I felt sharp and strong during the week with no noticeable negative effects. Eating a cup of berries in one sitting didn’t seem to affect my digestion in any perceptible way. I intend to continue eating blueberries every day, or at least several times per week.
How to eat more blueberries
Want to start your own daily blueberry habit? Use these tips to incorporate blueberries into your diet, courtesy of VanBeber:
- Add blueberries to oatmeal bowls, yoghurt, chia puddings, salsas, or cake and bread batters.
- Blend blueberries into hummus, smoothies, vinaigrette salad dressings, or sauce toppings for meat, fish, or poultry.
- Sprinkle blueberries onto salads.
The bottom line
Adding blueberries to my daily routine was simple, healthy, and delicious. You can incorporate blueberries into many of the foods you already eat to give your meals a boost of heart-healthy, brain-protecting nutrients. To stick with the habit without breaking your budget, try keeping frozen blueberries in the freezer.
Julie Stewart is a writer, editor and content strategist with over a decade of experience translating complex topics — health and medicine, science and engineering — into engaging, accessible stories. Her work has appeared in publications like Men’s Health, Women’s Health, AARP The Magazine, EatingWell and Prevention, and she has also led strategic communications for a top engineering college and a global oncology company.
summary: An author who ate a daily serving of blueberries for a week experienced a successful and enjoyable new habit that curbed their desire for sweet snacks. Blueberries offer versatile culinary uses, supplying fiber, vitamins, and anthocyanins that support various aspects of health. While research highlights potential benefits for cardiovascular, metabolic, and cognitive functions, experts note they are not proven to prevent specific diseases. Additionally, both fresh and frozen blueberries provide convenient and nutritious additions to everyday meals.
key_points: Eating a daily serving of blueberries provided a convenient boost of fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants without causing negative digestive effects.
Frozen blueberries offer a cost-effective, versatile, and readily available alternative to fresh berries.
Anthocyanins in blueberries have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties that may support cardiovascular and metabolic health.
The author found that the natural sweetness of blueberries helped curb their desire for sweet snacks like chocolate during the week.

title: RSPCA reveals ‘secret weapon’ to tackling common cause of food poisoning
author: Jane Dalton
content:
Higher-welfare chicken farming could be a “secret weapon” in curbing the UK’s most common cause of food poisoning, the RSPCA says, after a study linked factory-farmed birds to soaring rates of infection in people.
University of Oxford researchers last month revealed that the way in which most chickens are reared for meat in the UK increased the disease behind food poisoning more than 100-fold.
The scientists said industrial farming, and in particular densely populated chicken flocks, has allowed strains of a bacterium called campylobacter to spread widely in birds reared for meat.
Campylobacter is the most common bacterial cause of diarrhoea worldwide, causing more than 3.5 times as many gastroenteritis cases in the UK each year than all other monitored foodborne bacteria combined.
The RSPCA is calling on supermarkets, food companies and the government urgently to prioritise breeds that grow more slowly and to promote higher-welfare farming, to rein in the spread of the bacterium.
The animal-welfare charity says urgently switch to slower-growing chicken breeds will not only “drastically improve” animal welfare, but would also “offer a vital line of defence for public health” and reduce strain on the NHS caused by food poisoning cases.
Campylobacter is largely harmless to healthy adult chickens, but is a major infection risk for humans, causing severe stomach cramps, diarrhoea, fever, headache, nausea and vomiting.
The bacteria, which spreads via raw meat and raw and contaminated milk, can be killed by thoroughly cooking.
Most of the one billion-plus chickens bred for meat in the UK each year are “frankenchickens”, genetically engineered to put on weight so rapidly that their legs break under the strain and they suffer chronic pain, deformities and heart failure.
![Birds are bred to grow so rapidly that their legs cannot support them and their hearts fail](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/25/14/24/Copy-of-210522IMG_6401.jpg)
It’s been calculated that if human babies grew as quickly, they would weigh around 45 stone by two months old.
Evidence suggests that slower-growing chickens develop stronger immune systems, reducing the chances of bacteria such as campylobacter taking hold.
The researchers found the huge global expansion of chicken farming has created ideal conditions for the bacterium to spread, mix and adapt to survive.
As well as the Oxford study, research by the European Food Safety Authority has linked the practice of “thinning” – removing some chickens for early slaughter – to higher campylobacter rates because it causes distress and health risks for the remaining birds.
Charlotte Arthur, poultry welfare expert at the RSPCA said: “Evidence suggests more welfare-friendly poultry farming could be a secret weapon in efforts to reduce the spread of a bacteria that can be so dangerous to humans.
“Slower-growing chickens live longer, experience fewer welfare problems and may also be less susceptible to some of the biological processes that allow campylobacter to spread.”
The RSPCA says chicken with its Assured label takes at least eight days more to reach slaughter weight than standard supermarket birds.
![The way in which most chickens are reared for meat increases food poisoning risk more than 100-fold, experts say](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/25/14/10/w3-28_31813668088_o.jpg)
“These birds don’t just experience better lives - evidence suggests they may be better equipped to cope with infections such as campylobacter,” Ms Arthur said.
“That’s why slower-growing breeds of chicken must be part of a serious conversation about reducing risk, and building resilience that doesn’t involve more antibiotics - keeping people healthier, safer, and reducing the strain on the nation’s doctors’ surgeries, pharmacies and the NHS.”
Rising rates of antimicrobial resistance, in which bacteria resist drugs designed to kill them, are making campylobacter infections increasingly hard to treat.
Since the 1960s, global chicken numbers have increased seven-fold to approximately 31 billion birds.
A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “We are considering the best ways to promote the use of slower-growing chicken breeds to help boost animal welfare.”
The British Retail consortium has been approached for comment.
summary: The RSPCA states that higher-welfare, slower-growing chicken farming could help curb campylobacter, the UK's most common cause of food poisoning. A recent University of Oxford study linked densely populated factory-farmed chicken flocks to a 100-fold increase in the disease. The animal-welfare charity is urging supermarkets, food companies, and the government to prioritize slower-growing breeds to improve public health and animal welfare.
key_points: Campylobacter is the UK's most common bacterial cause of food poisoning and gastroenteritis.
A University of Oxford study linked densely populated industrial chicken farming to a more than 100-fold increase in the disease-causing bacteria.
The RSPCA is calling on the government, supermarkets, and food companies to prioritize slower-growing chicken breeds.
Slower-growing chickens generally develop stronger immune systems, which reduces the spread of campylobacter and improves animal welfare.

title: Trump lost patience with RFK Jr.’s autism research before vaccine shake-up
author: Bo Erickson
content:
Trump lost patience with RFK Jr.’s autism research before vaccine shake-up
- President Donald Trump signed an executive order scaling back the federal childhood vaccination schedule from 17 to 11 shots due to frustration over the pace of research into alleged autism links.
- The executive order calls for unbundling the combined MMR vaccine into separate doses and instructs the Justice Department to challenge state-level school vaccine mandates.
- Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is overseeing agency studies into potential vaccine dangers, though scientific consensus consistently shows no link between vaccines and autism.
- Leading medical associations warned that the directive will sow confusion, heighten vaccine hesitancy, and leave more children vulnerable to preventable diseases.
- Administration officials noted that the executive order does not fundamentally transform immunization policy on its own, with long-term changes dependent on ongoing agency reviews.
summary: President Donald Trump signed an executive order reducing the federal childhood vaccination schedule from 17 to 11 shots due to impatience with the pace of research into alleged autism links led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The directive also calls for unbundling the MMR vaccine and directs the Justice Department to challenge state-level vaccine mandates for schools. While medical associations have warned the order will increase vaccine hesitancy, administration officials noted that long-term policy changes will depend on ongoing agency reviews.
key_points: President Trump signed an executive order scaling back the childhood vaccination schedule from 17 to 11 shots.
The order instructs the Justice Department to challenge state-level school vaccine mandates and unbundle the MMR vaccine.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is overseeing agency studies investigating potential vaccine dangers, despite scientific consensus finding no link to autism.
Medical associations warned that the directive will cause confusion and leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases.

title: Worcester family's battle against motor neurone disease in mission for cure
author: James Connell
content:
THE family of a young mum diagnosed with motor neurone disease has described the devastating impact of the illness as they help in the fight to find a cure.
Friends and family of 38-year-old Stacy Bozward of Worcester have completed a fundraising walk to support the mum in raising awareness of motor neurone disease (MND)
The 26-mile walk was held in honour of Mrs Bozward from Worcester, who is living with MND.
It began at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham and ended at The White Hart pub in Fernhill Heath, raising more than £1,100 on the day.
  SUPPORT: Stacy Bozward inspired support from friends and family in the battle against MND (Image: Supplied by Bozward family)
Stacy’s husband, Barry Bozward, said: "I’m writing to share the story of a special fundraising walk completed yesterday in support of my wife, Stacy, and her charity, Stacy’s Kick For A Cure.
"Stacy is just 38 and is living with motor neurone disease.
"The illness has progressed rapidly, leaving her unable to use her arms or legs and reliant on non-invasive ventilation to breathe.
The JustGiving page is available here
"Despite everything she is facing, Stacy has remained determined to raise awareness of MND and help fund the fight for better treatments and, ultimately, a cure."
The walk was organised to support Stacy’s charity, Stacy’s Kick For A Cure, which she set up to raise funds and awareness for MND research.
  FINISH: Stacy Bozward at the finish of the walk between Queen Elizabeth Hospital and the White Hart in Fernhill Heath, near Worcester as part of a mission to raise funds to fight MND (Image: Supplied by the Bozward family)
A total of 32 of Stacy’s friends and family members took part in the walk, which ended with a raffle at The White Hart pub.
The pub also made a donation, bringing the total raised on the day to £1,112.
The JustGiving page is also continuing to receive donations and has now passed £8,000 as they try to reach the £10,000 mark.
All the money raised will go to Stacy’s own charity, Stacy’s Kick For A Cure, which she established to raise awareness and funds in the fight against MND.
Recommended reading:
- 
      First-time skydiver takes leap to raise funds for Macmillan
- 
      Family's tribute to Worcester musician aims to save lives
- 
      Steve Cram hails the 'amazing' power of this Worcester link
Stacy, a mum of two boys, Jenson, 12, and Josh, 17, was diagnosed with MND last summer after months of tests and uncertainty.
The disease has progressed quickly, leaving her wheelchair-bound and reliant on an oxygen machine for most of the day.
Her sister said: "Stacy went from playing football and working at the end of 2024, to being wheelchair bound relying on Barry and my parents to help her do the everyday mundane tasks that we all take for granted, and now relies on an oxygen machine for the majority of the day to help her breathe."
She also shared the personal connection of a friend, Joe, who lost his father, Kevin to MND when they were younger.
She said: "I had a small awareness of MND before Stacy was diagnosed.
"One of my best mates Joe; lost his Dad, Kevin to the disease when we were younger.
"I saw how hard it must have been for their family and sadly we are now living the same nightmare."
There is currently no cure for MND, and the average life expectancy following diagnosis is tragically short.
Despite her diagnosis, Stacy has remained focused on raising awareness and funds for research into the disease.
summary: Friends and family of 38-year-old Stacy Bozward, a mother of two diagnosed with motor neurone disease, completed a 26-mile fundraising walk to support her charity, Stacy's Kick For A Cure. The rapid progression of the illness has left her wheelchair-bound and reliant on ventilation, but she remains dedicated to raising awareness and funding for MND research. The recent walk raised over £1,100 on the day, with total donations on her JustGiving page surpassing £8,000 toward a £10,000 goal.
key_points: Stacy Bozward, a 38-year-old mother of two from Worcester, was diagnosed with motor neurone disease last summer.
The rapid progression of the illness has left her unable to use her arms or legs and reliant on an oxygen machine to breathe.
Friends and family completed a 26-mile walk from Birmingham's Queen Elizabeth Hospital to Fernhill Heath to support her charity, Stacy's Kick For A Cure.
The fundraising event and associated donations have raised over £8,000 toward a £10,000 target for MND research.

title: 'I was diagnosed with skin cancer aged 26 - unethical sunscreen tax must end now' - AOL
author: Sophie Huskisson
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![Jessica Zbinden-Webster, who was diagnosed with skin cancer at age 26, said 'the unethical tax on lifesaving sunscreen must end now'](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/24/4625d32b-5f3d-3456-bedf-360eba2387c6/3c223e40-d571-4d39-8950-ff2895ed4d78.jpg)
A woman who was diagnosed with skin cancer aged just 26 will today deliver a petition with almost 100,000 signatures to Downing Street calling for the 20% VAT charged on sun cream to be scrapped.
Jessica Zbinden-Webster, who is now 34 and cancer-free, had an excision, a skin graft and four ocular surgeries after what she describes as a “shock diagnosis”.
Her Change.org petition, which is signed by more than 99,000 people at the time of writing, comes after record temperatures and consecutive heatwaves ripped through the UK this summer. Up to nine in 10 melanoma skin cancer cases in the UK could be prevented by staying safe in the sun, such as using sunscreen and staying in the shade, and avoiding sunbeds, Cancer Research UK says.
But half (50%) of people in the UK think sunscreen is too expensive and 10% don’t use it at all because of the cost, a 2023 study by charity Melanoma Focus found. Some 67% of people said they would use it more if it was cheaper.
![Jessica Zbinden-Webster is now cancer-free](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/24/4625d32b-5f3d-3456-bedf-360eba2387c6/17929e97-7c7f-4143-9089-798fa07775f8.jpg)
![She described her cancer diagnosis as a 'shock'](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/24/4625d32b-5f3d-3456-bedf-360eba2387c6/7e5d567a-beab-45bd-b173-086e5d2b771c.jpg)
In her petition, Ms Zbinden-Webster said: "I had a shock skin cancer diagnosis at 26 years old. One excision, one skin graft and four ocular surgeries later, I'm lucky to be cancer-free, but there are many who aren't as fortunate."
Ahead of her No10 visit on Monday, the London-based campaigner continued: "The unethical tax on lifesaving sunscreen must end now. If you think this record-breaking summer has wreaked havoc on our environment, just imagine what it's done to our skin. And, in a cost-of-living crisis, the poorest are priced out of skin cancer prevention because of the 20% 'cosmetic' tax on sunscreen products. Sunscreen is not 'cosmetic' - it's critical."
She added to The Mirror that regularly applying sunscreen would have prevented her cancer. She said: "I didn't apply sunscreen regularly because I mistakenly thought it was a seasonal product, not an everyday essential. The 'cosmetic' VAT status of sunscreen reinforces this misunderstanding to consumers.
"Wearing sunscreen regularly would have prevented my skin cancer. My tumour was caused by UV damage in childhood, which is why it manifested to early in life. But parents are penalised to protect their kids' skin as the 'cosmetic' VAT on sunscreen also applies to sunscreen products for babies and children."
![Jessica will deliver a petition to No10 today calling for the 20% VAT charged on sun cream to be scrapped](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/24/4625d32b-5f3d-3456-bedf-360eba2387c6/66d23137-a43d-4ba7-8f6f-c5196b053647.jpg)
In June, a report on UV safety by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Beauty, Hair and Wellbeing said the current VAT classification that deems sunscreen a luxury cosmetic rather than vital preventative healthcare "inflates the cost in a way that deters regular use".
It called on the Government to reduce VAT to zero on all children’s sun protection products that are rated SPF 30 and above and engage with brands and retailers to ensure that the resulting savings are passed onto the consumer. It also demanded VAT be cut to 5% on all dedicated sun protection products designed for adults that are rated SPF 30 and above.
The report added: "Not only would this remove one of the barriers that stands in the way of people using a life-saving product but it would send a clear message to the population that UV safety is not only important to the Government, but that it should be a daily consideration for everyone."
A Government spokesman said: “As part of our 10-year plan to reform the health service, and through a national cancer plan, we will fight cancer on all fronts, from prevention, to diagnosis, treatment, and research. High-factor sunscreen is on the NHS prescription list for certain conditions and is already provided VAT free when dispensed by a pharmacist to these patients.”
VAT is the UK’s second largest tax and is forecast to raise £180billion in 2025-26. The 20% standard rate applies to most goods and services.
Cosmetic services are exempt from VAT where they’re undertaken as an element of a health care treatment programme. Where services are undertaken purely for cosmetic reasons, they will be standard-rated, gov.uk says.
In an advice page on sun safety, the NHS tells people not rely on sunscreen alone to protect from the sun. It also recommends wearing suitable clothing and spending time in the shade when the sun's at its hottest.
summary: Jessica Zbinden-Webster, who was diagnosed with skin cancer at age 26, is delivering a petition with nearly 100,000 signatures to Downing Street to scrap the 20% VAT on sunscreen. The petition argues that classifying sunscreen as a cosmetic product is a barrier to skin cancer prevention, particularly during a cost-of-living crisis. While a 2023 study found that half of people in the UK think sunscreen is too expensive, a government spokesperson noted that high-factor sunscreen is already provided VAT-free on NHS prescriptions for certain conditions.
key_points: Jessica Zbinden-Webster is delivering a Change.org petition with nearly 100,000 signatures to Downing Street.
The petition calls for the removal of the 20% VAT currently charged on sunscreen, which is classified as a cosmetic product.
A 2023 Melanoma Focus study found that 50% of UK people think sunscreen is too expensive and 10% do not use it due to cost.
Cancer Research UK states that up to nine in 10 melanoma skin cancer cases could be prevented by staying safe in the sun.
An All-Party Parliamentary Group report previously recommended reducing VAT to zero on children's SPF 30+ products and to 5% on adult SPF 30+ products.

title: Mobile beauty therapist charged with illegally selling weight loss jab Mounjaro
author: Simon Parkin
content:
A beauty therapist has appeared in court accused of illegally selling the weight loss jab Mounjaro to clients.
Karen Halton, 50, who runs a by-appointment beauty treatment business, denies selling injectable weight management and diabetes medication without a prescription.
Tirzepatide, also known by the brand name Mounjaro, is approved by the NHS to help manage obesity and related health conditions but is only available on prescription.
Halton, of Bury Road, Thetford, pleaded not guilty at Norwich Magistrates’ Court to having sold it illegally in September 2025.
She also denies selling or offering to sell suspected counterfeit medications purporting to be Mounjaro.
District Judge Matthew Bone granted her unconditional bail until a trial date of October 16.
The boom in use of weight-loss treatments has seen a spike in illegal sales and criminal gangs involved in the production of counterfeit products.
A spokesperson for the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) said: “Most authorised weight loss medicines are prescription-only, meaning that a consultation with a doctor or qualified healthcare professional must be conducted to assess the patient's suitability for the treatment.
“Sourcing weight loss medicines from unregulated suppliers significantly increases the risk of getting a product which is either falsified or not approved for use in the UK.”
summary: Karen Halton, a mobile beauty therapist, has appeared in court accused of illegally selling and offering to sell the prescription-only weight loss jab Mounjaro, as well as suspected counterfeit versions. Halton pleaded not guilty at Norwich Magistrates' Court to the charges stemming from September 2025. District Judge Matthew Bone granted her unconditional bail until her trial scheduled for October 16.
key_points: A beauty therapist is accused of illegally selling the weight loss medication Mounjaro without a prescription.
The defendant pleaded not guilty to charges of selling unauthorized and suspected counterfeit medication.
Mounjaro, containing tirzepatide, is an NHS-approved treatment for obesity that requires a professional prescription.
The defendant was granted unconditional bail until her trial date on October 16.

title: Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania
author: Madeline Halpert
content:
![Measles vaccine](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1008/cpsprodpb/4a64/live/340bd9d0-a091-11f1-b11c-1bea5fc925f5.jpg)
- Published
Two people who were not vaccinated against measles have died of the virus in Pennsylvania, health officials said.
The state has seen 393 cases of the highly contagious virus this year, as infections across the US have hit the highest point in 35 years.
Eighty-five percent of kindergarten-age students in Lancaster County, where the recent deaths occurred, are vaccinated against measles - well below the 95% rate needed for herd immunity to limit the spread and protect immunocompromised people.
Last year, two unvaccinated children in Texas died from a measles outbreak that infected over 1,000 people, primarily children.
"This is a serious and a growing problem across our country and in our commonwealth," Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said in a news conference on Tuesday. "This illness and death from measles is completely preventable."
He added that the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) vaccine was the best tool to protect against illness and death.
Officials said they would not share any additional information on the identities of those who died, including if they were children, who have face a higher risk of death and complications from measles.
The US has seen 2,777 confirmed cases of measles in 2026, just seven months into the year, up from last year's high of 2,289.
The rising number of cases comes as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates. The US recommends two shots to children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.
Earlier this month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that calls for fewer childhood vaccinations and recommends splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots. Public health experts worry the order will cause confusion about an already safe and effective vaccine and prove costly.
The executive order came after Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr took a number of steps to remake US vaccine policies over the past year, including the childhood vaccination schedule. Many of the changes were blocked by a federal judge earlier this year.
A vaccine skeptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the MMR vaccine, at times endorsing it and other times sharing unproven claims about its safety.
Speaking on Tuesday, Shapiro said he spoke with Kennedy over the phone that morning and that he had offered to send staff from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Shapiro said he was "very blunt" with Kennedy about vaccinations.
"I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that's coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America ... that there's real life consequences to spreading misinformation," Shapiro said.
The US is on track to lose its status of having eliminated measles, which will be determined by a panel in November. Canada lost its status last year.
summary: Two unvaccinated individuals have died of measles in Pennsylvania amid a nationwide surge in infections and declining immunization rates. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro criticized federal rhetoric and vaccine policies during a press conference following the deaths. US measles cases have reached a 35-year high, driven by increasing vaccine hesitancy and changes to federal health policies.
key_points: Two unvaccinated people died of measles in Pennsylvania, where 393 cases have been reported this year.
Lancaster County has an 85% kindergarten vaccination rate, falling short of the 95% threshold required for herd immunity.
US measles cases have reached 2,777 in 2026, marking the highest level in 35 years.
Governor Josh Shapiro criticized the Trump administration's vaccine policies and rhetoric following the deaths.
The US is currently on track to lose its status of having eliminated measles.

title: Scots girl, two, with rare sun allergy can play at home with curtains open
author: PA Media
content:
A Scottish toddler with a rare genetic disorder that makes her “allergic” to the sun can finally play at home without the curtains closed thanks to UV-resistant film installed at her home last month.
Two-year-old Mollie Murray, of Montrose, is the only child in the UK known to have her specific variant of xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), making her skin extremely sensitive to ultraviolet light.
The condition has no cure, and it puts Mollie at risk of severe sun damage all year round – meaning she can only safely go outside in protective full-length clothing or after dark.
Her mother, Kirsty Campbell, 35, a charge nurse, said: “She burns all year round and has burnt in November before.
“The only time it’s safe to go outside is in the dark. I want to keep her inside at all times to keep her safe, but we can’t do that – she needs some sort of normality.”
Ms Campbell has spoken out to raise awareness of Mollie’s condition and to thank The Archie Foundation for the “vital” funding they provided to help Mollie’s dad, Ryan Murray, 34, coat his home in UV-resistant film last month.
The film means that Mollie can now play inside without the curtains closed.
“Their support has been indescribable – they’ve been a massive help for us,” Ms Campbell said.
“I cried for about 20 minutes when I was told the money would come through. Mollie wouldn’t have the same quality of life at her dad’s house without it.
She added: “It means she can do simple things like look outside for the postman or draw in daylight. My ex-partner was having to take playpark equipment into his house as it wasn’t safe outside. She’s so happy running around like a normal child.”
Mollie was in and out of hospital from the time she was a baby, suffering from a range of symptoms including seizures and severe reflux.
She first experienced severe sunburn on an overcast day in May 2025. The situation escalated when it happened again two months later.
She was eventually diagnosed with XPF.
Doctors have advised Mollie is 10,000 times more likely to get skin cancer than other children and Ms Campbell has to use a UV monitor to check readings in every room to ensure it’s safe for Mollie to go inside.
“To go from thinking your child has sunburn to them having an extremely rare genetic disorder is mind-blowing,” Ms Campbell said.
“Everyday life is difficult as she needs full protective outer wear for going outside and sun cream every two hours under her clothes.”
She added: “We initially had to play inside in darkness with the curtains closed before getting the UV-resistant film on our windows.”
Ms Campbell and her family have been told that Mollie will likely have neurological impairment and mobility issues in her 40s and 50s, but that she should have a fairly normal childhood.
Mollie’s family are hoping to ensure she has the highest quality of life possible while continuing to keep her safe.
“I have a UV monitor as she can’t just walk into a room. I have to check there is absolutely no UV light there, so there are so many challenges along the way,” Ms Campbell said.
“She is an amazing wee girl and is coping with it so well. She’s very outgoing and friendly and the fact she’s been in hospital so much means she’s used to seeing different faces.”
The Archie Foundation provides support to babies, children and families during a hospital stay or after a bereavement.
The charity gifted Mollie’s family £600 to fund UV film for the whole downstairs of her dad’s house and Mollie’s bedroom upstairs, which was installed on July 15.
Rebecca Duncan, business development and fundraising manager for The Archie Foundation in Tayside, said it’s “wonderful” to hear how the charity’s support has helped make a difference for Mollie and her family.
“Caring for a child with complex needs can be incredibly challenging and, at times, isolating, so we’re committed to ensuring families never feel they have to face that journey alone,” Ms Duncan said.
“Mollie has shown remarkable resilience, and we’re proud to have played a small part in helping her experience the joy, opportunities and precious moments that every child deserves.”

![WhatsApp channel QR Code](https://news.stv.tv/wp-content/themes/stvnews/static/images/whatsapp-qr.png)
summary: A two-year-old Scottish girl named Mollie Murray, who is the only child in the UK with a specific variant of the rare sun-allergic genetic disorder xeroderma pigmentosum, can now play at home with the curtains open. Thanks to a £600 grant from The Archie Foundation, her father's home was fitted with UV-resistant window film last month. The condition leaves Mollie with a 10,000 times higher risk of skin cancer and requires her to wear protective clothing or go outside only in the dark.
key_points: Two-year-old Mollie Murray is the only child in the UK known to have her specific variant of xeroderma pigmentosum.
The incurable genetic disorder makes her extremely sensitive to ultraviolet light, putting her at severe risk of sun damage and skin cancer.
The Archie Foundation provided £600 to fund UV-resistant window film at her father's house, allowing her to play inside without closed curtains.
Mollie must wear full-length protective clothing and reapply sun cream every two hours when going outside, and can safely venture out only after dark.

title: Cases of bluetongue virus confirmed in Shropshire
author: Charlotte Benton
content:
![There is a herd of sheep in a field of brown grass and waste. There is around 50 and they have white and black heads and wool coats the same colour as the grass.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1539/live/23f41b40-9b08-11f1-b792-a710e56a11dc.jpg)
The locations of the cases was not revealed by the government
- Published
Four cases of the potentially fatal to cattle bluetongue virus have been confirmed in Shropshire.
They are part of the latest figures from the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which bring the total cases in the UK in 2026-27 to 618., external
The locations of the four premises affected in Shropshire have not been publicly revealed.
Defra has also not disclosed if the cases are in sheep or cattle but a spokesperson said, of the 25 new cases across the country in the latest update, 18 involved sheep, six cattle and one at a mixed farm affecting both.
Bluetongue is an insect-borne viral disease affecting sheep and cattle among other animals, mainly spread by biting midges, which thrive in long, hot summers like the one the UK is experiencing.
It is not dangerous to humans and poses no risk.
Earlier this month, a Shropshire farmer said he was concerned about the outbreak due to a shortage of vaccines used to protect the animals.
Of the current 618 cases, 580 are in England, with 29 in Wales and nine in Scotland, meanwhile Northern Ireland are yet to have a confirmed case.
Defra said it was "working closely with the industry and is putting processes in for additional vaccine supplies".
The Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) will hold a meeting in Shrewsbury on Wednesday evening, as part of a country-wide series, to offer an update on the virus to the county's farmers.
Industry experts with advice on the signs of the virus and updates around vaccinations are expected to attend the meeting at Shrewsbury Auction Centre.
According to the latest government figures there are currently 2,236 potential cases of bluetongue under investigation in Great Britain.
They are all at sites that have reported suspicious clinical signs.
Defra added that the total number of affected animals is likely to be significantly higher than reported as testing did not always include every animal on a premises.
summary: Four cases of the bluetongue virus have been confirmed in Shropshire, contributing to a UK total of 618 cases for 2026-27. The insect-borne viral disease affects livestock such as sheep and cattle, though it poses no risk to humans.
