Defra is working to secure additional vaccine supplies amidst concerns from farmers over shortages.
key_points: Four new cases of bluetongue virus have been confirmed in Shropshire.
The UK total for 2026-27 has reached 618 cases, with 2,236 potential cases under investigation.
The virus is spread by biting midges and affects sheep and cattle, but is not dangerous to humans.
Defra is working with the industry to provide additional vaccine supplies.
The AHDB is holding a meeting in Shrewsbury to update farmers on the virus and vaccinations.

title: The seven stages of a facelift
author: Hannah Coates
content:
The seven stages of a facelift
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Ultherapy
What An ultrasound treatment that works by directing micro-focused sound waves deep into the skin’s structural layers – including the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), a connective layer that sits between muscle and fat. This thermal energy stimulates fresh collagen production deep within the skin, gradually tightening, lifting and firming the jaw, chin, neck and brows. It remains the only FDA-cleared ultrasound device for skin lifting, though other well-regarded options exist, including Sofwave and HIFU.
Who Anyone who has noticed the creeping effects of skin laxity, which typically emerges as collagen begins to deplete. Safe for all skin tones, it is reportedly used by Jennifer Aniston and Helena Christensen.
What to expect After a conductive gel is applied, a practitioner moves the device over the face for between 30 and 90 minutes. Some spots may feel tingly or pleasantly warm, while more sensitive areas, such as those over bone, the neck or around the eye, may feel a piercing heat that quickly builds then is over in seconds. Results emerge gradually over three to six months and last for a year afterwards.
Downsides Tenderness and swelling are standard. Less common risks include temporary nerve irritation, which can cause facial asymmetry, and fat loss that could accentuate signs of ageing.
Where
Dr Jennifer Levine, New York City, drjenniferlevine.com
Dr Maryam Zamani, London, drmaryamzamani.com
Dr Costas Papageorgiou, London, Athens and New York City, drcostaspapageorgiou.com
Dr Lee Seung-Hyun at View Skin Clinic, Seoul, viewskinclinic.com
Price
From about £2,500 to £5,500 for a full face and neck treatment
Injectables
What Botulinum toxin (such as Botox or Xeomin), dermal filler and biostimulators are all used to sculpt, lift and plump, and can be combined in a “liquid facelift”. Biostimulators stimulate the skin’s collagen and elastin production, improving structure and firmness over time. Dermal filler, typically made from hyaluronic acid, restores volume. Botulinum toxin temporarily relaxes targeted muscles and can be deployed to lift the brows, slim the jawline and create a smoother appearance.
Who Biostimulators are a good entry point for those noticing the initial effects of ageing but don’t want intensive work. For hollowing under the eyes, cheeks and temples, or a loss of definition, dermal filler is ideal. Botulinum toxin is best for dynamic wrinkles – caused by repeated muscle movement – and can also lift brows that have begun to drop.
What to expect Most appointments take less than 30 minutes and downtime is minimal. But upkeep is required: botulinum toxin needs redoing every four months, dermal filler roughly every 18 months and biostimulators – which typically require three sessions about four weeks apart – every two years. Discomfort varies, but it isn’t much worse than having a quick injection. You may note some bruising or short-lived swelling.
Downsides Poor technique can result in an unnatural appearance, asymmetry or, in rare cases, vascular occlusion, leading to serious complications if not treated promptly.
Where
Dr Ashwin Soni at The Sonic Clinic, London, thesoniclinic.com
Dr Giulio Borbon at Studio Borbon, Milan, studioborbon.com
Dr Heyfa Ben Youssef, Paris, medecin-esthetiqueparis.com
Price
From about £300 up to £750
Blepharoplasty
What A surgical procedure that involves removing or repositioning excess skin, fat or muscle on the upper or lower eyelids – or both – to create a refreshed eye area. It was the third most common cosmetic procedure in the UK in 2024 and its popularity continues to grow. It won’t alter the face’s contours dramatically, but it’s a fairly easy route to a more youthful appearance.
Who Anyone troubled by under-eye bags or hooded eyelids (where excess skin on the brow bone obscures the eyelid crease). It can also be suitable for anyone whose peripheral vision is affected by loose eyelid skin. Most practitioners recommend waiting until at least 40, when changes to the eye area start to become more noticeable.
What to expect A relatively low-pain procedure done under local anaesthetic. Exceptionally fine incisions are made along the eyelid’s natural crease and just below the lower lash line, meaning scarring is nearly imperceptible. Upper and lower lids can be treated in the same session. Each lid takes up to an hour, with some bruising, swelling, light sensitivity and numbness to be expected in the first weeks. Most patients see full results in around eight weeks. Improvements last until further skin sagging occurs due to ageing.
Downsides As with any surgery, there is a risk of bleeding and infection. Dry eyes, temporary numbness, double vision and difficulty closing the eyes can also occur. In some cases, changes in eyelid position or asymmetry may require revision surgery.
![](https://images.ft.com/v3/image/raw/https%3A%2F%2Fd1e00ek4ebabms.cloudfront.net%2Fproduction%2F9e01d32c-9fa0-4595-aecc-dd06d4343191.gif?source=next-article&fit=scale-down&quality=highest&width=700&dpr=1)
The lunchtime (or micro) facelift
What A single small incision made just above the ear or at the temples, discreetly placed within the hairline. From there, a suture (stitch) is anchored into the SMAS layer – the same connective tissue targeted by Ultherapy – to suspend and elevate the mid-face, lifting areas such as the cheekbones and jawline for a subtly contoured appearance.
Who Best approached as an early intervention, the one-stitch lift occupies a middle ground between injectables and major surgery – most suitable for under-50s beginning to notice gravity’s pull on the face (early jowls, a slackening jawline). Those with more extensive laxity may find its scope limited; the smaller incision can only address mild cases.
What to expect The procedure’s name is due to the fact it can be performed within 45 minutes. It is done under local anaesthetic, meaning same-day discharge is standard. Expect some bruising and swelling, which typically returns to normal within 10 days. Results last between three and five years.
Downsides Less common complications include skin puckering around the stitches, asymmetry, raised scarring and infection. In rare cases, facial nerve injury can cause temporary numbness or weakness.
Where 
Dr Renato Calabria, Beverly Hills, Palm Springs and Milan, drcalabria.com
Mr Tunç Tiryaki, Istanbul and London, tunctiryaki.co.uk
Dr Ramtin Kassir, New York City and New Jersey, drkassir.com
Price
From about £3,500 up to £19,000
The ponytail lift
What The ponytail lift – also known as an endoscopic brow lift – takes its name from the snatched, eye-opening effect it can achieve. A surgeon uses a minuscule camera mounted on a thin tube to see and reposition the SMAS layer and deeper tissues without the need for large incisions.
Who Anyone whose eyebrows have descended, cheeks have fallen or who is experiencing a loss of youthful definition around the eyes or jaw. It suits those with robust, healthy skin – with good elasticity – who are in their late 30s to 50s and want to look younger without extensive surgery.
What to expect The endoscopic technique reduces visible scarring and the initial recovery period – which is often managed with prescription pain medication – lasts about one to two weeks. Performed under local or general anaesthetic as a day procedure, the surgery takes around 90 minutes, with stitches removed about a week later. Most patients see their final results within three to six months, lasting anywhere from five to 12 years.
Downsides Best suited to early signs of ageing; those with significant drooping, heavy jowling or excess neck skin are likely better served by a full facelift. Recovery typically involves bruising and swelling, while the risks of surgery include bleeding, infection, asymmetry and, in rare cases, temporary facial nerve weakness.
Where
Dr Chia Chi Kao, Santa Monica, kaoplasticsurgery.com
Dr Tim J Janssen at Waterhouse Janssen, London, waterhousejanssen.com
Dr Sam Rizk, New York City, drsamrizk.com
Price
From about £6,000 up to £190,000
SMAS facelift
What Unlike earlier methods that focused solely on tightening the skin, often creating results that looked overly stretched, the SMAS facelift focuses on treating the deeper structural layers of the face. It repositions the SMAS layer – made up of muscle, fat and connective tissue – before lifting the skin itself. It links the facial muscles responsible for expression to the skin above. By addressing this underlying structure, surgeons can create more defined contours while preserving natural movement.
Who Those with significant signs of ageing – pronounced jowls, a loose jawline, deep nasolabial folds or excess skin on the neck. The majority are in their 50s, 60s or beyond. Kris Jenner reportedly had one in 2025.
What to expect Incisions are made within the hairline and around the natural contours of the ear to keep scarring as imperceptible as possible. The procedure takes up to four hours and may require an overnight hospital stay. Recovery is gradual – swelling and bruising are to be expected in the first two weeks, and it can take three to six months for the tissue to settle into its new position. The results, however, are significant. Some claim to look a decade younger, with results lasting upwards of 10 years.
Downsides Beyond the expected downtime, there is a risk of delayed wound healing, bleeding, persistent swelling and changes to the skin’s contours. Rarer still, skin necrosis (the death of skin tissue), permanent numbness, facial nerve injury and complications related to anaesthesia are worth bearing in mind.
Where
Dr Steven Levine, New York City, stevenlevinemd.com
Dr Rajiv Grover, London, rajivgrover.co.uk
Dr Yannis Alexandrides at 111 Harley St, London, 111harleystreet.com
Price
From about £10,000 up to £190,000
Deep plane facelift
What Widely considered to be the most advanced facial rejuvenation procedure available. Building on the principles of the SMAS facelift, this goes a step further by releasing the ligaments that anchor the facial tissues to the underlying bone. As these ligaments weaken over time, the cheeks, jawline and neck begin to descend. By carefully releasing and repositioning the deeper layers of tissue as a single unit – including the SMAS – the procedure targets the underlying causes of facial ageing rather than simply tightening the surface.
Who Most candidates are in their 50s, 60s or beyond; the SMAS and deep plane facelifts are generally presented as alternatives rather than complements.
What to expect The deep plane procedure takes up to four hours and incisions are made around the natural contours of the ears and within the hairline. Because the surgery works at such a deep level, fewer superficial nerve endings are disrupted, so patients are more likely to experience a feeling of tightness and pressure rather than significant pain. While early improvements are visible within weeks, many patients find the face continues to refine and heal for up to a year after surgery.
Downsides The surgery carries broadly the same risks as an SMAS procedure but, because it is more extensive and involves deeper tissue dissection, the potential for complications is slightly higher. But when performed by an experienced surgeon, it is considered a safe procedure with low complication rates.
Where
Mr Georgios Orfaniotis, London, orfaniotis.co.uk
Dr Min-Hee Ryu, Seoul and Beijing, psryuminhee.com
Dr Andrew Jacono at New York Center for Facial Plastic & Laser Surgery, newyorkfacialplasticsurgery.com
Price
From about £15,000 up to £190,000
summary: The article outlines various cosmetic and surgical procedures aimed at facial rejuvenation, ranging from non-invasive treatments to advanced surgeries. It details methods such as ultrasound therapy, injectables, eyelid surgeries, and deep-structure facelifts like the SMAS and deep plane techniques. Each method is described with its target audience, expected outcomes, downtime, and potential downsides.
key_points: Ultherapy uses micro-focused sound waves to stimulate collagen production and tighten skin without surgery.
Injectables like botulinum toxin, dermal fillers, and biostimulators offer temporary volume restoration and wrinkle reduction with minimal downtime.
Blepharoplasty targets excess skin and fat on the upper or lower eyelids to create a more refreshed eye area.
The lunchtime facelift and ponytail lift act as intermediate, minimally invasive options for addressing early signs of aging.
SMAS and deep plane facelifts target deeper structural layers of the face to provide more significant and long-lasting anti-aging results for older individuals.

title: Birthday heartbreak as Louisiana girl, 8, dies from extremely rare brain infection
author: Owen Scott
content:
Girl, 8, dies after contracting brain-eating amoeba she likely caught swimming in Louisiana lake
![Girl, 8, dies after contracting brain-eating amoeba she likely caught swimming in Louisiana lake](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/7/27/782169146_122099375619446574_3374054569947885979_n-eeb42479.jpeg?quality=75&width=83&auto=webp 83w>)
Birthday heartbreak as Louisiana girl, 8, dies from extremely rare brain infection
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/7/49/783029300_122101208229446574_5316006533475584882_n-c570c64d.jpeg)
- Eight-year-old Lillian Smart of Ruston, Louisiana, has died after contracting the rare brain-eating amoeba Naegleria fowleri.
- Health officials believe the child likely contracted the infection while swimming at Lake Claiborne in Louisiana.
- The amoeba causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis, a nearly always fatal condition that travels to the brain when contaminated warm fresh water enters the nose.
- Lillian suffered severe symptoms including a fever, double vision, and significant brain swelling before passing away a day after her eighth birthday.
- The Louisiana Department of Health noted that such cases are extremely rare, with only 180 known cases reported in the U.S. between 1937 and 2025.
summary: An eight-year-old Louisiana girl named Lillian Smart has died from primary amebic meningoencephalitis, a rare and nearly always fatal brain infection caused by the Naegleria fowleri amoeba. Health officials believe she likely contracted the infection while swimming at Lake Claiborne. She passed away a day after her eighth birthday following severe symptoms including fever, double vision, and brain swelling.
key_points: Eight-year-old Lillian Smart of Ruston, Louisiana, died from a rare brain-eating amoeba infection.
Health officials believe she likely contracted Naegleria fowleri while swimming at Lake Claiborne.
The infection causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis when contaminated warm fresh water enters the nose.
Lillian suffered a fever, double vision, and brain swelling before dying a day after her eighth birthday.
Such cases are extremely rare, with only 180 known U.S. cases reported between 1937 and 2025.

title: The physical activity paradox: not all forms of exercise lower your dementia risk – this type raises it
author: Eef Hogervorst
content:
Not all physical activity is equal when it comes to protecting the brain from dementia. Where and why we move may matter more than most people realise.
A large new review of studies published in The Lancet Public Health found that leisure-time physical activity – such as sport, dancing or going to the gym – was linked to a 24% lower risk of dementia. Housework was linked to a 15% lower risk, although this finding came from just one study.
Occupational physical activity, on the other hand, was linked to a 20% increased risk of dementia.
The study compiled data from 74 studies involving more than 4.2 million people in 30 countries, making it one of the largest studies of its kind.
Brain protection is well established
Physical activity may protect the brain in several ways. It improves blood flow, helping to deliver oxygen and nutrients to the brain. It also causes muscles to release molecules that can reduce inflammation, help the brain use energy and encourage the growth of new brain cells.
That is one reason why reducing physical inactivity is a key part of the World Health Organization’s recently updated dementia prevention guidelines.
There is plenty of evidence that being active can help protect against dementia. A UK Biobank study tracked people’s activity using wearable devices for four years. Even less than 35 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a week was linked to a 41% lower risk of dementia compared with no such activity.
More vigorous exercise – the kind that leaves you too breathless to talk – was linked to a 63% lower risk of dementia compared with being inactive.
Meanwhile, the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing followed people for 17 years and found that the more active people were, the lower their risk of dementia. The most active group had about half the risk of the least active group.
Walking outdoors – even as little as two miles a day – and gardening have also both been linked to a 25 to 36% lower risk of dementia.
But the new Lancet study suggests that physical activity at work or while travelling to work may not offer the same protection. It may even be linked to a higher risk of developing dementia.
Physical activity paradox
Physical activity at work, based on the combined data from five studies, was linked to a 20% higher risk. And active commuting, such as walking or cycling, based on just two studies, was linked to a 10% higher risk.
Researchers call this the “physical activity paradox”. It is well documented in heart disease research: physical activity at work fails to deliver the same protective effect as the same activity done during leisure time, and can sometimes increase risk instead. Several explanations have been proposed.
People in physically demanding jobs may have had fewer opportunities for education than people in office jobs. Education and mentally stimulating activities throughout life are linked to greater reserve capacity in the brain – its ability to cope with damage and keep working normally.
![Person laying bricks.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/754831/original/file-20260819-69-pq2xal.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)
Manual workers may also be more likely to work in polluted environments, such as factories or building sites. And commuting, particularly by bicycle or on foot, can mean greater exposure to air pollution. Air pollution has separately been linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease.
Recreational exercise accounts for just 4% of active time in low-income countries, but 28% in high- and middle-income countries. So differences in income may shape the factors that influence dementia risk around the world.
The researchers say more research is needed, particularly in low-income countries, to understand what is behind the link between physical activity at work and dementia.
Not all physically demanding jobs are the same. Two physically demanding jobs can involve similar amounts of activity but very different exposures to noise, pollution, stress, heat and other hazards.
These findings point to a deeper inequality: leisure time itself is a resource – one that isn’t distributed evenly. People in low-income countries and those who do physically demanding jobs often have the least opportunity for the kind of activity that seems to protect the brain, while facing the working conditions that may undermine it. Understanding and addressing that imbalance may matter as much for dementia prevention as encouraging people to move more.
summary: A large new review of studies published in The Lancet Public Health reveals that not all physical activity carries the same dementia risk. While leisure-time exercise significantly lowers the risk of developing dementia, physical activity associated with occupations is linked to an increased risk. Researchers refer to this discrepancy as the "physical activity paradox," which may be influenced by factors such as education levels, working conditions, and environmental pollution.
key_points: Leisure-time physical activity like sports, dancing, or going to the gym is linked to a 24% lower risk of dementia.
Occupational physical activity is linked to a 20% increased risk of dementia.
The review compiled data from 74 studies involving over 4.2 million people across 30 countries.
Proposed explanations for the physical activity paradox include differences in education, exposure to air pollution, and work hazards.

title: Alopecia areata: Rheumatoid arthritis drug may treat hair loss
author: Corrie Pelc
content:
![blurred image of person seen from the back dressing their hair](https://media.post.rvohealth.io/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/getty_1386600233_header_1296x728-1024x575.jpg)
- About 160 million people around the world live with alopecia areata.
- There is currently no cure for alopecia areata.
- Alopecia areata is currently treated by medications like JAK inhibitors.
- A new study found a JAK inhibitor medication currently being used to treat rheumatoid arthritis may help people with alopecia areata regrow up to 80% of hair on their scalp within 24 weeks of use.
About 160 million people around the world live with alopecia areata, a chronic autoimmune skin disease causing hair loss on the head, face, and other parts of the body.
There is currently no cure for alopecia areata. The condition is treated with different types of medications, including corticosteroids, immunotherapy, and Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors.
“Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition causing hair loss that carries a profound psychosocial burden for patients,” Arash Mostaghimi, MD, MPH, vice chair of clinical trials and innovation in the Department of Dermatology at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston, associate professor at Harvard Medical School, told Medical News Today.
“Despite the introduction of FDA-approved medications over the past few years, many individuals still do not respond sufficiently to existing therapies. Developing new medications is critical to expanding effective options for these patients,” he noted.
Mostaghimi is the first author of a new study published in the journal 
For this randomized phase 3 clinical trial, researchers recruited almost 1,400 participants — including both adults and adolescents — with severe alopecia areata.
Study participants received either a 15 milligram (mg) or 30 mg dose of the JAK inhibitor upadacitinib, which is currently used to treat several chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s disease, and atopic dermatitis.
“Upadacitinib is a once-daily oral medication that targets the JAK/STAT pathway, a key cellular signaling route that drives inflammation,” Mostaghimi explained.
“Given its mechanism of action, along with real-world observations of hair regrowth in patients treated for eczema who also had co-occurring alopecia areata, investigating upadacitinib as a dedicated treatment for alopecia areata was a natural next step,” he told us.
At the study’s conclusion, Mostaghimi and his team found that about half of study participants taking the 15 mg dose of upadacitinib grew back enough hair to cover at least 80% of their scalp within 24 weeks. And 54% of participants taking the 30 mg dose had the same result.
“These findings demonstrate both rapid onset and substantial depth of response with upadacitinib,” Mostaghimi said. “While this was not a direct head-to-head comparative trial, the data suggest that upadacitinib may be among the most effective systemic treatments evaluated for alopecia areata to date.”
Additionally, researchers reported that study participants had improved eyebrows and eyelashes while on upadacitinib, and said they felt better emotionally and socially.
“The ultimate goal of treating alopecia areata is not just hair count, but restoring patients’ confidence and quality of life,” Mostaghimi explained. “Achieving regrowth in critical non-scalp areas like eyebrows and eyelashes, along with measurable improvements in emotional and social well-being, confirms that upadacitinib delivers clinically meaningful outcomes.”
“Based on these clinical data, upadacitinib has already been approved for severe alopecia areata in Europe,” he added. “The findings are currently under review by the FDA, and we are hopeful the therapy will be approved for patients in the United States in the near future.”
MNT had the opportunity to speak with Joseph W. Fakhoury, MD, dermatologist, clinical trialist, and director of the Alopecia Clinic at Henry Ford Hospital in Detroit, MI, and spokesdoctor for the National Alopecia Areata Foundation, who commented the results are encouraging.
“Upadacitinib works by blocking certain JAK pathways, which are involved in the abnormal immune response underlying alopecia areata,” Fakhoury, who was not involved in this study, explained. “By decreasing the immune system’s attack on the hair follicle, upadacitinib may help the follicle return to its normal hair-growth cycle.”
“Alopecia areata affects patients differently, and not all patients respond to currently available treatments,” he continued. “Having more treatment options will allow us to better personalize care and hopefully help more patients achieve meaningful and durable control of this condition.”
MNT also spoke with Alexis Young, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Hackensack University Medical Center (HUMC) in New Jersey, who likewise was not involved in this study.
Young said her first reaction to the study’s results was one of tremendous optimism.
“Seeing that up to 55% of patients on the 30-mg dose of upadacitinib achieved at least 80% scalp hair coverage in just 24 weeks is a massive step forward. It is especially exciting to see such rapid, robust results — with significant improvements observed as early as eight weeks — for both adult and adolescent patients, a demographic that currently has very limited systemic treatment options.”
– Alexis Young, MD
While the 24-week data demonstrates a highly positive benefit-risk profile with safety consistent with its other approved indications, Young said she looks forward to reviewing the longer-term data.
“This study program includes a 28-week blinded extension period, and seeing the 52-week and beyond results will be critical,” she continued. “That long-term data will help us understand the durability of the hair regrowth, identify any optimal dosing adjustments needed over time, and ensure there are no delayed adverse safety events before routinely prescribing it in clinical practice.”
summary: A recent phase 3 clinical trial found that the JAK inhibitor upadacitinib, a drug currently used for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can help patients with severe alopecia areata regrow significant scalp hair. Within 24 weeks, about half of the participants taking a 15 mg dose and 54% taking a 30 mg dose achieved at least 80% scalp hair coverage. Participants also experienced improvements in eyebrows, eyelashes, and emotional and social well-being. The medication has already been approved for severe alopecia areata in Europe and is under review by the FDA in the United States.
key_points: Alopecia areata affects approximately 160 million people globally and currently has no cure.
A phase 3 clinical trial involving nearly 1,400 participants tested the JAK inhibitor upadacitinib for severe alopecia areata.
Within 24 weeks, up to 54% of participants taking the 30 mg dose of upadacitinib regrew hair covering at least 80% of their scalp.
The treatment also improved eyebrow and eyelash regrowth, as well as patients' emotional and social well-being.
Upadacitinib is already approved for severe alopecia areata in Europe and is currently under review by the FDA.

title: Woman diagnosed with rare eye cancer after lights 'flickered' in work meeting
author: Benjamin Paessler
content:
A woman was diagnosed with a rare eye cancer after complaining to confused colleagues that the office lights were 'flickering'.
Lara Vivo, 41, started to notice 'flickering lights' in work meetings which gave her headaches around March 2019, despite colleagues saying the lights were working fine.
She put it down to stress, but ended up going for an eye test as she thought she needed glasses.
Instead, Lara was referred straight to an emergency eye unit in a hospital, where further tests led to a doctor diagnosing her with eye cancer - uveal melanoma.
  Lara Vivo, after the operation.
She flew from her home in Bournemouth to see a highly-recommended private specialist eye doctor in Barcelona who found a 1cm tumour on her right eye, and it had caused her retina to detach, causing the flashing lights and headaches.
Lara, who is originally from Valencia, Spain, underwent three surgeries costing £30k in Barcelona, aiming to destroy the tumour and prevent spread of cancer, although it left her with just 10% vision in that eye.
Read more
    National Highways gives date for A31 reopening with 40mph speed limit in place
    Son of Beaulieu Motor Museum founder speaks out over plans to leave New Forest
    Car wash in Bournemouth ordered to stop jet washing after noise breaches
  
For the following seven years she had regular checks and was believed to be cancer-free - until January this year where doctors found the cancer from her eye had metastasised in her liver.
At this point the cancer was deemed incurable, and NHS doctors told Lara and her partner, Roy, that there was no NHS-funded treatment available for her.
Lara is now fundraising for £120,000 of private chemosaturation therapy - a targeted chemotherapy delivered by needle directly into the liver - which is not available on the NHS due to limited research and it not being considered cost-effective.
  Lara Vivo, after the operation.
Lara, a supermarket store assistant, said: "I had this funny vision at work but I couldn't explain it, it just didn't feel right.
"Everyone else said the lights hadn't bothered them at all.
"I went for this eye test and I was shocked to be referred straight to the emergency eye unit.
"Even then, I never thought it was serious - I just thought I needed glasses.
"So when the consultant told me it was cancer, it was like a stab in the heart.
"I had three operations over six months where I had to move back to Spain and live with my family, leaving behind my partner and dog.
"After that I thought it wasn't coming back, and even at the start of this year my oncologist told me I was past the point of it returning.
"Then they found cancer in my liver. Now this is life or death for me, if I don't do anything this will kill me. But I'm not giving up, I want to live."
Lara's vision issues first started in early 2019, although she struggled to pinpoint the exact issues beyond "flickering lighting".
She said: "I asked my colleagues 'did that lighting bother you?' after the meeting. But they said it didn't.
"Then I was scrolling through Facebook and it showed me an advert for a free eye test, so I went, thinking I must need glasses."
But the optician referred her straight to the emergency eye unit at Royal Bournemouth Hospital instead.
Soon she had been diagnosed by a consultant with uveal melanoma, a rare malignant cancer, found in the eye's uvea - the middle layer of tissue in the wall of the eyeball.
She said: "I remember saying 'hold on a minute, did you say cancer?'. I don't remember much else.
"I came out the waiting room and burst into tears to my partner."
Despite her impression that 'melanoma' would be related to skin, Lara later learned it had been caused by a random cell mutation at the back of her eye.
Lara visited a doctor in Barcelona who confirmed the diagnosis and agreed to operate.
The operation comprised of three separate surgeries over six months to reattach the retina, remove half the tumour and apply a radioactive plaque to it which aimed to attack the remaining cancer, and which would later be removed.
The three surgeries left her with just 10% vision in that eye, but with the hope that it had got rid of the cancer once and for all.
She returned to the UK and had regular check-ups but remained cancer-free.
Seven years on, Lara felt more reassured - and Lara and Roy, a firefighter, had discussed getting married and starting a family.
But in January, a scheduled MRI scan revealed the cancer had metastasised in the liver.
She said: "I had originally been told I was a high risk for metastases in the liver, but by now I thought maybe I was fine.
"But as of March 2026, I am considered stage four terminal."
Because of the rarity of uveal melanoma, NHS's Clinical Commissioning Policy of 2016 for chemosaturation says there isn't enough evidence of success to support making the procedure available on the NHS.
It reads: "No studies were identified of high quality to draw firm conclusions on the safety of the procedure in patients with liver metastasis from ocular melanoma.
"No cost-effectiveness studies were identified to comment on the cost-effectiveness of this procedure."
But Lara says it's her only hope - and is fundraising via GoFundMe to cover the cost of a round of three £40,000-a-go treatments at Southampton General Hospital.
She said: "I've been given a grim diagnosis but I've been researching and I'm not giving up, I want to live.
"These seven years it's just been appointments, cancer, hospitals. We had planned to get married, and maybe have children.
"It will never happen now. It's ruined my life.
"I don't look ill, but I'm fighting for my life now. And this cancer is persistent, but I'm not giving up.
"If you're sensing something is wrong with your eye, get it checked."
Lara's fundraiser: https://gofund.me/deb9eb466
summary: Lara Vivo was diagnosed with a rare eye cancer called uveal melanoma in 2019 after noticing flickering lights in work meetings. Following treatments in Spain that left her with 10% vision in her right eye, she was told she was cancer-free until an MRI in January revealed the cancer had spread to her liver. Now facing a terminal stage four diagnosis and lacking NHS-funded treatment options, she is fundraising £120,000 for private chemosaturation therapy.
key_points: Lara Vivo noticed perceived flickering lights during work meetings in 2019, which prompted her to get an eye test.
She was diagnosed with uveal melanoma, a rare eye cancer caused by a random cell mutation that had detached her retina.
After undergoing three surgeries in Barcelona costing £30,000, she retained only 10% vision in her right eye.
In January, a scheduled MRI scan revealed the cancer had metastasised in her liver and was deemed incurable by NHS doctors.
She is currently fundraising £120,000 for private chemosaturation therapy not available on the NHS due to limited research and cost-effectiveness.

title: Oxford cancer trial hopes to reduce risks for rare condition
author: Sarah Farmer
content:
![A white woman, with fair shoulder-length hair looks into a microscope in a laboratory. She is wearing a white lab coat and blue latex gloves. Her colleague observes in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/7215/live/eb147510-9fa6-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
People with Li-Fraumeni syndrome can have an increased cancer risk of about 90%
- Published
Researchers are hoping a new clinical trial could delay or reduce the risk of cancer for people with a rare condition.
Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) can increase an individuals likelihood of developing cancer during their lifetime by about 90%.
It is known to affect about 700 people in the UK - but scientists believe as many as one in 20,000 may have it.
The team behind the trial at the University of Oxford hope to gain a better understanding of the condition and are aiming to create a vaccine to protect people from cancer.
![A white woman, with fair, shoulder-length hair sits in a blue office chair. She is wearing a checked shirt and grey cardigan. On the desk behind here there is a computer monitor, books and a lamp.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a504/live/db3b68c0-9fa5-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Professor Sarah Blagden, Professor of Experimental Oncology at the University of Oxford, hopes her team can develop a vaccine to protect against cancer
Sarah Blagden, Professor of Experimental Oncology at the university, is leading the trial.
She said many people with LFS develop multiple forms of cancer in succession.
"It's more than just a risk of cancer, it's like a biological guarantee," she said.
The study has been funded by Cancer Research UK, the National Institute for Health and Care Research, the Medical Research Council and The George Pantziarka TP53 Trust.
It is considering the use of Metformin, a drug routinely used to treat diabetes, after successful lab studies in the US.
Blagden said: "We have in our cells 'organelles', little structures called mitochondria, and they help convert our food into energy.
"We know with somebody with LFS that their mitochondria are overactive and so Metformin tunes that down, preventing the damage to the cell."
Blagden hopes focusing on the specific cell mutations in LFS - known as P53 mutations - will help in the bigger picture of tackling cancer.
She said: "P53 mutations are commonly seen in all types of cancers and when they occur, they often signify that the cancer is more aggressive.
"So for us it's really important to understand why that mutation not only starts LFS, but makes other cancers more aggressive."
The team hopes to develop a vaccine that can be used to protect people once they get a LFS diagnosis.
Blagden said: "The plan would be to use the samples that we've collected to really help us engineer the perfect off-the-shelf vaccine that we can give to protect people from cancer."
summary: Researchers at the University of Oxford have launched a clinical trial aimed at delaying or reducing cancer risks for individuals with Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS), a rare genetic condition that carries an increased lifetime cancer risk of about 90%. Led by Professor Sarah Blagden, the study is investigating whether the diabetes drug Metformin can tune down overactive mitochondria and prevent cell damage in LFS patients. Ultimately, the team hopes to use data from the study to engineer a vaccine to protect diagnosed individuals from developing cancer.
key_points: Li-Fraumeni syndrome increases an individual's lifetime cancer risk by about 90% and affects an estimated one in 20,000 people.
The Oxford trial is investigating the use of Metformin, a routine diabetes drug, to reduce cell damage by calming overactive mitochondria in LFS patients.
The study is funded by organizations including Cancer Research UK, the Medical Research Council, and the National Institute for Health and Care Research.
Researchers plan to use collected samples to engineer a vaccine that can protect people against cancer following an LFS diagnosis.

title: Sir Chris Hoy: Campaigning for cancer screening should not be down to me
author: Jane Lewis
content:
Chris Hoy says men must understand their prostate cancer risk
- Published
Sir Chris Hoy believes the onus to encourage men to get tested for prostate cancer should not just be on high-profile individuals like him.
Hoy told BBC Scotland he felt privileged to have the public platform to spread awareness and would continue to do so even if there was a national screening system in place.
But he said: "It shouldn't just be down to high-profile individuals like Jeremy Clarkson or myself or any number of men who've been in a similar situation.
"There should be a more systematic and proactive approach to let men know about their own risk."
Sir Chris was diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer when was 47. He turned 50 in March.
![Sir Chris Hoy is pictured walking out of the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome with the Wales family - Prince William, Princess Catherine and their children George, Charlotte and Louis at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/819/cpsprodpb/5fb5/live/1ba38130-9d54-11f1-aac2-870643eea2ac.jpg)
Hoy uses his profile as a well-known and well-loved public figure to campaign for prostate screening
He told BBC Scotland: "I turned 50 recently and I got a letter through the post with a bowel screening test.
"I understand the PSA test (a blood test that can help detect prostate cancer) isn't perfect, you know you can get results - not false positives, but it can be that men can be treated when they maybe didn't need to be treated.
"But actually, I think that's not a diagnosis issue, that's a treatment issue, that's a decision for the doctors to make.
"I think knowing your situation is really important."
Hoy said 10,000 men a year in the UK find out too late that they have prostate cancer.
He said there should be some kind of formal process to at least make men take responsibility and ownership and to understand their personal risk.
"In the short term, until something more proactive happens you've got to take it on your own shoulders," he said.
"It's not what you want to think about and it's always the thing you push down the list of priorities. You forget about it because life's busy."
![An image of Sir Chris, on his bike, cycling around a park with a large group of cyclists in Tour De 4 cycling tops. They are all punching the air and smiling. He is in the centre, all the cyclists are wearing helmets.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/23c2/live/6d2bca90-9fa6-11f1-bff6-57f1422ebb0b.jpg)
Sir Chris Hoy meets employees from Tour de 4 backer ScottishPower for a special training session at Bellahouston Park, Glasgow.
The six-time Olympic gold medallist, was speaking ahead of his "'Tour De 4" charity cycle, the event he founded after his diagnosis which, in his view, is "doing something positive from a very difficult situation."
"The aim is to try and change perceptions of what living with stage 4 cancer can mean," he said.
As well as raising money, he said the event aimed to "bring together people who are in a similar situation to me, to bring together families, people who are remembering loved ones".
"It's really a celebration of life," he said.
While Sir Chris is an ardent campaigner for prostate cancer, he admits to being "moved" by Scottish swimmer Archie Goodburn's impassioned plea to the prime minister for increased funding for brain cancer, and hopes something will come of it.
"So far, it seems that the powers-that-be are listening," he said.
'I'm not going to give up'
"My concern is that you get a lot of publicity from something like that and then the politicians, or the people in power or whoever the decision-makers are, will do something as a reaction - 'oh yes we're going to have a chat' or 'we're going to do this', but actions speak louder than words.
"You want to see some practical change that will actually be implemented, not just a sit-down-and-talk and 'we might address this' and 'we'll have a look at it' because often that means 'we're just going to kick the can down the road' and nothing actually changes."
"But Archie's not going to give up and I'm not going to give up."
Sir Chris said he was "doing really well" at the moment.
He added: "Right now life just goes on. You could spent your time sitting worrying about the future but that doesn't help you in any shape or form."
The Tour De 4 takes place on Sunday 6 September, starting and finishing at the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome in Glasgow.
summary: Sir Chris Hoy believes that encouraging men to get tested for prostate cancer should not rely solely on high-profile figures like himself and Jeremy Clarkson. Diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer at 47, Hoy advocates for a more systematic and proactive approach to inform men about their personal risks. He is also speaking out ahead of his "Tour De 4" charity cycle, an event aimed at raising funds, changing perceptions of living with stage 4 cancer, and celebrating life.
key_points: Sir Chris Hoy stated that encouraging prostate cancer screening should involve a formal, systematic process rather than relying on public figures.
Hoy was diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer at the age of 47.
He emphasized that 10,000 men in the UK each year discover they have prostate cancer too late.
Hoy founded the "Tour De 4" charity cycling event to raise awareness, change perceptions of stage 4 cancer, and bring affected families together.

title: AI trial aims to detect depression in new mothers
author: Liz Johnson; Miya Chahal
content:
![Woman using a phone in front of a baby in a cot](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9641/live/02b81e50-9bb6-11f1-ae8a-8d57110c5ba6.jpg)
The technology uses women's speech and facial expressions to determine their mood
- Published
A medical study is testing whether Artificial Intelligence (AI) could be used to detect depression in pregnant women or those who have recently given birth.
Researchers from the University of Nottingham and Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust have worked with AI firm BlueSky to develop an app that tracks participants' mood and behaviour.
The app works by asking users to complete tasks while software analyses their facial expressions, speech and automatic movements.
After finishing the task, the technology flags if patients are getting above a certain depression score. Researchers hope it will help women speak to their GP about mood changes during and after pregnancy.
The study, which started in 2024, is now in its final stages and researchers are aiming to finish in October.
A report by the University of Oxford, external last year found that in the UK, 39% of maternal deaths between six weeks and one year after pregnancy are suicides.
Dr Neil Nixon, one of the leading researchers on the project, said: "One thing we should remember is that suicide remains a really important cause of mortality in women in the post-natal period.
"Being able to identify clinical problems early on, at a point where we can intervene for those women, could really make a big difference."
The tasks vary from reading a few paragraphs of a novel to journalling their mood.
Nixon said that so far, about a third of women who have been through the study have been flagged for depression.
"The worry is that women don't realise their mood is changing. This software could change that," he said.
![Dr Neil Nixon standing in front of a bookshelf](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/960/cpsprodpb/8b35/live/83805ee0-97e1-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
Dr Neil Nixon is one of the leading researchers on the project
Lizzie, a mum from Long Eaton who took part in the trial, has two children and used the app when her youngest child was seven months.
She said people underestimate how hard it can be once you leave the hospital.
"You are so obsessed with the pregnancy, and you have so much support through the birth... and then you are just at home.
"That's when it really can be tricky.
"It's not all rainbows and butterflies. It's a really difficult time mentally for you, your identity and your mental health."
Sally Bunkman. from the charity PANDAS, which helps women suffering with perinatal mental illness, added: "People that use our services are often dismissed when they see a healthcare professional - they are told it's just the 'baby blues'.
"This technology has lots of potential and could empower women to talk more openly about their feelings to a doctor.
"But, women need to get support from an actual human - we don't want women being supported by an AI. We need human to human support. That is crucial."
Nixon said the technology will not be used to diagnose conditions, but instead support clinicians in their work.
He added: "We hope this will help women check in with their feelings at a time that is so important in their lives."
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this article, support is available via the BBC Action Line
Listen to BBC Radio Nottingham on Sounds and follow BBC Nottingham on Facebook, external, on X, external, or on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to eastmidsnews@bbc.co.uk, external or via WhatsApp, external on 0808 100 2210.
summary: A medical study is testing a new AI-powered app designed to detect depression in pregnant women and new mothers by analyzing their facial expressions, speech, and movements during tasks. Developed by researchers from the University of Nottingham, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, and AI firm BlueSky, the tool aims to help women identify changing moods and speak with their GPs early. Researchers emphasize that the technology is intended to support clinicians rather than diagnose conditions, while charities stress the ongoing necessity of human support.
key_points: Researchers from the University of Nottingham, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, and BlueSky developed an app to track mood and behavior using AI.
The app analyzes facial expressions, speech, and automatic movements as users complete tasks like reading or journalling.
The study, which began in 2024, is in its final stages and aims to conclude in October.
Developers state the technology is designed to support clinicians and help women discuss mood changes with their GP, rather than provide a medical diagnosis.
Charity representatives note the potential for the app to empower women, while stressing that actual human support remains crucial.

title: I’m a cardiologist. This is what you need to know about the side effects of statins
author: Damon Syson; Dr Ricardo Petraco
content:
![Dr Ricardo Petraco specialises in cardiovascular screening, coronary artery disease and intervention](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000497961165_17873041445140_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Dr Ricardo Petraco specialises in cardiovascular screening, coronary artery disease and intervention](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000497961165_17873041445140_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dr Ricardo Petraco is an internationally recognised consultant cardiologist and researcher based at Imperial College London and the Mayo Clinic in London. He specialises in cardiovascular screening, coronary artery disease and intervention.
Around seven to eight million people in the UK are on statins, and every week I see patients who are either on or considering taking them. More than with any of their other pills, many are worried about side effects. So what are their real risks?
First, an important disclosure: I have no conflict of interest in recommending or prescribing statins. I don’t make money from doing so, and I have no relationship with the pharmaceutical companies that make and sell them to the NHS.
It’s mystifying to me that statins are so vilified, because if you had to pick the one medication in the history of cardiology with the clearest benefit, it would be them.
Statins work by lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL), the so-called “bad” cholesterol in the blood that leads to heart attacks, strokes and early death. Across the board, people taking a statin are roughly 25-40 per cent less likely to have a heart attack or stroke, regardless of their cholesterol level at the start of treatment. And the myths about the alleged risks – cancer, dementia, cognitive impairment, sexual dysfunction – have all been robustly debunked.
A study led by Oxford Population Health and published in The Lancet in February 2026 pooled 23 blinded trials involving more than 154,000 people. It found no excess risk from statins for 62 of the 66 conditions listed in their package leaflets, including memory loss, depression and sleep disturbances.
However, side effects can happen and some patients have genuine concerns. Dismissing them is wrong. What we should say is: “Yes, there is a small risk of side effects with statins, but let’s talk about it. Let’s weigh that risk against the risk of having a heart attack, and then you can make a rational decision about your treatment.”
Whatever you do, don’t give up on statins because you’re worried about side effects. That daily pill could save your life.
![Around seven to eight million people in the UK are on statins](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499018171_17873045168230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The side effects – should you be concerned?
Muscle aches
It is estimated that around one fifth of patients refuse or stop taking statins because of muscle aches, fatigue or joint pain. Yet true statin-caused muscle ache is uncommon. A 2022 study led by researchers from Oxford Population Health found that “for every 1,000 people taking a moderate intensity statin, the treatment would cause 11 generally mild episodes of muscle pain or weakness in the first year, with no significant excess in subsequent years”. The occurrence is just over 1 per cent, and only at the start.
A lot of complaints around muscle ache are largely down to the “nocebo effect”. That means the symptom is real but the drug is not causing it – the expectation of feeling unwell is. In studies where people don’t know whether they’re taking a statin or a dummy pill, aches are reported at nearly the same rate in both groups.
At Imperial, where I’m based, my colleagues carried out a study in 2020 that recruited 60 people aged between 37-79 who had stopped taking statins because of side effects, and restarted them, but with a twist. Over a year, each patient received bottles containing a statin, bottles containing a dummy pill, and bottles containing nothing at all, rating their symptoms each day via an app. The results were illuminating. Symptoms were nearly identical whether people took the statin or the placebo.
Nonetheless, it does occasionally happen, and it is a genuine concern. If a patient feels that statins are causing aches and pains, we monitor the situation, temporarily stop the statin and restart it to see how they feel. For many, symptoms lessen with time, particularly if you start on a lower dose and increase gradually. And if muscle problems persist, we can find another way to lower their LDL cholesterol. There are always alternatives.
Severe muscle damage
Rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle breakdown) is a genuine but extremely rare side effect of statins. It happens in about one to three people out of every 100,000 taking statins each year, and less commonly still at lower doses. It is more likely if you’re on a higher dose, if you’re taking certain other medications at the same time, or if you have kidney or liver problems or an underactive thyroid.
The problem is that because people occasionally experience muscle aches on statins, they immediately associate this with rhabdomyolysis and become very concerned. Yet the chances of it occurring are negligible, and that small risk needs to be weighed against the benefit.
A 2016 report published in The Lancet remains the clearest quantification: treating 10,000 people for five years with a type of statin called atorvastatin at 40mg would cause about five cases of muscle injury. One of those five might progress to rhabdomyolysis, and 50 to 100 people would report muscle symptoms.
Over the same five years, it would prevent 500-1,000 major vascular events, including deaths and disability from strokes and heart attacks. The benefits outweigh the harms many times over.
Slightly higher risk of diabetes
Taking a statin does slightly increase your average blood-sugar level, and over five years it raises the chance of being diagnosed with diabetes by about 0.5 to 1 per cent – somewhere between one in 200 and one in 100 people.
If you are fit and well, with a normal blood sugar, you will not suddenly become diabetic by going on a statin. It’s the patients who are already borderline – with insulin resistance or obesity – who may be taken over the line from pre-diabetes to diabetes. But those are precisely the patients at highest risk of a future cardiac event, so they are the ones the statin protects most. In these cases, lifestyle interventions such as diet changes, exercise and quitting smoking are recommended alongside taking statins.
Raised liver enzyme levels
With many medications, such as paracetamol, ibuprofen and antibiotics, there is a very small risk of liver failure. With statins, this is not a clinical concern: they do not measurably increase your risk of dying from liver failure.
It’s true that about four in 1,000 people have raised liver enzyme levels on blood tests when they start taking statins, but this usually causes no symptoms and is rarely a reason to stop.
Dementia (and the brain cholesterol myth)
There is a widespread myth that taking statins causes dementia. It is based on the fallacious claim that “20 per cent of your brain is cholesterol and yet your doctor is giving you medication to lower your cholesterol”. Biologically this makes no sense. Your brain cholesterol is produced locally, by specialised cells, and has nothing to do with the cholesterol circulating in your bloodstream in LDL particles.
Cognitive impairment is not a side effect of taking statins – The Lancet’s 2026 review confirmed as much. If anything, there is a theoretical gain, because you are decreasing the chance of vascular damage in the brain. Observational studies suggest that long-term statin use may even reduce your risk of developing dementia, although that is not yet proven.
Sleep problems
Clinical trials have shown no consistent association between statins and sleep problems, but this is something patients do worry about. Again, the picture is confounded: people on cardiac medication tend to be older, and to have other conditions that disturb sleep. The statin itself has never been shown to cause them.
A few people taking statins that cross the blood-brain barrier – such as simvastatin or atorvastatin – report vivid dreams or disturbed sleep. This is rare, and although it’s hard to conclude whether the drug is the cause, we pragmatically recommend moving the dose to the morning; and if symptoms persist, an alternative such as rosuvastatin can be tried, as it is known not to cross into the brain so easily.
Erectile dysfunction
Statins causing erectile dysfunction is another common chapter in the book of online misinformation, but the link is unfounded. Sexual dysfunction is common among patients with cardiovascular disease, and some heart drugs, such as beta-blockers, can indeed cause it.
That confuses the picture, as those are the same patients who take statins. But there is no scientific evidence that statins cause sexual dysfunction. In fact, some studies suggest they can help, possibly by improving vascular health which then improves blood flow to the genitals.
Oedema (swollen ankles)
Oedema – essentially swollen ankles – does happen, but the numbers are very small and it’s not something we worry about. The 2026 analysis previously found roughly seven extra cases per 10,000 people per year, or 0.07 per cent. For comparison, amlodipine, a blood pressure tablet frequently prescribed alongside statins, causes dose-dependent ankle oedema in 5-10 per cent of users.
summary: Statins are highly effective medications that significantly reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes by lowering LDL cholesterol. While patients frequently worry about side effects like muscle aches, dementia, and diabetes, large-scale studies show that the vast majority of feared risks are myths or exceedingly rare. The significant cardiovascular benefits of statins far outweigh the minor risks of side effects.
key_points: Statins reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke by roughly 25 to 40 percent.
Many reported muscle aches are linked to the "nocebo effect" rather than actual statin toxicity.
Severe muscle damage, or rhabdomyolysis, is extremely rare, occurring in only one to three out of every 100,000 users annually.
Statins can slightly increase the risk of a diabetes diagnosis by 0.5 to 1 percent over five years, mostly in individuals who are already borderline.
Myths regarding links between statins and dementia, cognitive impairment, or sexual dysfunction have been robustly debunked by clinical data.

title: NHS England to offer women ‘gamechanging’ free home testing kits for cervical cancer
author: Andrew Gregory
content:
Millions of women in England who have missed cervical screening appointments will be offered free home testing kits on the NHS.
The move comes amid concerns that only two-thirds of women attend in-person cervical screening appointments when asked to do so, leaving as many as 4 million women not up to date.
The rollout is being described as a “gamechanger”, offering a “discreet and convenient option” to encourage more women to get screened.
The kits contain a swab to collect a sample from the vagina. This is then posted back to the NHS free, where it is tested in labs for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV).
If high-risk HPV is detected, patients will then be asked to attend a cervical screening appointment with a clinician.
HPV is a group of viruses that can be passed on through sexual contact and cause no symptoms. About 13 high-risk types of the virus are known to cause 99.7% of cervical cancers.
Starting on Tuesday, eligible women between 30 and 65 who have not attended screening appointments will be sent invitations via the NHS app, text message, email or letter.
They will then be able to order a kit through the app or website. The scheme is part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040.
Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two-thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS.
“Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.”
Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, or more often if HPV is detected.
The latest figures from NHS England show 68.8% of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80% target. It means about 4 million women are not up to date, according to NHS estimates.
“There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test,” said Mann.
after newsletter promotion
“So, if you’re invited to take part, please order a test – it’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.”
Athena Lamnisos, chief executive of the Eve Appeal, welcomed the move, saying that self-testing at home would be a “step-change” for many women.
Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK, said: “Cervical screening is a powerful tool that saves lives – it can prevent cervical cancer or spot it at an earlier stage when treatment is more likely to be successful.
“While it’s best for cervical screening to be done by a nurse or doctor, there are barriers that make it challenging for some people to attend. At-home HPV self-testing kits will help more people take part in a way that works for them.”
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the aim was to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening. She said: “This is the future NHS we are building – there for all of us when we need it, and acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths.”
summary: NHS England is introducing free home testing kits for cervical cancer to reach millions of women who have missed in-person screening appointments. Eligible women aged 30 to 65 who are behind on screenings can order a kit containing a vaginal swab via the NHS app or website. Samples are mailed to the NHS to test for high-risk HPV, with patients who test positive subsequently asked to see a clinician. The initiative aims to overcome barriers like lack of time and embarrassment, supporting the NHS target to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.
key_points: Millions of women in England who missed cervical screening will receive free at-home testing kits.
Only about two-thirds of women currently attend in-person appointments, leaving roughly 4 million women not up to date.
The kits use a simple vaginal swab to test for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) in a lab.
Eligible women between 30 and 65 can order the kits through the NHS app or website starting Tuesday.
The scheme is part of an NHS target to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.

title: Ebola cases in DRC hit 5,515 as Pope Leo urges global action to save lives
author: Faisal Ali
content:
![FILE PHOTO: Displaced people watch a health worker in full personal protective equipment (PPE) preparing to disinfect the area during the burial of suspected Ebola victims at the Kigonze displaced persons camp in Bunia, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, on June 18, 2026, one month after the outbreak was declared. REUTERS/Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/File Photo](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-21T112538Z_1019628448_RC23WLAWITCL_RTRMADP_3_HEALTH-EBOLA-UN-1787523055.jpg?resize=730%2C410&quality=80)
DR Congo miners risk Ebola to make a living
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 5,515 confirmed cases of infection and killed 2,642 people, with 51 new cases detected in Ituri and North Kivu provinces, according to the latest government figures.
The update on Sunday came as Pope Leo called for international action to help contain the epidemic, which is now the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the DRC’s history.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How the deadliest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak can be stopped
- list 2 of 3DR Congo miners risk Ebola to make a living
- list 3 of 3Ebola continues to spread in the DRC as 16,000 vaccine doses arrive
Declared in mid-May, it is the DRC’s 17th Ebola epidemic and was designated a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization (WHO), its highest alert level, also covering neighbouring Uganda.
The outbreak is now on track to surpass the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record, which was the 2014–2016 outbreak in West Africa that killed more than 11,000 people.
According to government figures, the case fatality rate in the DRC has climbed from about 20 percent in early June to nearly 48 percent now, meaning almost one in two people infected are dying.
Contact tracing, however, has improved sharply, from 30 percent in June to more than 85 percent.
The disease has also proved deadly for those fighting it. About 160 health workers have been infected, and about 45 have died, according to the WHO.
Efforts to contain the outbreak, however, have been hampered by armed conflict in the affected provinces, displacement, attacks on medical personnel and facilities, a mobile working population and a lack of critical infrastructure.
Vaccines arrive in DRC
There is no approved vaccine or treatment for this particular strain of Ebola, known as Bundibugyo, which is rarer than the virus type behind most past outbreaks.
The WHO has pledged 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, which is licensed for Ebola and has been effective in past outbreaks. According to the global body, early data from animal trials suggest it may offer some protection against Bundibugyo.
Some 16,250 doses of the vaccine arrived in the DRC on Friday.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and other officials said the response in the DRC needs to be scaled up two to threefold to contain the outbreak and reach every affected area.
They also called for more support and protection for front-line health workers, including protective equipment, timely payment, and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill.
Abdulsalami Nasidi, a public health consultant who helped establish the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, told Al Jazeera that the outbreak was “getting out of hand”.
He blamed weak infection control measures and a lack of trust between authorities and affected communities for the continued transmission.
“This is no longer just a national or regional issue; it is a global issue. If it spreads to neighbouring places with lower immunity, it will be a disaster,” Nasidi added.
The WHO currently rates the risk to the global public as low, but warns that the danger inside the DRC remains very high.
Despite the surging cases, Uganda and several health zones in DRC’s Ituri and South Kivu have interrupted transmission, which the WHO said is evidence that rapid detection, decisive leadership, and community cooperation can break the chain of transmission.
At the Vatican on Sunday, Pope Leo offered prayers for the DRC, “in light of the spread of the Ebola epidemic, which is sadly claiming many lives”.
The pontiff also called for global action to help save lives.
“I urge the international community to respond in a way that also involves local communities in prevention efforts to save as many lives as possible,” he said.
summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reached 5,515 confirmed cases and 2,642 deaths, making it the deadliest in the country's history. Pope Leo has called for international action to help contain the epidemic, which faces containment challenges due to armed conflict, attacks on medical personnel, and a lack of critical infrastructure. Meanwhile, thousands of vaccine doses have arrived in the DRC as health officials work to scale up the response.
key_points: DR Congo's Ebola outbreak has reached 5,515 confirmed cases and 2,642 deaths, with a case fatality rate nearing 48 percent.
Pope Leo urged international action and community involvement to help contain the epidemic and save lives.
Efforts to combat the outbreak are hampered by armed conflict, displacement, attacks on medical personnel, and a lack of infrastructure.
A shipment of 16,250 vaccine doses arrived in the DRC following WHO pledges to supply doses for the response.

title: Girl, 8, dies after contracting brain-eating amoeba likely caught in Louisiana lake
author: Owen Scott
content:
An 8-year-old girl has died after contracting a brain-eating amoeba likely contracted while swimming at a lake in Louisiana.
Lillian Smart was infected with Naegleria fowleri, an amoeba that thrives in bodies of warm, fresh water.
Her family confirmed her death on the Love for Lillian Facebook page, where they have been sharing updates about her battle with the illness.
“Last night Lillian ran from our arms to the arms of Jesus,” they posted. “The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from.
“Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?”
![Lillian Smart, an 8-year-old from Louisiana, has died after becoming infected by a brain-eating amoeba](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/7/27/782169146_122099375619446574_3374054569947885979_n-eeb42479.jpeg)
Without naming Lillian, the Louisiana Department of Health confirmed a case of infection with Naegleria fowleri on August 19, adding that it had most likely been contracted at Lake Claiborne.
According to the LDH, Naegleria fowleri can cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), which can occur when water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain.
The LDH warns that Naegleria fowleri can cause victims to suffer severe headaches, fever and vomiting that progresses to a stiff neck, seizures and a coma. Although rare, PAM is nearly always fatal.
In a post on Facebook uploaded earlier in August, Lillian’s mother said that the little girl had been admitted to hospital after suffering a fever before experiencing double vision.
![Lillian was described as a ‘sweet little girl’ and a ‘happy child’](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/7/49/783029300_122101208229446574_5316006533475584882_n-c570c64d.jpeg)
Lillian died just a day after her birthday, according to the Love for Lillian page, with doctors telling her family that the swelling caused by the infection was “significant.”
Members of the community in Ruston, where the 8-year-old was from, held a Love for Lillian fundraiser on Friday to mark her eighth birthday.
“She’s just always a happy child,” Patricia Willis, a local business owner, told KNOE. “Every time you see her, she has a smile on her face.”
Louisiana senator John Kennedy said in a statement that he and his wife are “heartbroken” at the news of Lillian’s death.
“Our hearts and prayers are with Lillian’s family, Ruston and all of Louisiana as we mourn this sweet little girl,” he wrote. “May God comfort her family and give them strength in the days ahead.”
![Naegleria fowleri (pictured) can cause a deadly infection known as primary amebic meningoencephalitis](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/7/31/Naegleria-4.jpg)
The LDH says that there have only been 180 known cases of PAM in the U.S. from 1937 to 2025, with just three cases of Naegleria fowleri occurring in Louisiana during that period.
The agency warns that swimmers should keep their heads out of the water and plug their noses while swimming. Swimmers have also been urged to not dig up or disturb sediment while taking part in water-based activities.
summary: An 8-year-old girl named Lillian Smart has died from a brain-eating amoeba infection she likely contracted while swimming at a Louisiana lake. Her family confirmed her passing after severe brain injuries left her unable to recover from the illness caused by Naegleria fowleri. The rare infection leads to primary amebic meningoencephalitis, which is nearly always fatal.
key_points: Lillian Smart, 8, died from an infection of Naegleria fowleri, commonly known as a brain-eating amoeba.
The Louisiana Department of Health stated the infection was likely contracted at Lake Claiborne.
Naegleria fowleri causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), an infection that enters through the nose and is nearly always fatal.
The Louisiana Department of Health reports only 180 known U.S. cases of PAM from 1937 to 2025, with just three in Louisiana.
Health officials advise swimmers to keep their heads out of the water, plug their noses, and avoid disturbing sediment.

title: Salmonella outbreak affecting UK 'may have spread to chicken'
author: Craig Munro
content:
![A butcher's hands hold a piece of chicken meat in a butcher shop. The butcher stores the chicken meat in a bag; Shutterstock ID 2694404125; purchase_order: -; job: -; client: -; other: 15829173](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_297936224-4e92.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
A Salmonella outbreak affecting the UK and six other countries around Europe may have spread to chicken, experts have suggested.
The outbreak, which was first detected in August last year, has already led to one death in the UK while 34 have been hospitalised across all seven countries.
There have been a total of 207 confirmed British cases with contaminated eggs the ‘strongest’ possible cause, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).
Research published last week by the body said: ‘At this time there is no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry.’
Austria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany and the Netherlands have also reported cases, though the outbreak is hitting the UK and Netherlands hardest.
Sign up for all of the latest stories
On Friday, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) again highlighted UK investigations pointing to imported eggs as ‘the suspected source of infection’.
The organisation added: ‘The investigation done in the Netherlands in 2026 pointed towards chicken meat, although it is based on a small number of patient interviews.’
What is Salmonella?
Salmonella is a bacteria which is spread via contaminated food such as eggs, poultry, meat, unpasteurised dairy products and fresh produce.
Consumption can result in an infection called salmonellosis, which can be fatal.
Typical symptoms of salmonella infection can include diarrhoea, stomach cramps, vomiting and fever.
But for those who are particularly vulnerable – such as young children, older adults and immunocompromised people – it can result in more severe illness such as blood stream infection and sepsis.
The particular variation of Salmonella in the current outbreak is S. Enteritidis, which is the most common type in England.
Its assessment reads: ‘The multi-country outbreak of Salmonella Enteritidis ST11 remains ongoing, with increasing case numbers since May 2026, particularly in the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.
‘Epidemiological investigations are ongoing and indicate eggs and chicken products as potential sources of infection.
‘More cases are expected until proper control measures are implemented on the source.’
The UKHSA reports that the British outbreak is most prevalent in London, which has had 47 cases, and Yorkshire and Humber, which has had 38.
Only eight of the 207 total cases were resident outside England, including six in Scotland, one in Wales and one in Northern Ireland.
![Fresh, organic chicken eggs in recyclable egg cartons are being arranged for customer orders by a Japanese owner of a zero-waste whole foods refill store, as seen in a close-up.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309389386-df05.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Last week, the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) called for the government to ensure adequate checks are being carried out on all food coming into the country.
- 
	![ABC News coverage of the Second Inauguration of Donald Trump airs Monday, January 20, 2025 on ABC. (ABC/Jose Alvarado, Jr.) Barron Trump](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309359472-58f9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646&h=363&crop=1)
- Drunk Brit, 30, admits pulling down underwear and 'squatting' on packed plane
- Five youngsters who died after crashing into police car pictured
- Twelve arrested after deadly A66 crash that killed seven
Will Raw, chair of the NFU Poultry Board, described the news that the serious outbreak was being linked to eggs from abroad as ‘hugely concerning’.
He said: ‘This undermines the excellent work British egg producers have undertaken over decades, adhering to the highest standards, abiding by rigorous testing and building a world-leading reputation.
‘Food produced to standards that would be illegal in the UK is still being allowed into our market. This simply cannot be allowed to continue.’
Get in touch with our news team by emailing us at webnews@metro.co.uk.
For more stories like this, check our news page.
