summary: An ongoing multi-country outbreak of Salmonella Enteritidis has affected the UK and six other European nations, resulting in one death and 34 hospitalizations in the UK alone. While contaminated imported eggs have been identified as the strongest suspected source by health agencies, recent investigations suggest the outbreak may have also spread to chicken. The UKHSA reports 207 confirmed British cases, with the UK and the Netherlands being hit the hardest.
key_points: A Salmonella Enteritidis outbreak has caused 207 confirmed British cases and one death in the UK.
The outbreak spans seven European countries, with the UK and the Netherlands experiencing the highest impact.
Health investigations point to imported eggs as the suspected source, while Dutch research also indicates chicken meat as a potential source.
The UKHSA states there is currently no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry.
The National Farmers' Union has called for increased government checks on food coming into the country.

title: Antidepressant use in Britain is surging, and it’s not OK
author: James Kirkup
content:
![Taking medicine](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499432917_17875806495170_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Taking medicine](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499432917_17875806495170_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Where does sadness end and depression begin? Why do more and more people report problems with their mental health? Should we give those people drugs, or send them for a walk in the sunshine? Why are British youngsters even more miserable and anxious than those in similar countries?
And can we find a way to deal with the country’s growing mental health problem that is based on kindness and humanity yet still makes better use of public resources and gets more people off welfare into work?
These are crucial, complicated questions that anyone who would lead Britain should try to answer. To help with that, they should read a new book by Norman Lamb, a former health minister.
After leaving Parliament in 2019, Lamb embarked on a second career, thinking seriously about mental health while also confronting its realities as chair of the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust.
His book – Be More Human: Why Mental Health Care is Broken – and What We Can Do to Fix It – is a thoughtful account of how Britain thinks and acts on mental illness and how our services respond to it.
Often that response is poor. Consider antidepressants. In England, the number of antidepressant prescriptions issued rose from 47.3 million in 2011 to 89 million in 2023-24. More than 8.7 million adults are now prescribed them.
For some doctors, that’s no big deal and maybe even a positive – a sign that people are now getting the medication they need, rather than soldiering on and suffering in silence.
But can it really be the case that Britain is almost twice as depressed as it was 15 years ago? That one in six adults are depressed to the point of medication? Or have we become more inclined to reach for medicine to manage distress that is caused by things that are just too hard to fix?
One reason Lamb deserves to be listened to is that he refuses to reach for simple answers to complex questions, instead touring the modern British mental health landscape for real stories – happy and sad – that illustrate the nuance of the issue.
For some critics, the rise of antidepressants is just proof of NHS failure. Others see medical overreach or even the malign influence of pharmaceutical companies. Lamb accepts that antidepressants work for some people and can be vitally important. But why are we prescribing so many of them, and what are we treating? In some cases, the treatment ends up suppressing symptoms instead of addressing root causes.
Lamb describes GPs who have tried doing things differently: finding time to understand why somebody is distressed and making greater use of “social prescribing” – connecting people with exercise, sport, art, music, nature, companionship or community activity. Such approaches aren’t a cure-all, but they do show that there is often an alternative to medication.
The real reason to focus on antidepressants is that the alarming numbers on their use point to the more fundamental question about Britain and mental health: what is causing more and more people to report sadness and distress so severe as to warrant a medical response?
All too often these people are young. Most mental health problems begin in childhood or adolescence, the start of what Lamb calls a “conveyor belt” of despair and failing services delivering people to a life of distress and missed opportunities.
We must stop that conveyor belt, and soon. Otherwise, Britain is on course for a depressive future, because so many of our young people today are troubled and anxious. OECD figures show around a quarter of British 15-year-olds reported low life satisfaction, putting Britain at the bottom of 27 European countries. Among British girls, the proportion was almost one in three.
The troubles of the young are well-documented, often by people offering neat explanations. Depending on which guru you pick, the distress of British children can simply be explained by any one of the following: smartphones; social media; Covid lockdowns; poverty, inequality; racism; family breakdown; bad schools; bad parenting; bad government; a weak economy; the housing market; climate change.
In reality, of course, the truth is complicated and messy. Mental health problems, at both a personal and societal level, are multifactorial. This is where Lamb’s book should start a debate about doing things differently.
Today we have a fractured and incoherent response to a society-wide problem. Parts of the state try to curb and manage children’s access to technology and online content. Other services focus, generally badly, on the health and welfare of the most vulnerable children. Schools are left trying to do everything – educate, counsel, nurture, support – for all children while lacking the time and resource to do any of those things well. And at the end of the conveyor belt, an over-burdened, fragmented and fundamentally reactive NHS is left trying to address the mental health symptoms of causes it cannot ever hope to treat. When that fails, it’s the police, or nothing.
The consequences of systemic failure are not just measured in human suffering. Mental health problems are taking a growing toll on our economy too, removing more people from the workforce, often early in life, and transferring them into the welfare system. Many politicians offer answers to that, promising to tighten the qualifying criteria for mental-health-related benefits. Much harder is explaining and fixing the range of issues that have driven the growth of mental health problems in the first place.
![Close up of palm with pills from pill bottle. Man is sick, taking medication, painkillers, man with cold](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499432921_17875806641290_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Lamb offers suggestions that are worth exploring. He supports the argument that schools should pay more attention to wellbeing rather than measuring success purely through academic attainment. He highlights programmes empowering parents and families of children with poor behaviour. He wants children to have greater access to nature and play. He argues for a reduction in school exclusions, which too often push vulnerable children away from education and towards criminality, addiction and serious mental illness.
More widely, he makes a convincing case for an entirely new mindset on mental health policy, measuring spending not on treatment but on prevention and refocussing local services on supporting relationships: Wigan and Gateshead are pioneers worth studying.
Lamb doesn’t pretend to have all the answers, but his book should prompt some real national reflection. The answer to our national mental health problem won’t be simple, but it must surely involve doing things differently if we are to escape a future of depression and despair. As the old cliché puts it, the definition of insanity is doing the same thing again and expecting different results.
summary: Antidepressant prescriptions in England have surged significantly, raising questions about whether medication is overused to manage distress caused by complex societal issues. A new book by former health minister Norman Lamb examines Britain's mental health crisis, highlighting how services often suppress symptoms rather than address root causes. The article notes that young people in Britain are particularly troubled, with OECD figures showing high rates of low life satisfaction. Lamb argues for a shift toward prevention, better support for families, and alternative approaches like social prescribing to address the nation's growing mental health challenges.
key_points: Antidepressant prescriptions in England rose from 47.3 million in 2011 to 89 million in 2023-24, with over 8.7 million adults now prescribed them.
OECD figures indicate that around a quarter of British 15-year-olds reported low life satisfaction, placing Britain at the bottom of 27 European countries.
Norman Lamb's book, Be More Human, argues that current mental health services are broken and often rely on medication instead of treating root causes.
Alternative approaches, such as social prescribing, connect people with exercise, nature, and community activities as an alternative to drugs.
Lamb suggests focusing mental health policy on prevention, supporting families, prioritizing wellbeing in schools, and refocussing local services.

title: Largest review of its kind confirms benefits of tai chi and other Chinese exercises
author: Andrew Gregory
content:
Traditional Chinese exercises such as tai chi can offer wide-ranging benefits for people with musculoskeletal disorders, improving physical function, pain, mental health, sleep quality and bone mineral density, according to the largest review of its kind.
More than 1.7bn people have musculoskeletal conditions worldwide. While prevalence varies by age and diagnosis, people of all ages in every country and every continent are affected.
Musculoskeletal conditions significantly limit mobility and dexterity, leading to early retirement from work, lower levels of wellbeing and reduced ability to participate in society. They are also the leading contributor to disability worldwide, with low back pain being the single leading cause of disability in 160 countries.
There was already evidence indicating traditional Chinese exercises were associated with beneficial health outcomes in people with musculoskeletal disorders, but much of it was fragmented and contained inconsistencies.
The overarching review of pooled data analyses of systematic reviews by researchers at hospitals and universities in China, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, drew on 92 data syntheses from 1,744 randomised controlled clinical trials.
It found “high certainty evidence” for the effectiveness of traditional Chinese exercise – such as tai chi, qigong, baduanjin, wuqinxi and yijinjing – for a range of health outcomes for people with musculoskeletal disorders.
These included improving movement in knee osteoarthritis, mental health associated with neck pain and knee osteoarthritis, and sleep quality associated with fibromyalgia.
Tai chi, in particular, significantly eased chronic musculoskeletal pain and stiffness in several conditions while increasing bone mineral density in participants with osteopenia or osteoporosis, the research found.
Maximum benefits were achieved when people did these exercises for longer than six months, at least three times a week, clocking up a total of at least 150 minutes a week.
“This comprehensive [umbrella review] provides a definitive, high-level evidence synthesis supporting [traditional Chinese exercises] as effective interventions for a range of musculoskeletal conditions],” the researchers concluded.
“The evidence, particularly for tai chi, reaches high certainty for improving key outcomes such as physical function in knee osteoarthritis, mental health in neck pain, sleep in fibromyalgia and bone density in osteoporosis.”
The findings suggested traditional Chinese exercises should be included in clinical guidelines and rehabilitation programmes worldwide, the researchers added.
“[These] exercises represent a safe, accessible, and cost-effective strategy that can complement conventional therapies, reduce pharmacological reliance, and empower patients in self-management.”
While the prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions increases with age, younger people are also affected, often during their peak income-earning years.
And with global population growth and ageing, the number of people living with musculoskeletal conditions and associated health problems is rapidly increasing.
“For healthcare systems and policymakers, promoting the adoption of traditional Chinese exercises, particularly in community and primary care settings, could be a strategic component of public health initiatives aimed at healthy ageing and chronic disease prevention,” the researchers said.
summary: The largest review of its kind, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, confirms that traditional Chinese exercises like tai chi provide significant health benefits for people with musculoskeletal disorders. Analyzing data from 1,744 trials, researchers found high-certainty evidence that these practices improve physical function, pain, mental health, sleep quality, and bone mineral density. Maximum benefits were observed when participants practiced for more than six months, at least three times a week, totaling 150 minutes or more per week.
key_points: Traditional Chinese exercises improve outcomes such as knee osteoarthritis movement, neck and knee pain mental health, and fibromyalgia sleep quality.
Tai chi significantly eases chronic musculoskeletal pain and stiffness while increasing bone mineral density in osteopenia or osteoporosis patients.
Maximum health benefits require exercising for over six months, at least three times a week, for a minimum of 150 minutes weekly.
Researchers recommend incorporating these safe, cost-effective exercises into global clinical guidelines, rehabilitation programs, and public health initiatives.

title: Vaping could lead to health harm in children and young people, doctors warn
author: Hugh Pym; Olivia Ireland
content:
![A young fair-haired woman wearing a grey hooded sweatshirt and white T shirt is standing in a kitchen with vape and mobile phone in her hands](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/ae91/live/be34ef00-9bfc-11f1-bbc9-198f60b94eaf.jpg)
- Published
Vaping could lead to health harms in children and young people and should be made "less attractive" to them, doctors have said.
The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) has reviewed about 81 studies into vaping and said it is linked to higher rates of breathing problems and evidence of harm in babies whose mothers used vapes while pregnant.
The review said vaping should not be seen as a "harmless part of growing up".
The RCPCH is calling on the UK government to go further in its proposals to place new restrictions around the sale of vapes and suggests limiting the number of flavours that are available.
The review into vapes has been published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood. Experts from the college looked at the studies involving health or social outcomes of vaping on children and young people.
It said vaping had an association with problems including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.
Co-author of the systematic review, Prof Will Carroll, said the evidence showed "clear links" with respiratory symptoms, nicotine dependence and subsequent cigarette smoking.
"We must act to make vaping less attractive and accessible to children," he said.
Vice-president for policy of the RCPCH, Dr Mike McKean, added: "Vaping is still a relatively new product, and there is much we do not yet know about its long-term impact on children and young people but a clear and concerning picture is emerging."
"We need to keep pace with a rapidly evolving market and continue to take action to protect children from nicotine products."
In July, the government launched a 12-week consultation on the appearance, packaging and display of vapes with the aim of reducing the appeal of the products to children.
As part of the new proposals, packs would need to be plain with strict limits on branding and only simple flavour descriptions like "apple" or "cola" used.
Other restrictions would move vapes out of sight in shops, similar to how cigarettes and tobacco are currently sold.
The 100-day consultation follows the recent passing of the Tobacco and Vapes Act,, external which sets out proposals to create the UK's first smoke-free generation.
Children aged 17 or younger now face a lifelong ban on buying cigarettes, since it will be illegal for shops to sell tobacco to anyone born after 1 January 2009.
Dr McKean said the new act was "an important step towards protecting children from nicotine addiction, but it must not be seen as a one-and-done solution".
Prof Carroll said the government needed "to go further and limit the types of flavours available to them as opposed to just their descriptions".
![A photo of many bright, multicoloured vapes in different shapes and sizes.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/f2b3/live/aaac8d00-7b93-11f1-897a-ebe8a20106d3.jpg)
Ministers say they are consulting on proposals to crack down on packaging of vapes that appeal to children
According to a poll for the charity Action on Smoking and Health (Ash), almost one in five 11 to 17-year-olds in Britain have tried vaping,
Ash chief executive Hazel Cheeseman said: "The evidence remains clear that vaping is less harmful than smoking but is not risk free."
She said: "As it was with tobacco, strong controls on marketing and promotion will be key to reducing youth vaping."
Andrew McCracken from the charity Asthma + Lung UK said: "Vapes can play an important role for current smokers looking to quit, but anyone who doesn't smoke, shouldn't vape, and that is especially true for children."
The Department of Health and Social Care said "children should never vape and this evidence shows just some of the risks associated".
A spokesperson said: "We have already banned single-use vapes and have legislated to ban advertising and sponsorship from next year too.
"We're also consulting on proposals to crack down on packaging that appeals to children."
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/b804/live/8df619c0-9c62-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
![A thin, grey banner promoting the News Daily newsletter. On the right, there is a graphic of an orange sphere with two concentric crescent shapes around it in a red-orange gradient, like a sound wave. The banner reads: âThe latest news in your inbox first thing.â](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/73ad/live/179bc000-9c61-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
summary: The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health has warned that vaping poses significant health risks to children and young people, linking it to breathing problems, nicotine dependence, and other health issues. Following a review of roughly 81 studies, doctors are urging the UK government to implement stricter regulations, including limiting available vape flavors and reducing the appeal of packaging. While acknowledging vapes can help adult smokers quit, experts emphasize that non-smokers and children should avoid them.
key_points: A review of about 81 studies by the RCPCH linked youth vaping to breathing difficulties, nicotine dependence, and potential harm to babies whose mothers vaped during pregnancy.
Experts are calling on the UK government to go further than current proposals by actively limiting the types of vape flavors available.
The UK government previously launched a consultation on plain packaging and moving vapes out of sight in shops to reduce their appeal to minors.
Data from an ASH poll indicates that nearly one in five children aged 11 to 17 in Britain have tried vaping.

title: Cheltenham's new Â£12m cancer centre reaches 'significant milestone'
author: Duncan Cook
content:
![A computer generated image showing plans for a new cancer care centre. It shows the outside of a building with brown bricks, a number of windows and a door. There are two benches outside in a garden with two seat sat on one on the benches and a person being pushed in a wheelchair along a path](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/6e3f/live/92f18ef0-9fb4-11f1-bff6-57f1422ebb0b.jpg)
Therapeutic gardens will be created as part of The Big Space
- Published
Proposals for a new Â£12m cancer care centre have reached a "significant milestone" after planning permission was approved.
About Â£9.8m has already been raised for the new centre at Cheltenham General Hospital, which will include modern consulting rooms, access to digital consultations and a therapeutic garden.
Kevin McNamara, the hospital's chief executive, said it was a "significant milestone" to secure the planning approval.
Cancer patient Gillian Hayward, from Wotton-Under-Edge, is one of the 10,000 people who has donated towards the project, she said: "When someone is telling you how your life is going to change, you want to be in a place where you feel safe, comfortable and secure."
More from Gloucestershire
Hayward added she wanted to support the appeal to say thank-you to "the fabulous people who saved my life twice".
The project is mainly being funded by the Cheltenham and Gloucester Hospitals Charity.
A charity spokesperson said some patients had described the current oncology department's rooms as "small and dark", with clinicians sometimes having to sit on beds when discussing patients' health and futures.
The new centre will include light and spacious consultation rooms, with indoor and outdoor space that offers patients places to think and reflect.
Richard Smith, the charity's associate director, thanked the "amazing community" for their fundraising efforts.
"We are closer than ever to transforming cancer care for our patients and their families, as well as our incredible NHS teams, we are so grateful," Smith said.
summary: Planning permission has been approved for a new £12m cancer care centre at Cheltenham General Hospital, marking a significant milestone for the project. The facility, primarily funded by the Cheltenham and Gloucester Hospitals Charity with about £9.8m already raised, aims to replace small and dark rooms with light, spacious consultation areas and therapeutic gardens. The new centre is supported by thousands of donors, including cancer patients and local community members.
key_points: Planning permission has been granted for the new £12m cancer care centre at Cheltenham General Hospital.
Approximately £9.8m has already been raised toward the project, which is mainly funded by the Cheltenham and Gloucester Hospitals Charity.
The new facility will feature modern consulting rooms, digital consultation access, and indoor and outdoor therapeutic spaces.
Current oncology rooms were described by patients as small and dark, highlighting the need for the upgraded environment.

title: How do you vaccinate 1,000 tiny penguins against bird flu in the wild? It’s ‘really tricky’ but there is a way
author: Petra Stock
content:
More than 1,000 little penguins have received their first dose of bird flu vaccine in Victoria, in what is believed to be the world’s largest vaccination program involving wild birds.
Catherine Basterfield, the chief executive of Phillip Island Nature Parks, said vaccinations began early last week and were ramping up.
“This is the first time anyone around the world has attempted something like this at this scale,” she said.
“It is really tricky and penguins are difficult to handle, but we have very well trained people.
“The penguins come up the beach, they’re able to trap them in a little pen, and then move them into smaller pens to be able to then go through the vaccination administration process.”
About 5,000 birds across Phillip Island and St Kilda would receive two doses of the H5N1 vaccine, an effort that was only possible because penguins returned to the same burrows each night.
“Everybody loves little penguins,” said the state’s environment minister, Jaclyn Symes. “They’re an iconic little creature, they’re adorable, but they have a significant economic value to this region and to the state of Victoria.”
In recent nights, about 300 penguins were weighed, measured and microchipped, before being vaccinated and released. Those same birds would receive a second dose in three weeks’ time.
![Phillip Island Nature Parks rangers administer an injection](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/7a66c6f5f1550ae091ae3f14f357d8440dd54afd/0_0_5600_3733/master/5600.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Little penguins are the world’s smallest species of penguin – about a ruler’s length in height – and found only in southern Australia and New Zealand. The birds, which are not listed as threatened under federal environment laws, are considered at “very high risk” from the deadly bird flu, according to a national risk assessment.
The population on Phillip Island is about 40,000 birds. The island’s “penguin parade” is a major tourist attraction, drawing about 700,000 visitors each year and contributing about $500m to the state’s economy.
![People arrive at the viewing platforms on Phillip Island.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6f81d5194fa90121656d6c8f8f774bc947f0f167/0_0_7755_5170/master/7755.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The large-scale wildlife vaccination program was announced by the Victorian government on 12 August, with vaccines supplied by the federal agriculture department.
Positive bird flu cases on Phillip Island, including one in a little penguin, have increased the sense of urgency, with the team working to vaccinate as many as possible over the coming weeks.
after newsletter promotion
![Rangers are weighing, microchipping, scanning and vaccinating penguins as part of the H5N1 bird flu vaccination program at Phillip Island.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5c46b38b997575ffa85753c03d2b9b4aaefe301d/0_0_5600_3733/master/5600.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
South Australia also reported a confirmed case in a little penguin on Kangaroo Island on Sunday. On King Island in Tasmania, 51 of the animals died, with the deaths presumed to have been caused by bird flu, after one sample tested positive.
An Arthur Rylah Institute report published last year said it would take 10 weeks for penguins to reach peak immunity, and that administering vaccines after H5N1 arrived could be “too late, because significant mortality is likely to occur before adequate vaccine coverage is achieved”. In a worst-case scenario, the report said, up to 16,000 little penguins could die.
A federal agriculture spokesperson said vaccination was “one tool” that could reduce the impact on vulnerable native birds, but was “not a standalone solution”. “It does not replace effective biosecurity, which remains critical.”
![Little penguins roam in their enclosure at Summerlands in Philip Island.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a054dec81fd89542baf377e906c1470f37b18036/0_0_6594_4396/master/6594.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
James Todd, Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, said vaccines weren’t a “silver bullet”, and wouldn’t be suitable for many of the hundreds of other wild species at risk from the virus.
“In the case of little penguins, we know that they are at risk from H5, they’re a colonial species that nest together. They are a seabird that will come in contact with other seabirds that carry the virus. And we also know that they’re an iconic species that have high value to Victorians.”
Dr John Cockrem, an emeritus professor at Massey University in New Zealand, who researches little penguins, said H5 bird flu was an added threat to the species, which were already affected by severe storms, sea level rise and changes in food availability due to the climate crisis.
“So avian flu then is a threat that has arisen and comes on top of other threats that the little penguins are facing, and will increasingly face in coming years.”
summary: More than 1,000 little penguins in Victoria have received their first dose of an H5N1 bird flu vaccine in what is believed to be the world's largest wild bird vaccination program. Officials plan to administer two doses to about 5,000 birds across Phillip Island and St Kilda because the penguins return to the same burrows each night, making them accessible to rangers. While the species is considered at very high risk from the deadly virus, experts emphasize that vaccination is only one tool and not a standalone solution for wildlife protection.
key_points: Over 1,000 little penguins in Victoria have received their first H5N1 vaccine dose in a world-first large-scale wild bird vaccination effort.
About 5,000 penguins across Phillip Island and St Kilda are targeted to receive two doses of the vaccine.
The vaccination program is aided by the fact that little penguins return to the same burrows each night, allowing rangers to trap and handle them.
Little penguins face high risks from bird flu in addition to other environmental threats such as climate change and severe storms.
Officials and experts note that vaccination is a helpful tool but not a standalone solution or silver bullet for managing the virus.

title: Mum says painful condition 'overlooked' during pregnancy
author: Brett Tremble
content:
![A young baby wearing an orange onesie is held up to her mother's face as the two exchange smiles](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/ea56/live/9ec4ca90-9e2d-11f1-bed9-2f55a7feabfd.jpg)
Grace, 28, from Manchester, started noticing how "physically taxing" her pregnancy had become
- Published
A mum who suffered from pre-eclampsia during pregnancy said she felt her symptoms were "overlooked" due to her underlying sickle cell disease.
Grace, 28, from Manchester, was in her second trimester when she started noticing how "physically taxing" her pregnancy had become including "extreme pain".
It was only when she was admitted to St Mary's Hospital in Manchester with a sickle cell disease (SCD) unit that she was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy-related condition that can cause high blood pressure, and went on to have an emergency Caesarean.
She has called for urgent research and more awareness of SCD so people do not suffer the same trauma ordeal she did.
She said: "It's not often you get pre-eclampsia present itself and not be flagged up.
"It was just something that was so overlooked that any symptom that was raised or any issue that was raised, they just put it down to sickle cell."
A spokesperson from Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust said: "We are proud to see Grace share her story to help raise awareness of sickle cell disease.
"Grace has been working closely with us in collaborative efforts to improve awareness of the condition within the wider health system."
During Grace's pregnancy she was under the care of various services, including midwifery teams in Accrington, Burnley and Blackburn.
She was treated by Blackburn Hospital for SCD and was later transferred to a specialist sickle cell unit at St Mary's Hospital in Manchester, where she remained as an inpatient until giving birth.
Due to having the condition, Grace believes a lot of her symptoms were overlooked until she was transferred to St Mary's Hospital, where doctors discovered that she was suffering from the SCD-related condition known as pre-eclampsia.
Pregnancy with SCD is high-risk and carries an increased risk of serious conditions. It is the fastest-growing inherited blood and genetic condition in the UK and can cause severe pain and other complications including shortness of breath, strokes and vision problems.
By the time that Grace's symptoms were eventually diagnosed her condition was so bad that she needed to have an emergency Caesarean section.
Her daughter Lana is now two, and while she does not have sickle cell disease herself she has inherited the trait for it.
Grace has urged women to speak to their doctors if they have any concerns.
"I cannot emphasise strongly enough how much we need more research into sickle cell disease, funding into sickle cell disease, and understanding of the disease itself," she said.
"It's so much more important now that we raise as much awareness as possible to help people understand what this condition is and how it presents itself."
She continued: "I just want women who are sickle-celled to know really, that if you are pregnant or planning to have a baby, be very, very prepared that you may experience a higher rate of crises than is normally expected, and if you feel like anything isn't right, vocalise it.
"You are your own advocate, no one can advocate for you like yourself," she said.
Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust said: "We are glad Grace is using her experience to raise awareness of sickle cell disease.
"We continue to be one of the region's only trusts providing this specialist care, with our teams at Manchester Royal Infirmary and Royal Manchester Children's Hospital also delivering specialist services for sickle cell patients."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio Manchester on Sounds and follow BBC Manchester on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230.
summary: A Manchester mother has spoken out after her pre-eclampsia symptoms were allegedly overlooked during pregnancy because medical staff attributed them to her underlying sickle cell disease. Grace experienced extreme pain during her second trimester and was eventually diagnosed with pre-eclampsia only after being admitted to a specialist sickle cell unit at St Mary's Hospital, where she underwent an emergency Caesarean. She is now calling for urgent research, increased funding, and better awareness of sickle cell disease to prevent similar trauma for other women.
key_points: Grace felt her pre-eclampsia symptoms were dismissed and attributed entirely to her sickle cell disease during pregnancy.
Her condition was diagnosed after she was transferred to St Mary's Hospital in Manchester, leading to an emergency Caesarean section.
Sickle cell disease is a high-risk, fast-growing inherited blood and genetic condition in the UK that can cause severe complications.
Grace is advocating for increased research, funding, and awareness regarding sickle cell disease.
She encourages pregnant women with the condition to be prepared and to vocalize any concerns they have.

title: People urged to get tested for syphilis in Swansea Bay health board area
author: Danielle Herbert
content:
![Blood sample tube for syphilis test analysis.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b375/live/9d4643f0-9fb9-11f1-b703-13ae65ccf6b5.jpg)
Swansea Bay University Health Board have said they continue to see higher levels of syphilis than many other areas of Wales
- Published
People in an area of Wales with some of the highest rates of syphilis are being urged to get tested for the sexually transmitted infection.
Swansea Bay University Health Board have said they continue to see higher levels of syphilis than many other areas of Wales.
Advanced Nurse Practitioner Carly Porter said: "Anyone who is sexually active can be affected and we have seen cases in people aged from 17 to 70 plus."
Syphilis, external is a bacterial infection that can be cured with antibiotics but many people experience no symptoms at all, meaning infections can go undetected and be passed on unknowingly.
Advanced nurse practitioner Carly Porter said: "As far as I am concerned, the sooner you test, the sooner you are diagnosed and the sooner you are treated."
The health board said providing access to free and confidential testing regularly is the most effective way to lower transmission rates, along with general prevention work to help reduces the spread of the infection.
![Carly is holding up posters advertising testing for syphilis. She is wearing dark purple medical scrubs and a rainbow NHS lanyard around her neck. She has short curly blonde hair and is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/3631/live/23fcb220-9fbb-11f1-9828-47742d0f1032.jpg)
"If you are concerned, get tested, even if you don't have symptoms. This helps us to identify cases, start treatment and reduce the spread", said Advanced Nurse Practitioner Carly Porter
Porter believes many people are not aware syphilis can be contracted via oral sex alone.
Early symptoms can include a rash on the palm of your hands, the soles of your feet, or on your chest or stomach.
Small painless ulcers might affect genital area but can also be found in other areas of the body. You may also experience swollen lymph nodes.
"Education is important, as is destigmatising syphilis," said Porter.
"What we want is for people to have sex safely. Using condoms is a brilliant start. But if you are concerned, get tested, even if you don't have symptoms. This helps us to identify cases, start treatment and reduce the spread.
Porter said negative results are just as important as the positive.
"If you test now and get a negative result that's a good benchmark because if you test again and get a positive result, we will have an idea of how long you have had the infection," she added.
![Side view close-up of pregnant woman touching her belly.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/982/cpsprodpb/fe9b/live/6b9a15f0-9fc5-11f1-b3e7-331c6d9a8046.png)
Nurses at Swansea Bay University Health Board continue to see high rates of cases, including pregnant women
Senior public health practitioner Sarah Johnson said cases of syphilis have risen steadily across Wales over the last decade.
Across the UK, diagnoses have reached their highest level since 1948, external.
"We have seen a slight drop in cases over the past two years in Swansea Bay, but Carly and her colleagues still see a lot of patients, including pregnant women, which is why we want to start the conversation," said Sarah.
Syphilis can be passed from mother to baby, external, known as congenital syphilis and can increase the risk of miscarriage, premature birth and stillbirth.
Pregnant women are offered screening for syphilis so it can be found and treated before it causes any serious problems.
More top stories
- ![Emily pictured outdoors in a natural setting, wearing a pale pink top against a backdrop of softly blurred greenery.
She has shoulder length blonde hair with a fringe coming down to her blue eyes.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/5c42/live/ea1f8de0-9e1e-11f1-bc51-19e4b5ccc0f6.jpg)
  - Published2 days ago
 ![Four semi-detached modern homes at the end of a street. There are solar panels on the roof and wooden cladding on the top of the buildings. Each home is painted a different colour. They are grown, green, yellow and grey.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c3e5/live/6a091240-9def-11f1-898b-91bf436c749f.jpg)
  - Published3 hours ago
 ![People wearing coats and backpacks queue to reach the top of a mountain, against the backdrop of a blue sky.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7191/live/600d5190-9f7d-11f1-994f-5b14ccb35057.jpg)
summary: People in the Swansea Bay health board area are being urged to get tested for syphilis as the region continues to report higher infection levels than many other parts of Wales. Health officials emphasize that the bacterial infection can be cured with antibiotics, but many infected individuals experience no symptoms at all. Cases have affected individuals ranging from 17 to over 70 years old, including pregnant women, prompting health workers to encourage regular testing and safe sex practices to lower transmission rates.
key_points: Swansea Bay University Health Board continues to see higher levels of syphilis compared to many other areas in Wales.
Syphilis is a bacterial infection that can be cured with antibiotics, but it often presents no symptoms and can go undetected.
Health officials note that cases span a wide age range, from 17 to over 70, and include pregnant women.
The infection can be contracted through oral sex alone, and early symptoms can include rashes and painless ulcers.
Pregnant women are offered screening because untreated syphilis can be passed to a baby and cause miscarriage, premature birth, or stillbirth.

title: After 100 days of the deadliest Ebola outbreak, it can be stopped. Here’s how | Jean Kaseya and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
author: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
content:
Each time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we go first to listen. In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas.
Their message was direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They were right.
Ebola spreads through communities – and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it.
They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response will move faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.
![An African man in a pale blue suit sits on a rostrum by the green flag of the African Union](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/909507d1791e0a05317e2d0939167793531e6d11/0_0_4000_2667/master/4000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The government of the DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak 100 days ago after confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus.
The outbreak has since become the deadliest ever recorded, with about 2,500 deaths.
Behind this unprecedented toll are families grieving and communities confronting Ebola alongside conflict, displacement and fragile access to care.
At the centre of it all are the people who show up every day. Health workers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.
They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure areas.
Some have contracted Ebola in the line of duty; some have paid with their lives.
Their service must be met with action: protection, training, reliable equipment, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to vaccination, testing and treatment. Their safety is central to stopping transmission.
The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.
Uganda has interrupted transmission and declared the end of its outbreak, proving the Bundibugyo Ebola virus can be stopped. Decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities broke the chains of transmission.
The emergency continues in the DRC. Cases are still being detected outside known contact lists. Each one points to a chain that has not yet been found. Every delay gives the virus another opportunity to spread.
The next phase must reach the village.
The DRC’s village-centred strategy takes the response to the places where transmission occurs. Surveillance, testing, treatment, vaccination, infection prevention and community engagement must operate together, close to affected families. Teams need the authority and resources to act quickly.
This is how we stop Ebola at its source: identify infection early, isolate and care for patients safely, follow every contact and prevent the next transmission.
Community leadership will determine whether this works. Women’s groups, young people, religious leaders, traditional healers, survivors and community health workers know where families seek care, how information moves and where trust is weakening. They can identify concerns early, challenge dangerous rumours and help response teams reach people who may otherwise remain invisible.
Their knowledge must shape the response. When they raise concerns, they must see action.
Trust is earned through delivery. A family that reports a suspected case needs safe transport and immediate care. A community that supports vaccination needs clear information about what the vaccine can do. Families who lose loved ones need dignity, compassion and support through safe burial procedures.
![An older Ethiopian man with the World Health Organization logo behind him](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f198a8b570bb5bc9d63442f4881f8fa667dc3fd6/0_0_4709_3139/master/4709.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Health facilities also require urgent protection. As of 18 August, 163 health workers have been infected and 47 have died in the DRC, while Uganda has recorded four health worker infections. Every facility needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water and sanitation.
An infection in a health facility places workers, patients and families at risk. A protected health facility becomes a centre for early detection, safe care and public confidence.
Financing remains a decisive test. Governments and partners have made commitments that must now reach the response.
National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, vaccination, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.
Delayed financing costs lives; fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both.
Cross-border coordination must remain strong. People move to trade, work, study, seek care and support families. Countries need rapid information-sharing, aligned surveillance and prepared health facilities along major routes.
The first 100 days have made the priorities clear: find every case; follow every contact; protect every frontline worker; bring testing, treatment and vaccination closer to every affected community. Turn every pledge into action.
Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, alongside neighbouring countries, communities and partners, to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally led response.
This outbreak can be ended. Uganda has shown what focused leadership and community action can achieve. The DRC can do the same.
summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo is facing its deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, with about 2,500 deaths 100 days after it was declared. Stopping the virus requires centering the response around affected communities, protecting frontline health workers, and providing predictable financing. Uganda has successfully interrupted its transmission, proving that decisive leadership and community cooperation can end the outbreak.
key_points: The DRC's 17th Ebola outbreak has caused about 2,500 deaths in 100 days, making it the deadliest ever recorded.
Community leadership and local knowledge are essential for early detection, contact tracing, and building trust.
Frontline health workers face severe risks, with 163 infected and 47 dead in the DRC as of 18 August.
Uganda successfully interrupted transmission and ended its outbreak through decisive leadership and community cooperation.
Predictable financing, protection for health facilities, and a village-centred strategy are critical to stopping the virus at its source.

title: South West animal attractions open despite bluetongue outbreak
author: Cameron Weldon; Alison Stephenson
content:
![A close up sheep which is looking away from the camera. It is stood in a grass field.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/9b69/live/ffd26810-9e69-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Paignton and Newquay Zoos are among many attractions which had precautions against the virus
- Published
It is "business as usual" for zoos and animal attractions across the South West despite an ongoing bluetongue outbreak among livestock.
Attractions including Paignton and Newquay Zoos, Totnes Rare Breeds Farm and The Big Sheep, near Ilfracombe, said they had all taken precautions and vaccinated their animals most at risk from the insect-borne viral disease.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) confirmed zoos and attractions could stay open because there was no risk to visitors.
So far this year there have been cases recorded of the bluetongue virus (BTV) at 556 sites in the UK, including 327 in Devon and 110 in Cornwall, according to latest government figures, external.
![A close up picture of a cow eating at a farm trough. It is looking at the camera while there are two others with their heads down eating.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/51a0/live/60912ea0-9e6c-11f1-bd18-3f8c7915b51c.jpg)
Bluetongue can affect sheep, cattle, deer, goats and camelids
BTV affects cattle, goats, sheep, deer and camelids, with signs including fever, lameness, facial swelling, nasal discharge and mouth ulcers.
While it can be potentially fatal for livestock, the virus does not affect humans or food safety.
Lisa Britton, head of living collections at Paignton Zoo in Devon, said the virus was "not something that would or should affect our footfall" and sheep and yaks on the site had been vaccinated.
She said sheep were regularly tested for tuberculosis (TB) and were used to being jabbed, whereas some of the other animals would need to be trained to willingly take the vaccine and that could be one or two doses annually for bluetongue.
'Monitor the situation'
Britton said there was a programme of vaccination being looked into at the zoo for potential risk species.
Potentially infected animals would not have to isolate because the virus could not be spread through direct contact like saliva or nose to nose, she added.
Britton said the virus had not been reported in exotic animals but the zoo was liaising with its teams and colleagues across Europe and adhering to Animal and Plant Health Agency guidelines.
A spokesperson for Defra said it "recognised how concerning bluetongue is for animal keepers" and it was working to put in processes to bring in additional vaccine supplies, whilst urging keepers and vets to place orders to ensure access.
"There is a wide range of support available to help keepers protect their livestock and we will continue to monitor the situation closely."
Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.
summary: Zoos and animal attractions across the South West of England are remaining open during an ongoing bluetongue virus outbreak among livestock. Attractions like Paignton and Newquay Zoos have implemented precautions, including vaccinating vulnerable animals. Defra confirmed that the attractions can safely stay open because the virus poses no risk to humans or food safety.
key_points: Bluetongue virus cases have been recorded at 556 sites in the UK.
The virus affects livestock such as cattle, sheep, goats, deer, and camelids, but does not affect humans.
Paignton and Newquay Zoos, Totnes Rare Breeds Farm, and The Big Sheep have taken precautions and vaccinated at-risk animals.
Defra confirmed that attractions could remain open as there is no risk to visitors.
Infected animals do not need to isolate because the virus cannot be spread through direct contact.

title: Charity donates skincare to radiotherapy patients in Northampton
author: Sam Read
content:
![A dark glass table is at the centre of the picture. On top of the table are white and blue pots, tubs and bottles of skin care products. Seven adults and one child are standing around the table looking at the camera. Some are wearing hospital uniform, three are wearing white t-shirts. They appear to be in a radiotherapy room with a large piece of medical equipment behind them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/ef78/live/7a7e0a50-9d49-11f1-a3dc-c3f8cfe34ff8.jpg)
Niven Whatley (third left), received care from the radiotherapy team at Northampton General Hospital
- Published
A co-founder of a charity has donated about 100 skincare products to cancer patients at the hospital where he received radiotherapy treatment.
Niven Whatley, who established the charity Ailsa's Aim, based in Olney, Buckinghamshire, was admitted to Northampton General Hospital with bowel cancer in May.
Radiotherapy patients can have skin reactions to targeted radiation treatment including itching, irritation and soreness.
Whatley said while undergoing treatment he experienced "uncomfortable" skin irritation which meant he could not forget about the therapy even at other times of the day.
Whatley said the radiotherapy treatment, which he has now finished, was "scary", but providing the products to the hospital was "a ray of sunshine and a bit of normality".
He added he was still receiving cancer treatment and hoped the products would help break down any "taboo" for other patients.
![The picture shows the top half of a man on the right of the image smiling looking at the camera. He has his hands on the shoulder of a girl who is looking at the camera and you can see head and shoulders of. They are standing in a corridor with white walls. Behind them you can see a light brown door with a window in it, a window covered by a blind and part of a notice board.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7ae7/live/68f43460-9d82-11f1-adf5-2dc21c9cc109.jpg)
Niven Whatley co-founded the charity shortly after the birth of his daughter Ailsa
His wife and co-founder Sara Whatley said: "During radiotherapy treatment, skincare becomes incredibly important, yet many specialist products are expensive and out of reach for people already facing the financial impact of a cancer diagnosis."
The couple set up Ailsa's Aim in 2020, to support cancer patients and families who have babies in neonatal care after Sara received a cancer diagnosis while pregnant with her daughter Ailsa, now seven.
The products, which include moisturisers, cleansers and toners, have been donated as part of a trial to better understand patient needs and how the products can be used alongside others that the hospital can prescribe.
Jane Wilkinson, the hospital radiotherapy manager, said: "[The products] will provide some additional skincare support at a difficult time for patients and because they are free it will ease some of the financial strains people experience around their cancer diagnoses and treatment."
Do you have a story suggestion for Northamptonshire? Contact us below.
summary: Niven Whatley, co-founder of the charity Ailsa's Aim, has donated about 100 skincare products to radiotherapy patients at Northampton General Hospital, where he previously received cancer treatment. Whatley experienced uncomfortable skin irritation during his own therapy and hopes the donation will help others. The hospital is using the products as part of a trial to support patients and ease financial strain.
key_points: Ailsa's Aim donated approximately 100 skincare products to Northampton General Hospital.
Co-founder Niven Whatley was treated for bowel cancer at the hospital and experienced uncomfortable skin reactions from radiotherapy.
Specialist skincare products can be expensive for patients facing the financial impact of a cancer diagnosis.
The products are part of a trial to better understand patient needs and complement hospital-prescribed treatments.

title: St Neots girl gets brain tumour diagnosis 12 hours after eye test
author: Aimee Dexter
content:
![Phoebe is laying on a hospital bed with white sheets. She has ginger hair in a loose ponytail and has a bandage on her arm. She is wearing pink striped pyjamas and is hugging a pink teddy bear.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1056/cpsprodpb/5eec/live/d099d0e0-9cae-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Phoebe had two surgeries within 72 hours of her brain tumour diagnosis
- Published
A mum said she "fell apart" after finding out her four-year-old daughter had a brain tumour, just 12 hours after an eye test.
Katie, 41, said her daughter Phoebe, now five, started to be sick and was getting severe headaches in February, but was told "it was just migraines" by a GP.
Following an eye test in May, Katie was called by the optician who told her to take her daughter straight to A&E at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. Just hours later, she was diagnosed with a brain tumour.
"I fell apart and just sobbed and sobbed," said the mum from St Neots, Cambridgeshire. Thankfully, Phoebe's tumour was not cancerous and she is now under the care of specialists.
Katie said: "I felt like we were probably wasting the hospital's time because Phoebe was running around playing like normal but, looking back, she was probably the sickest kid there.
"I kept thinking, how am I going to tell her dad and the other children?
"I kept asking if Phoebe would survive but the doctors said they were unable to answer that at that time, which is the worst thing in the world as a parent."
![Phoebe is laying on a hospital bed with white sheets. She has ginger hair in a ponytail and has a bandage on her arm. She is wearing patterned pyjamas and has her thumbs up.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/7e55/live/0627fd90-9caf-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Remarkably, Phoebe went back to school three weeks after her surgeries
The day after her diagnosis, Phoebe had her first surgery where a drain was inserted to relieve the pressure on her brain, caused by a build-up of cerebrospinal fluid.
She underwent a second surgery the day after that, with surgeons removing most of the tumour during a 10-hour procedure, where it was confirmed to be a pilocytic astrocytoma.
Astrocytomas are the most common type of brain and spinal cord tumour in children and are also known as gliomas, according to Cancer Research UK, external.
It said about 175 children were diagnosed with an astrocytoma each year in the UK.
![A selfie of Phoebe and Katie who are next to each other. Phoebe, on the left, has shoulder length ginger hair and is wearing a gold crown. Katie, on the right, has brown hair and is wearing a black T-shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/45e2/live/f40dbe60-9cae-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Katie said her daughter "was incredible" during and after her surgeries
Katie told BBC Radio Cambridgeshire: "Within three weeks of coming out of hospital she was back at school part-time, and by the end of the term we managed to get into school full-time again."
Phoebe's progress is now being monitored.
She will have her first follow-up MRI scan in November, and is likely to need one every six months until post-puberty or into her early adulthood, as the condition is hormone-related.
If MRI results are positive, Phoebe is unlikely to need further care, but if the tumour returns she would most likely be suitable for targeted treatment.
More stories from Cambridgeshire
![Phoebe is standing in front of a brick wall. She has ginger hair in a ponytail and is wearing a pink T-shirt. She is holding her thumbs up and smiling.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/5393/live/1046ffc0-9cb8-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Phoebe now wears glasses "which are mega strong, but she's very comfortable wearing them", said her mum
Speaking of Phoebe's resilience, Katie said: "She is incredible.
"If the opticians hadn't spotted us or told us straight away, who knows what would happen."
Katie added that she wanted to "bring more awareness" to getting children's eyes tested.
"She now wears glasses which are mega strong, but she's very comfortable wearing them.
"If it's just that she now has bad eyesight and wears glasses, then so be it."
After the diagnosis, Katie started to work for the charity Brain Tumour Research, and has been calling on the government to increase spending on science.
"Funding for research into brain tumours is so important because this really could happen to anyone," she said.
"You never think something like this will happen to you, but it does."
The Department of Health and Social Care said it was establishing a "national Brain Tumour Research Consortium" and announced a Â£13.7m investment to support research to develop new treatments.
Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below.
summary: A four-year-old girl from St Neots was diagnosed with a non-cancerous brain tumour just 12 hours after an optician recommended she go straight to A&E. Following two surgeries within 72 hours, including a 10-hour procedure to remove most of the tumour, she remarkably returned to school part-time three weeks later. Her recovery is now being monitored with regular MRI scans, and her mother has begun working for Brain Tumour Research to raise awareness and funding.
key_points: Phoebe's symptoms of severe headaches and sickness were initially dismissed as migraines by a GP before an optician spotted the issue.
She underwent two surgeries within 72 hours of her diagnosis at Addenbrooke's Hospital to relieve brain pressure and remove most of the tumour.
The tumour was confirmed to be a non-cancerous pilocytic astrocytoma.
Phoebe returned to school part-time within three weeks of leaving the hospital and will require ongoing monitoring with MRI scans.
Her mother is now advocating for increased government funding and awareness regarding children's eye tests and brain tumour research.

title: Toddler with sun allergy can now play in daylight thanks to UV film
author: Calum Watson
content:
![A woman with a spotty top sits on a sofa next to a child in a red outfit](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/fc73/live/8a0f1420-9f9a-11f1-a83c-33ebef033ca4.jpg)
Mollie's mother Kirsty says installing UV film on windows has meant she can live a far more normal life
- Published
A Scottish toddler with a rare genetic disorder that makes her "allergic" to the sun can play indoors without the curtains closed thanks to UV-resistant film installed on the windows.
Two-year-old Mollie Murray, of Montrose, is the only child in the UK known to have her specific variant of xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), making her skin extremely sensitive to ultraviolet light.
The condition, which has no cure, means Mollie can only safely go outside while wearing protective full-length clothing or after dark.
Her family was able to install the film last month with funding from a charity originally established to support the build of Aberdeen's children's hospital.
![A young girl in a red outfit playing with an etch o sketch type toy in a living room](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/3c6b/live/bb5f1ec0-9f96-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Mollie previously could only play indoors with the curtains drawn
Mollie's mother, Kirsty Campbell, 35, a charge nurse, said her daughter is at risk of sunburn all year round - and has previously burnt in November.
She said: "The only time it's safe to go outside is in the dark. I want to keep her inside at all times to keep her safe, but we can't do that â she needs some sort of normality."
The NHS had paid to install the film at Kirsty's home, but Mollie's parents live apart and there was no funding for it at her father Ryan's home, where she spends much of her time.
The Archie Foundation, which provides support to babies, children and families during a hospital stay or after a bereavement, has now stepped in to cover the Â£600 cost.
"Their support has been indescribable â they've been a massive help for us," Kirsty said.
"I cried for about 20 minutes when I was told the money would come through. Mollie wouldn't have the same quality of life at her dad's house without it.
She added: "It means she can do simple things like look outside for the postman or draw in daylight.
"My ex-partner was having to take playpark equipment into his house as it wasn't safe outside. She's so happy running around like a normal child."
![A child in a red outfit wearing a sun hat, gloves and sunglasses outdoors](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/968e/live/c9740250-9f96-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Mollie has to wear full-length clothing to protect herself from the sun when she is outdoors
Mollie was in and out of hospital from the time she was a baby, suffering from a range of symptoms including seizures and severe reflux.
She first experienced severe sunburn on an overcast day in May 2025. The situation escalated when it happened again two months later.
She was eventually diagnosed with XP.
Doctors have advised that Mollie is 10,000 times more likely to get skin cancer than other children.
Her mother has to use a UV monitor to check readings in every room to ensure it is safe for Mollie to enter.
"To go from thinking your child has sunburn to them having an extremely rare genetic disorder is mind-blowing," she said.
"Everyday life is difficult as she needs full protective outer wear for going outside and sun cream every two hours under her clothes."
She added: "We initially had to play inside in darkness with the curtains closed before getting the UV-resistant film on our windows."
Quality of life
The family have been told that Mollie will likely have neurological impairment and mobility issues in her 40s and 50s, but that she should have a fairly normal childhood.
They are hoping to ensure she has the highest quality of life possible while continuing to keep her safe.
"She is an amazing wee girl and is coping with it so well," said Kirsty. "She's very outgoing and friendly and the fact she's been in hospital so much means she's used to seeing different faces."
Rebecca Duncan, business development and fundraising manager for The Archie Foundation in Tayside, said it was "wonderful" to hear how the charity's support has helped make a difference for Mollie and her family.
She said: "Caring for a child with complex needs can be incredibly challenging and, at times, isolating, so we're committed to ensuring families never feel they have to face that journey alone.
"Mollie has shown remarkable resilience, and we're proud to have played a small part in helping her experience the joy, opportunities and precious moments that every child deserves."
summary: A two-year-old Scottish toddler with a rare genetic disorder called xeroderma pigmentosum, which makes her extremely sensitive to ultraviolet light, can now play indoors in the daylight without closed curtains. Funding from a children's charity allowed her father's home to be fitted with UV-resistant window film, giving her a more normal quality of life. The incurable condition means she is at a significantly higher risk of skin cancer and can only safely go outside after dark or while wearing full protective clothing.
key_points: Two-year-old Mollie Murray is the only child in the UK known to have her specific variant of xeroderma pigmentosum.
The genetic condition makes her skin extremely sensitive to ultraviolet light and puts her 10,000 times more likely to get skin cancer.
The Archie Foundation provided £600 to install UV-resistant film on the windows of Mollie's father's home.
The window film allows Mollie to play in daylight and look outside without needing to keep the curtains closed.
Mollie must still wear full-length protective clothing and sun cream or stay indoors during the day to remain safe.

title: ‘An amazing relief’: implant offers hope for those with refractory angina
author: Denis Campbell
content:
“It’s an amazing relief, both physically and emotionally, to be able to live my life again normally, without feeling that I’m limited all the time in what I can do.”
Cristian Jensen is describing the difference that an implant inserted in his chest – to reduce the symptoms of his debilitating angina – has had on his life.
The 64-year-old used to have five angina attacks a week, each involving a sharp, acute pain that reminded him of the heart attack he once had. Now he has an attack every week or two.
He used to have to limit the amount of exercise he did, in case strenuous activity induced an attack. Now he’s walking further and faster and no longer worries about climbing stairs.
“It’s made a huge difference to my confidence,” the packaging designer adds. “Angina is a reminder that something isn’t right with your body. It’s like a sharp pain in the middle of your chest that stops you doing what you are doing.
“The fear that the pain of an episode of angina could be a heart attack. Suddenly not having that anxiety at the back of your mind changes your life.”
Angina, a common form of heart disease, involves pain in the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arm.
Jensen had a long and troubled history of heart problems before consultant cardiologist Dr Ranil de Silva fitted him with the implant – a coronary sinus reducer (CSR) – at the Royal Brompton hospital, a renowned centre of specialist NHS heart and lung care in London, in 2021.
![Cristian Jensen holds his hand against his chest](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/57ea6f4deb7ccdc106f4d73350cb106717584466/178_0_3333_2667/master/3333.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In 1990, he was diagnosed with angina at an unusually young age – at just 28 – after an angiogram showed he had blocked arteries.
Open heart surgery helped. “That fixed me, for a while at least,” he says. “I was angina-free for 17 years until I had a heart attack in 2007.” That led to him having the first of what became eight stents put in, to help his arteries stay open and his heart to keep pumping blood around his body.
But in 2015 he began taking drugs to lower the high level of bad cholesterol in his bloodstream – fatty deposits that narrow the arteries. He also started using another drug, a spray called gylceryl trinitrate (GTN), to banish the pain each of his angina attacks brought.
Jensen is one of an estimated 300,000 people in England with refractory angina. That is angina that remains problematic despite the patient having drugs, stents and heart bypass surgery.
When Jensen’s symptoms persisted, de Silva suggested he have the implant fitted. Despite the large number of people with the condition, only a handful have had what is still an experimental treatment.
The small, hourglass-shaped device is implanted near the heart using keyhole surgery through the patient’s neck. It works by narrowing a vein at the back of the heart. That helps to redirect the person’s blood flow to the parts of the heart muscle that are getting too little oxygen. Each device costs the NHS £11,400.
A new study – the largest of its kind worldwide to date – has found that the device brings about a significant fall in chest pain in 75% of people with refractory angina within six months of its implantation.
“In this respect it is potentially a gamechanger,” says de Silva, who co-led the study with his colleague Dr Kevin Cheng. It was based on observation of 491 people with refractory angina between 2014 and 2024, 474 of whom had the implant fitted at 19 hospitals in England and Scotland.
Most patients went home the day of the procedure or the day after and serious complications were rare, the study also found.
According to de Silva, it shows that the device can greatly reduce the debilitating symptoms of refractory angina that significantly compromise quality of life and the ability to undertake normal day to day activities, and can help people avoid being admitted to hospital and boost their mental wellbeing.
“Many patients report their lives being transformed and that it helps them to achieve the quality of life they wish for, that they were unable to enjoy prior to the reducer implant – they get their life back,” says de Silva.
Despite the apparent success of the implant, and that only “a tiny fraction” of the 300,000 people with refractory angina have had one fitted, it is too early to yet see CSR as a standard treatment for people with this very painful form of coronary artery disease, he says.
More trials are needed and the NHS needs to approve the funding needed to expand access, he adds.
Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and the British Heart Foundation’s clinical director, said: “The findings are reassuring as they show that in routine clinical practice the device is being delivered safely and is resulting in fewer symptoms for patients.”
The device “offers hope for people living with this challenging condition”, she said.
summary: A new experimental chest implant called a coronary sinus reducer offers significant relief for patients suffering from refractory angina, a debilitating form of heart disease. A recent study of 491 patients found that the hourglass-shaped device successfully reduced chest pain in 75% of individuals within six months of implantation. While the procedure has proven safe and transformative for patients like Cristian Jensen, further trials and NHS funding approvals are required before it becomes a standard treatment.
key_points: Refractory angina affects an estimated 300,000 people in England whose symptoms persist despite medication, stents, and bypass surgery.
The coronary sinus reducer is a small, hourglass-shaped device inserted via keyhole surgery in the neck that redirects blood flow to oxygen-deprived heart muscle.
A major study found that the implant significantly reduced chest pain in 75% of patients within six months.
Despite promising results and safe outcomes, the implant remains an experimental treatment that requires more trials and NHS funding to become standard practice.

title: 'I had 9 organs removed after true cause of pain discovered' - AOL
author: Steven Smith
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![Claire Gerring in hospital](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/23/cbaec5b1-c16d-3387-b0ba-e5b6d1f4af3d/d2236bf9-23c9-4961-8401-0a38df3cbc69.jpg)
A woman's condition turned out to be so rare that it required nine of her organs to be removed during “the mother of all surgeries”.
Claire Gerring, 42, had initially been referred to John Radcliffe Hospital after an ultrasound in November 2022 with suspected endometriosis and was put on the wait list in May 2023 for an investigative laparoscopy. But after intense pain on her right side, a positive Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) test led to a colonoscopy.
Doctors discovered her appendix was inverted and a CT scan revealed she had malignant tissue on the organ and needed investigative surgery. A biopsy on May 6, 2025, confirmed she had stage four Pseudomyxoma Peritonei (PMP) - a rare cancer that typically originates from a tumour in the appendix.
She was referred to Basingstoke and North Hampshire Hospital, as it is one of only two hospitals that specialise in PMP. The cancer in her appendix had ruptured, meaning there were other nodules in the rest of her body.
![Claire Gerring after her first hospital discharge](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/23/cbaec5b1-c16d-3387-b0ba-e5b6d1f4af3d/58be2c1e-5f69-4883-a3f0-8be146c17046.jpg)
On July 15, 2025, Claire, who is mum to sons Oscar, 15, and Spencer, 14, underwent a 10-hour operation to remove nine organs - her appendix, ovaries, fallopian tubes, gall bladder, spleen, uterus and cervix.
She also had removed her greater omentum, belly button, peritoneum lining and part of her bowel Her liver was also partially cut away, as well as having her diaphragm scraped and bladder stripped.
During the surgery Claire had HIPEC chemotherapy – heated chemotherapy circulated around her abdomen. After four-and-a-half weeks in hospital, she was discharged and has been left with bowel problems, but has no evidence of disease at the moment and will be monitored for the next 20 years.
Claire, a hairdresser from Wantage, Oxfordshire, said: “I felt really quite scared and quite alone after my diagnosis. When you’ve got a rare cancer and it’s not something you’ve heard of before, there are not a lot of people to talk to about it.
“I was told by surgeons before my operation what they would remove. On top of that they cut part of my liver away and scraped my diaphragm and stripped my bladder.
“It’s a lot to process. It’s quite scary, but I’m lucky I had professionals who knew what they were doing. It’s called the mother of all surgeries because of the severity of it."
After struggling with pain in her side and asking for her laparoscopy surgery to be expedited by her GP, a positive FIT test and colonoscopy in March 2025 revealed Claire’s inverted appendix, which needed a CT scan. Her original endometriosis surgery was set to go ahead on April 11, 2025.
“But on April 10, I phoned up just to double check they’d got my CT scan results back as the next day I was now having investigative surgery,” Claire told Talk to the Press. “That’s where I was told I had malignant tissues in my appendix.
“At that point I wasn’t too worried because I thought, ‘well I don’t need my appendix’. Thirty seconds later, my gynaecology lady rang and said ‘Claire this is serious’ and that my surgery wouldn’t be happening tomorrow."
![Claire Gerring with her husband, Tom](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/23/cbaec5b1-c16d-3387-b0ba-e5b6d1f4af3d/db0e4351-e120-4d01-a6ad-72df6949af9a.jpg)
Investigative surgery on May 6 revealed the cancer was not contained to her appendix.
“When the tumour ruptures it releases mucin, which is a jelly-like substance,” Claire said. “It’s often called ‘jelly belly’. Your abdomen fills up and coats all your organs with mucin."
As a result, Claire needed vital cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC to remove all her affected organs.
"I’m coming up to my year's anniversary and I’m still left with complications in my bowel and I’ve been back in hospital in between,” she said. “With a lot of cancer you’re told you lose weight, but with this one I put on weight and looked four months pregnant.
“I thought I’d just got to 40 and it was my middle-aged spread. But it was actually inside my abdomen.
“Recovery is a slow process, obviously, like most surgeries, if you have your appendix out the recovery time is six to eight weeks.
“Times that by 11 (and) it’s a long time. I had a bowel obstruction and was back in hospital for a 10-day stay recently.
“I’m still grateful, it’s a small price to pay. Basically what they say is you’re never back to your old self, you just get used to the new you."
Now a year into her recovery, Claire has thrown herself into fundraising for charity Pseudomyxoma Survivor, throwing a masked ball on July 11, 2026.
On the night, she said: "I just feel my main purpose for doing this is raising awareness about the rare cancer and Pseudomyxoma Survivor. I believe deeply that if you’re willing to take, you must also be willing to give back. And here I am today, standing in front of you, living that promise.
