The road to recovery has been challenging for the life-long Derry City supporter.
Before her diagnosis, McConnellogue described herself as a "non-stop Duracell bunny, on the go 24/7".
"The physical part is very tough; I walk with a zimmer frame or a crutch and I have to be helped up the stairs, my husband has to physically put me to bed," she added.
She said the diagnosis had "floored" her and she had relied on counselling services to keep her going.
"My independence is gone. I cannot drive, I can't go to the shop on my own - all those things I took for granted," she said.
Country music singer Lisa McHugh spoke publicly last year about being diagnosed with FND.
According to the NHS, there is no cure for FND but it is treatable providing you adapt your life as much as possible to manage it.
McConnellogue has been sharing her recovery journey on social media.
"I do believe FND is misunderstood and I want people to know they are not alone," she said.
"It is a very real neurological condition, and I want to show others you can recover."
'Postcode lottery'
![A woman wearing a pink top looking at the camera. She is wearing a gold necklace and green glasses. She has red hair and earrings. There are red curtains behind her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a62f/live/0a6a36b0-9d55-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Helen Dickson was diagnosed with FND in 2022
FND Matters NI is the only FND charity in Northern Ireland.
The charity estimates there around 5,000 people living with FND in Northern Ireland but they have struggled to obtain specific figures as Northern Ireland's health trusts do not record FND as a primary condition.
Trustee Helen Dickson was diagnosed with the condition in 2022.
"Treatment for FND can be a postcode lottery," she said.
"More awareness and changes in attitudes are needed, and we need FND specific services.
"There can be a misconception that FND symptoms are imagined or 'all in someone's head' but it's very real."
She said healthcare professionals have asked the charity for advice.
![A woman smiling with her hands int he air wearing a red and white zipped up jacket. She has glasses and short brown hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/58b1/live/0bd97f20-9d4a-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
McConnellogue is a supporter of Derry City Football Club
The Department of Health has previously said in response to a question put forward at Stormont that precise numbers of patients with a diagnosis of FND are not currently captured due to limitations in coding and data systems.
The department estimates there are several thousand people in Northern Ireland with FND.
For Carmel McConnellogue, her next recovery goal is to be able to go to watch a football game.
"I am working towards being at Derry City's next home game, I have come through a lot in life and I will overcome FND," she vowed.
"I know my brain computer is going to come back online, and I will be at the Brandywell again."
summary: While being treated for dehydration in a hospital, Carmel McConnellogue suddenly lost the ability to move and speak, with initial symptoms pointing toward a stroke. An MRI confirmed she had Functional Neurological Disorder (FND), a condition where the brain struggles to properly send and receive signals. McConnellogue spent five weeks in the hospital undergoing rehabilitation and now relies on a zimmer frame and assistance from her husband. She is sharing her journey to raise awareness and hopes to overcome the condition.
key_points: Carmel McConnellogue was diagnosed with Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) after suddenly losing movement and speech while hospitalized for dehydration.
FND is a real neurological condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals, often compared to a computer with too many tabs open.
McConnellogue spent five weeks in the hospital and now requires mobility aids and assistance from her husband for daily tasks.
There is no cure for FND, but it can be treated through rehabilitation therapies and lifestyle adaptations.
Charities and patients in Northern Ireland highlight that FND treatment is a postcode lottery and that health trusts do not record FND as a primary condition.

title: 80 Medical Professionals Share The Diagnoses That Made Their Stomachs Drop
author: Gabija Palšytė
content:
![A female doctor, in a white lab coat with a stethoscope, sits hunched over with her face in her hands. She looks distraught, contemplating difficult diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/medical-professionals-hard-diagnosis-cover_675.jpg) 
80 Medical Professionals Share The Diagnoses That Made Their Stomachs Drop
Healthcare workers have an incredibly important job. They help us through illnesses, injuries, and some of the hardest moments of our lives. Unfortunately, though, medicine can’t fix everything, and sometimes even the most skilled specialists have to deliver news they wish they didn’t have to.
One Redditor recently asked medical professionals to share the diagnoses that gave them the worst pit-in-the-stomach feeling, and they came through with plenty of heartbreaking responses. Scroll down to read some of them. Just be warned that the following stories contain upsetting and sensitive content.
 ![A doctor with a stethoscope sits at a desk with his head in his hands, reflecting the difficulty of delivering diagnoses. A doctor with a stethoscope sits at a desk with his head in his hands, reflecting the difficulty of delivering diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-CZod2AuO0UE-unsplash-1-6a82cfc288dac__700.jpg) My dad is a radiologist. Back when he was doing his residency rotations, he had an elderly woman come in, full of joy, talking about how happy she was that she was officially one year cancer free. He had to tell her that her scans were absolutely riddled with cancer. Everywhere. He cried telling her and she comforted him.
 ![A doctor in blue gloves examines a patient's foot, illustrating a medical examination for diagnoses. A doctor in blue gloves examines a patient's foot, illustrating a medical examination for diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-CFV7FeTbmcI-unsplash-6a82d033dfc1f__700.jpg) In my field (Neuromuscular Medicine) the biggest pit in my stomach comes when I am doing an EMG for something otherwise non-concerning and it starts to look like ALS. I’ll catch myself going from talking and joking with the patient to not talking at all and adding on more body parts to the test, which tends to confuse the patient. For example I’ll be checking the leg for weakness with pulling the toes up and I’ll then have to test the arm, muscles by the spine in the back, and sometimes the tongue.
When the patient asks why I am testing so many body parts, I have to tell them that I’m concerned about a disease that impacts the nerves that move the muscles. I try not to use the word “ALS” at this time because more confirmatory testing needs to take place before confirming a diagnosis.
It reminds me of a quote that I won’t get exactly right but you’ll get the idea. 
“Each physician carries with them a tiny graveyard, where, every now and then, they go to pray.”
For anyone considering becoming a physician, please know that you’ll care so deeply about so many people while being told by the public that you do not. This job was absolutely the right choice for me, but cases like this take a toll that will wash over you in your most private moments. 
If my rambling comment resonates with any other healthcare providers, or anyone for that matter, please consider seeing a therapist. Many of us don’t recognize how much we are suppressing until we look inward. 
Sorry for the long comment that got off track a bit. Please take care of yourselves. 
 ![A pregnant woman undergoing an ultrasound, potentially revealing a difficult diagnosis for doctors. A pregnant woman undergoing an ultrasound, potentially revealing a difficult diagnosis for doctors.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/curated-lifestyle-PrkjUA_SgFo-unsplash-6a82eee50567e__700.jpg) Term stillbirth.
There’s never a good way to tell someone their baby [passed away] before it could even be born. No combination of words makes the delivery any easier. And you know when you see there’s no heartbeat on the ultrasound. You scan again because you gaslight yourself into hoping you’re wrong, even though you’re not new to scanning babies and the heart is obviously not moving. You add color flow to prove to yourself that what you’re seeing is the truth. And then you have to say it even though everyone in the room knows it. It’s not official until you say the words. 
Those screaming sobs will always stay with me. 
 ![A man with clasped hands looking down, receiving a hard diagnosis from a doctor. A man with clasped hands looking down, receiving a hard diagnosis from a doctor.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/429050-6a82f7c073842__700.jpg) ED nurse here. I remember one time a patient was diagnosed with a dissecting abdominal aortic aneurysm; the MD told the patient he'd be rushed into surgery soon and to immediately settle any affairs and talk to his loved ones, as the likelihood of him not making it off the table was high.
It was just surreal seeing this guy talking to his wife and kids knowing it may be his last. 
 ![A male doctor speaking with a young girl holding a teddy bear, discussing a hard diagnosis. A male doctor speaking with a young girl holding a teddy bear, discussing a hard diagnosis.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-KO2TcT_Fluw-unsplash-6a82efc379c67__700.jpg) Healthy kid has some new minor neurological symptom (tremor, headache, poor balance) and MRI shows big, huge, bad brain tumor.
 ![A child peeks from under blankets, representing sad and horrifying diagnoses. A child peeks from under blankets, representing sad and horrifying diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-dvzbR7Djy4Y-unsplash-6a830157ab046__700.jpg) Non accidental trauma (NAT) in kids. I was taught during residency that if you have never diagnosed NAT, you aren’t looking hard enough. I think about those words a lot, and now I teach them to trainees.
 ![A doctor sits alone, appearing distressed and holding her head, reflecting the hardest diagnoses. A doctor sits alone, appearing distressed and holding her head, reflecting the hardest diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-8OBmzKlzhdI-unsplash-6a82f5b18e71e__700.jpg) Patient with the same exact birthday as me, has a one year old in the waiting room, pregnant with her second, and I’m doing biopsies of her cancer, which was at least stage 3. So humbling and scary.
 ![A woman looking distressed, head in hands, experiencing a difficult diagnosis. A woman looking distressed, head in hands, experiencing a difficult diagnosis.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/curated-lifestyle-COX0vuquK6Y-unsplash-2-6a82f80cdf9de__700.jpg) Late teens patient diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease but CT showed metastatic colon cancer.
 ![A tired male doctor leaning against a wall, appearing distressed by the hardest diagnoses he delivered. A tired male doctor leaning against a wall, appearing distressed by the hardest diagnoses he delivered.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/77360-6a8306e36aeac__700.jpg) OR Scrub Nurse
STAT Necrotizing Fasciitis cases. 
Flesh eating disease. Advancing faster than we can pump high dose antibiotics into them. We basically rush them in and cut away everything infected we can as fast as we can while racing the clock on the patient being too sick to be under anesthesia safely anymore. Pack with iodine and race to the icu. I’ve seen a doctor follow the stretcher still wrapping the packing while they took off out of the OR. 
Not only does my stomach drop for the patient, but it’s just the most awful case in every way imaginable. From equipment to smell to clean up all the way to the other end of the spectrum of watching what is actually happening to another human in front of you. No matter what reason you got into medicine, it wasn’t for that feeling. 
 Teenage girl came in, with only some trouble eating and other vague discomforts. Nothing serious. Doctor doesn't trust it and kind of by chance sends us her samples. My lab diagnoses her with a rare metabolic disorder. This has no cure, and her version means she will likely pass within a few years after symptoms start. Transplant from an uncle to extend her life got rejected. But it got worse: my lab tests the rest of the family as these are genetic diseases. 3 of the 4 daughters have the disease and will likely not make it through puberty. I didn't get the full details of the mutations but mom has a weird variant but she's fine, but the dad has a known late onset version. Combined, they are deadly during puberty, and dad will likely get sick soon and pass as well. 
In a few years, it will just be the mother and her one daughter, having lost everyone else as they slowly lose their bodily functions. 
From minor discomfort to losing your entire family. There were a lot of tears. 
 ![A stressed doctor in scrubs and a mask sits outside, highlighting the emotional toll of delivering hard diagnoses. A stressed doctor in scrubs and a mask sits outside, highlighting the emotional toll of delivering hard diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-dAjwssdnsDs-unsplash-2-6a82f025c64f6__700.jpg) Obviously very advanced, previously undiagnosed cancer presenting to ED for anything. Feeling multiple golf ball and baseball sized lumps or an abdomen full of tumor is sobering.
 ![A patient with gray hair and glasses gestures with open palms while talking to a doctor about hard diagnoses. A patient with gray hair and glasses gestures with open palms while talking to a doctor about hard diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-5vFNfXZ_Cko-unsplash-6a8462d11bfba__700.jpg) Specific to my field (occupational therapy) when patients get spinal cord injuries and plateau after improvements. It all looks like they’ll recover mobility but you know they won’t, but they still think they will.
Or when you get a post stroke and you know recovery is minimal but they think they’ll recover fine. 
 ![A doctor wearing a mask and lab coat looks into a microscope, symbolizing medical diagnoses and research. A doctor wearing a mask and lab coat looks into a microscope, symbolizing medical diagnoses and research.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-7DvSNNwQaVg-unsplash-6a82d603f364a__700.jpg) Bacterial meningitis. In the lab we are the first to see it. It’s very scary to think about how close someone could be to the end while you look at their spinal fluid on a slide.
 ![A pregnant woman touches her belly. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver. A pregnant woman touches her belly. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/natalia-blauth-EDiSQjFAIcA-unsplash-1-6a83075504d6d__700.jpg) Advanced cervical cancer in a pregnant patient. In a state with the most restrictive ban.
 ![A mother cradles her newborn baby. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver. A mother cradles her newborn baby. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/daiga-ellaby-DXZPaq7Sbds-unsplash-6a83095382b92__700.jpg) Im an ED nurse and was working triage one day. I had a lovely 22 year old lady come in who had given birth to her first child 3 months prior. She had a large, non-painful lump come up on her chest overnight. I knew it was cancer. I checked her chart the next week, and sure enough she was diagnosed with metastatic cancer, it was so far along that they couldn't find the primary. Poor thing. 22 years old and a brand new mother. I couldn't bring myself to check her chart again.
 ![A doctor speaks to a distressed patient. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver. A doctor speaks to a distressed patient. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/5598-1-6a83099c2e5e5__700.jpg) 18 year old kid was worried about an STD because his girlfriend found a lump. My stomach dropped when I examined him. Metastatic testicular cancer.
 MD here.
Pronouncing kids d**d with their parents there.
Seeing an intoxicated man smiling while continuously vomiting pure blood from esophageal varices while trying to get a line in and he just dies right there sitting up.
Schizophrenic patient who tore her own eye out and swallowed it because it would help her “see inside herself”. 
 ![A vet holds a cat, symbolizing the empathy doctors have delivering diagnoses, even for pets. A vet holds a cat, symbolizing the empathy doctors have delivering diagnoses, even for pets.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/jsb-co-19n_ippcypQ-unsplash-6a82f94a2cdc6__700.jpg) Veterinarian here to mix up the just horribly depressing human stories with a hopeful one.
The worst ‘pit-in-your-stomach’ diagnosis for me used to be FIP. (Feline Infections Peritonitis) It is caused by corona viruses, but seems to be more due to viral interactions, not one specific causative agent so no vaccine was ever able to be developed successfully.
Horrible, slow disease that, until recently, was entirely incurable. And it usually, but not exclusively, hit young cats. I’m never going to forget the family with the 8 month old kitten who hadn’t even wanted a cat…but whose kids just fell in love with this kitten…and eventually wore the parents down only to learn like 3 months later that this new member of the family was going to [perish] slowly and painfully and the best thing we could do was offer to euthanize it now.
BUT I promised hope and uplifting…this disease now has a CURE! Turns out Remdesivir (and a couple of its related molecules) works GREAT on this disease, like 80-99% cure rate great. While Gilead won’t actually license any of the family of molecules, or produce a veterinary labeled medicine, thanks to Remdesivir hitting the market (and being largely not that helpful) for COVID-19, there are legal ways to get ahold of a cure now. AND, despite not licensing it, they’ve (tacitly at least) made no move to enforce their patent against compounding pharmacies making versions of the medicine commercially for use in cats.
There’s lots of times I’ve felt that sinking feeling…but the feelings I got from FIP cases a decade ago still top the list. So to get to watch a cure be developed and become more and more accessible has been a career highlight. 
 ![A young girl sleeping in a hospital bed, hugging a teddy bear, illustrating a patient receiving diagnoses. A young girl sleeping in a hospital bed, hugging a teddy bear, illustrating a patient receiving diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/curated-lifestyle-lOicquPBEjY-unsplash-6a8304d09e45e__700.jpg) Paramedic here
0500 in the morning we were called to a house, mother was worried about her pre-teen daughter acting depressed and weird. Normal house, siblings having breakfast. I was tired, after 10 mins of waffling words from Mum where I semi zoned out she said something my partner picked up on, she had described a seizure. We recommended she see her GP. 
That night I got called in for a transfer. Daughter had advanced metastatic brain tumour, off to a major hospital for treatment which essentially meant make her comfy while she [passes]. 
 ![A close-up of a warm fireplace with burning logs, offering a sense of comfort amidst discussions of difficult diagnoses. A close-up of a warm fireplace with burning logs, offering a sense of comfort amidst discussions of difficult diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3140-6a8561908a110__700.jpg) Third-degree burns covering 50% of the total body surface. During my general surgery internship, I was on my trauma rotation. We brought in a 75-year-old woman who had fallen into her large fireplace at home. After evaluating her in the trauma bay, where she was alert and oriented, we transferred her to the burn unit. Once the plastic surgeon in charge of the burn unit was briefed and examined her, he immediately ordered intubation and quietly informed our team that she would be gone in 72 hours, regardless of our interventions. She received aggressive resuscitation and serial debridements in the OR. Like clockwork she died almost exactly 72 hours later. I will never forget the pit in my stomach when i heard that prognosis. Her fate was sealed.
Patient came into the ED for difficulty finding her words. MRI after admission concerning for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, the human version of mad cow disease. Prion disorders scare the [hell] out of me.
 ![A doctor gives a boy a check-up. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver. A doctor gives a boy a check-up. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-1KRiK2V5fLI-unsplash-6a845f644accd__700.jpg) 6yo boy comes in with limping. MRI done - aggressive brain cancer. The surgeon and pediatrician explained it was inoperable - that he would start having issues swallowing, and he might need a nasogastric for nutrition. The parents stood up, grabbed the child and just left. It didn’t make sense to them and they were in complete denial and even anger. They said we were quacks and we must be wrong and were quite aggressive.
The child and his family represented 2 weeks later. He died soon after. 
 ![A female doctor performs an ultrasound on a pregnant woman, often delivering difficult diagnoses. A female doctor performs an ultrasound on a pregnant woman, often delivering difficult diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-i_kwjZ9JcvE-unsplash-6a84615418e6f__700.jpg) When I didn’t find a fetal heart beat on a patient at her 39 week prenatal appt. It’s happened twice in the last year. Full term fetal demise.
 ![A happy mother holds up her baby, a joyful moment contrasting the serious topic of hardest diagnoses. A happy mother holds up her baby, a joyful moment contrasting the serious topic of hardest diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/836-6a8561cc8ba53__700.jpg) As a nurse of 11.5 years I’ll have to say yesterday when my husband and I got the news our baby has a rare structural brain abnormality that will never allow him to live a normal life.
 Any time someone tells me they are just glad their cancer didn’t come back and the scan says “the cancer is back and it’s everywhere.”
I can still feel the sinking feeling I had when I read the results. 
 Had someone come in to my OCED for a migraine and left with a referral to neurology and oncology once they got back home for a suspected glioblastoma. The look on their partner’s face as they whispered, “but it was just a headache…” as I went over their discharge instructions about broke me. Never heard from them again as they were on a work trip.
It was one of our last before end of shift so it was pretty d**n somber the rest of the night. 
 ![A male doctor looking stressed at a computer, reflecting the difficulty of delivering diagnoses. A male doctor looking stressed at a computer, reflecting the difficulty of delivering diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/7586-6a8302b760fb9__700.jpg) Fairly young patient came in with no symptoms after having low hemoglobin caught incidentally on routine bloodwork. Baseball-sized tumour in the stomach... these cases always haunt you.
 ![A female patient in a mask listens to a doctor during a consultation, representing challenging medical diagnoses. A female patient in a mask listens to a doctor during a consultation, representing challenging medical diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/cdc-GqFxZ5lfMxs-unsplash-6a82d5c31c9f2__700.jpg) Neurologist here. Seeing patchy muscle wasting, fasciculations in the tongue, asymmetric weakness onset over a couple of months and brisk reflexes in a young healthy, usually very friendly and lovely person.
(ALS). 
 ![Doctors in an operating room preparing for a difficult surgery, revealing the hardest diagnoses to deliver. Doctors in an operating room preparing for a difficult surgery, revealing the hardest diagnoses to deliver.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/piron-guillaume-U4FyCp3-KzY-unsplash-1-6a845f98ac493__700.jpg) Glioblastoma is a pretty bad one.
Also, any time I wake up a patient WAY earlier than they or their family were expecting. That means the cancer (usually something in the belly) was worse and had progressed more than anyone knew and the surgeons couldn’t even attempt to remove it. 
 ![A male doctor sits on stairs looking sad, having delivered hard diagnoses. A male doctor sits on stairs looking sad, having delivered hard diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2148535651-6a82f88cc0c5c__700.jpg) My neighbor was babysitting my then 11 month old for the day. Her dad was my last patient of the day. Coming in for “sternal pain.” Initially suspected costochondritis as he told me he does 500 crunches and 100 pushups a day. Very well known legend in our town, the fittest of fit, non smoker. Chest Xray showed advanced incredibly rare type of lung cancer. No known successful treatment. She walked in to drop my son off right as I was pulling up the X-rays. My heart has never sunk that low. He [passed away] within 3 months.
 ![A doctor walks towards ambulances, reflecting on the hardest diagnoses to deliver. A doctor walks towards ambulances, reflecting on the hardest diagnoses to deliver.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty-images-INDsmWsDtDo-unsplash-6a8461a4ce21f__700.jpg) Arriving on the scene of an accident and you can’t tell what kind of vehicle you’re looking at.
 ![A doctor discusses difficult diagnoses with a patient in a medical office, showing the gravity of the situation. A doctor discusses difficult diagnoses with a patient in a medical office, showing the gravity of the situation.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/32027-6a85624845ccb__700.jpg) Older guy came in with a lump on his back that his wife told him to get checked out 6 months prior. He being the typical 50s rural male patient decided to wait until it was the size of a golf ball. He finally comes into clinic, we can see his chief complaint is the mass and swelling in his armpit in the EMR.
I was a resident at the time, my attending and I both knew it'd be bad before we went in the room. I watched my attending do a shave biopsy and the underlying tissue was just gray and black with pigment, obviously melanoma without even sending off for pathology.
Guy was a d**d man walking at that point. We basically told him so in the room before even sending it off for pathology. He no showed his follow up appointment. 
 ![A doctor reviews a chart with a young patient. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver. A doctor reviews a chart with a young patient. Doctors reveal the diagnoses that were the hardest to deliver.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2148868111-6a8562ccd1c01__700.jpg) I rotated in a pediatric PM&R clinic during my training. We had a young family come in with their two boys age 2 and 4. The attending physician (who already knew what their diagnosis was) asked me to observe the kiddos and tell him what I thought was going on.
I start watching the older one playing and oof it hit me hard. Positive Gower's sign.
For the non-medical people here, it basically means the kid was moving from sitting to standing like an old man which is seen in neuromuscular diseases.
I talked with the attending and yep, both boys had Duchenne's. The older one was showing symptoms but the younger one hadn't yet. It's weird looking at 2 perfect-looking kiddos giggling and playing when you know they'll be lucky to live into their 40s. 
Harlequin disorder in a NICU baby and explaining to the parents that it does not go away. Don’t google it unless you’re okay with grotesque. Listening to the attending explain that there is no chance it will go away as mom stared off into space because Im sure it was all too much to take in shortly after an unplanned section. The way her eyes lost every bit of light was startling.
 Patient discharged from the ER a couple days ago due to high blood pressure, readmitted for Bell's Palsy.
CT of the brain was negative for stroke.
I did his swallow eval. Oral stage was unremarkable...but he could not swallow anything no matter the texture or amount. Would start coughing, choking etc.
Bell's Palsy can affect the oral stage of swallow but never the pharyngeal stage. 
I told his nurse "I know his CT was negative but can we ask the attending for a stat MRI of the head, this definitely isn't Bell's Palsy."
The agreed. MRIs will show fresh strokes whereas it may take a few days to show up on a CT.
I was right. MRI showed he had a brainstem stroke, too fresh for the CT to pick up on.
I got a certificate and a biiiiig plate of cookies for my "Good Catch!" . 
Necrotizing fasciitis. She went from walking to the bathroom under her own power while casually chatting about her pets to floridly septic and unconscious in about 30 minutes. She didn’t make it.
My patient who had only delivered her baby (vaginally, but had prior c section) started having severe shoulder pain. Immediate red flag. She looked pale and clammy which is common with people in shock. I let the OBs know, immediately did an ultrasound, and she was back in the OR STAT. Her previous c section scar had ruptured and she ended up needing a ton of blood. The rupture had led to her abdomen filling with blood which is what made her have shoulder pain. As soon as she said shoulder pain it was red flags all around. If that had been ignored or minimized she could have definitely died.
 I work as a radiology tech, and there are so many moments that stick with me. You talk to patients, joke with them, hear them make plans for vacations, family gatherings, all while you are staring at their scan and realizing something is terribly wrong.
One case still haunts me. A middle‑aged guy came in just for persistent back pain, convinced it was just muscle strain from work. He told me he was going to take his kids camping the next weekend. Pulling up his CT scan, I saw his lungs were covered in metastatic lesions. He had absolutely no clue.
The worst part is we cannot break the news directly. We just hand the report over to the doctor, and send the patient home, knowing their whole world is about to fall apart in a day or two.
Healthy young adults, active parents, kids with tiny, harmless‑seeming symptoms. Nothing prepares you for seeing a life‑ending diagnosis pop up on screen out of nowhere. You learn to hide your shock on your face, but that heavy, sinking feeling in your stomach never really goes away. 
When I was in residency, I was rotating in peds ED. A kid came in for anemia. The blood counts came back and my attending went really quiet and then goes “aw frick”. She had critically low white blood cells and platelets as well as severe anemia. Multiple cell lines being low is usually a sign of bone marrow dysfunction, usually hematologic cancer. I still remember the grandma’s wailing in the hallway when she heard the news. I don’t know what the final diagnosis was but the attending was pretty sure leukemia.
 Former EMT here. Had a patient who started with shortness of breath that just got worse and worse, and nothing helped. He started panicking as we loaded him up. He was clawing at the oxygen mask.
"Am I going to d*e?!" he asked my partner. 
"We're going to do everything we can for you to make sure that doesn't happen," my partner replied after a pause. And in the end, we did. 
But so did he. 
About 15 minutes after we got him to the hospital, he died. Pulmonary embolism.
That pause, though... I don't know if he noticed it, but I did. I mean, you're never supposed to tell them they're going to be fine cause you can't know, but my partner really didn't know if the patient was going to make it. That pause was carefully selecting the right words. And I knew it. 
 Not a diagnosing professional, but a first responder. 
There have been many, many instances of responding to 911 calls where family is like “help!” and the patient is clearly not salvageable. The sinking feeling in your stomach when you know you’re gonna do your best, but the outcome isn’t going to be good, and the family is in denial - it’s awful. 
Was working on the open heart team in a pediatric hospital when we had a teen come in with an enlarged heart and infectious processes going on. We opened his chest to remove fluid from around the heart and do something else that I just cannot recall after so many years. However, what I do recall is what this child’s heart looked like once we got in there.. it was like wet tissue paper and incredibly friable. There was nothing we could do. This poor kid was beyond saving and the whole team knew it. In my experience, there is such a sense of somberness and quiet that blankets the OR in times like this. In the OR, we are fixers… and we just couldn’t fix this. We were able to close the chest and whisk the teen back to the ICU for their parents to be with them when they passed away. Sigh….
Participating in a right pneumonectomy for necrosis on a 17 year old who had vaped for 2 years.
 Quite specifically it’s pancreatic cancer. There’s something like a 5% survival rate. And I’m not sure about reoccurrence after remission. 
The pancreas is a unique little organ and any time it gets angry it goes scorched earth. Some of the things that make it unique help the cancer spread rapidly before it’s detected. After I became a nurse the first time someone I knew was diagnosed with this I just thought, clear as day “oh, he’s already d**d”. And I was so *mad* at everyone trying to push him into treatment and all of the “rah rah rah” of it. Because treatment would take the time he had and make it so much worse. 
As a medical laboratory scientist, seeing blasts (immature cells) in a pediatric spinal fluid. This generally means that treatment is going to have to be altered/more intense for those kids that have already gone through leukemia treatments.
 Anytime I see pathological fractures, meaning fractures not caused by a fall or trauma but fractures that just happen. Especially if it’s in a femur. 
9/10 it’s cancer that has metastasized to bone. The outlook is not great, and the pain is awful. 
It wasn’t when I opened up the imaging for a “back pain” referral and saw a whole spine of cancer. What got me was when I loaded his screening chest CT from 7 months prior and saw the primary tumor on that scan, which was unnoticed. I had to tell an otherwise healthy active man I had never met that he had cancer, it had spread everywhere, he needed to go to the ER…*over video*.
Anoxic brain injury in a teenager who took a few of their mom’s Percocets.
I saw a patient for severe uncontrolled itch. I always order an SPEP as standard of care. It can be a clue that there’s underlying cancer, but I’ve never seen it be positive… until it was. I told the patient that one of the proteins was off, and it could very rarely be a sign of a serious underlying issue. She interrupted to ask if I thought she had cancer, and I said it’s possible. She looked devastated and said her uterine cancer must be back. Sure enough— she had no other signs, but her heme/onc said without this test, the cancer would have been caught at a more advanced age.
 Huntingtons.
Kursed_Valeth:
I'll never forget the first the I was caring for a patient with Huntington's. It still haunts me. If it ever happens to me I'm going to take myself out before I lose myself. 
When I was a medical student, I did a sub-i in psych. I was seeing this pt who was the same age as me and in for psychosis. Turns out she had schizoaffective disorder, but she was in medical school during her first break and had to drop out. Her entire career as a physician was ruined because of it. She retained a lot of info from school too so she believed she was a surgeon / ER physician etc. Just hit reallly close to home. Not that I have a very extensive career or anything yet, but I think about her often.
 I was an intern doing my OBGYN rotation. My sister’s childhood friend (female early 20s) came in as a patient, sent in from the ER for ascites. Imaging suggested ovarian cancer with peritoneal implants.
Definitely not the worst case I’ve seen, but it was a devastating diagnosis in someone I’d known for over a decade. She was d**d within a year. 
I'm a paramedic in a really advanced, but semi rural system. We can do a lot for most things these days. The exception? That unexplained hypotension when you do a quick ultrasound and suddenly the abdominal aorta jumps to like 5cm+. It's just so defeating because there's so little I can do to even slow down d***h from a ruptured AAA and best case scenario if I'm at the closest point in the county to them my closest hospital that can treat it is 20min away. Some places it's an hour.
The first covid patient we intubated in the ICU I worked at... we were all watching that point where bipap was failing and we would need to go in there for a more advanced airway. Knowing we were also at risk of contracting covid was pretty terrifying early days. My unit had seen one of the first cases of H1N1 and lost staff to it many years earlier, I think there was a lot of dread and PTSD with covid.
Veterinary medical professional here, I work in ER/Critical care and oncology. Anytime a cat comes in with an ATE (arterial thromboembolism) my heart breaks. If you don't know, it's basically throwing a clot, this usually occurs secondary to unknown heart disease, and presents as a cat that is suddenly paralyzed in the rear legs and is vocalizing in pain. The sounds from the cat are always terrible and the family is always in shock. There really isnt anything we can do unless the event is treated within 30 mins and it isnt something that can be medically managed. These patients always get me when they come in cause I know 99% of the time there is nothing we can do to make them better except for strong pain meds and ending their suffering.
 ![A female doctor taking notes while a male patient holds his head, discussing difficult diagnoses. A female doctor taking notes while a male patient holds his head, discussing difficult diagnoses.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2148396692-6a856125e3cc3__700.jpg) In my field - brief psychotic disorder or schizophreniform disorder. It doesn’t always happen, but often they convert to schizophrenia.
 ![A male doctor examining a patient's throat, representing a common medical diagnosis procedure. A male doctor examining a patient's throat, representing a common medical diagnosis procedure.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/823-6a856162ab8fe__700.jpg) “I’ve had a sore spot on the side of my tongue for two months and it just isn’t going away”. It was squamous cell carcinoma, the patient was gone about 12 months later. The initial treatment actually went quite well apparently, but it metastasized.
 I'm a nurse.
A good friend of mine was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. As soon as he said the diagnosis, I knew it was likely in the late stages, and likely to be a terminal diagnosis. 
 Five year old carried in through the ER doors by dad, in complete cardiac and respiratory standstill due to a ping pong ball stuck in his throat. 
It was too late. So so sad. 
30yo single mom with two kids and new onset ALS.
First time I saw cervical cancer. Placed a speculum to do a Pap smear and just immediately knew I was looking at very advanced cancer. There was nothing that remotely looked recognizable as cervix.
I transported a woman with advanced CJD more than a decade ago. Her husband rode in the back with me and we chatted about it and her. He showed me the progressive imaging of her brain and told me that approximately two weeks prior she experienced unresolved tingling in her hands, so she went to the hospital and now she was going home for hospice. He explained she was a successful CFO, very active, etc. He generally looked bewildered and said everything was happening so fast he did not have time to process anything.. he was just trying to keep up with taking care of things as they came and keeping the family informed. I think about them a few times a year.
Liver failure in a 37 year old. Came in walking and talking, he thought it was his gallbladder. He died 48 hours later.
Advanced myelo-mesothelioma. Tragic. Gentleman worked his whole career at an asbestos plant.
My first week of clinicals as a family nurse practitioner student. Woman came in with advanced breast cancer. Had the peau d’orange skin covering half of her breast. First saw her by myself for the whole health history and exam. Part of me died inside when I saw it.
I used to work for a queer PCP in Manhattan, and I remember the doctor’s anxiety before having to tell a gay man that he had tested positive for HIV. (This was around 2010 or 2011.).
Miscarriages.
 I work in a long term acute care hospital, so we see all kinds of illnesses, wounds, etc. 
After many surgeries, attempts at wound care and A LOT of pain for the patient the doctors had to change their diagnosis to "Skin Failure".
Basically no matter the intervention, the skin, like any other organ can, just quit doing what it needed to do. Wouldn't heal, wouldn't regulate fluid balances or temperatures, etc.
Of course, with it came the inevitable comfort care conversation and a very sad family. 
An autoimmune disorder that attacks your own red blood cells. Patient had a hemoglobin in like the fours. But a transfusion could send her body into a spiral. That one was crazy. But the one that always makes me terrified is epiglottitis. Where you're epiglottis swells up and you can't breathe.
I used to work on a leukaemia unit and even though I worked with leukaemia patients all day every day a brand new acute leukaemia patient would always fill me with dread. I never stopped feeling absolutely terrible for these patients.
 Got a patient who was supposed to be a simple stroke workup, which didn’t turn out to be so simple. His symptoms were non focal and really all over the place. Multiple sclerosis was on the top of the list for the differential, but was not what it actually ended up being. Turns out the guy had Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease. Over the few days of admission his symptoms significantly worsened. He initially asked for a second opinion but ultimately decided against it. He was discharged home in less than a week, died at home on hospice 2 weeks later.
He was the second person I have known of to get CJD. My coworker’s mom died the same way a couple years earlier. 
I am a therapist and there are a few. I used to work primarily with kids and I specialize in neurodevelopmental disorders. Rett's is awful. I worked with a teenager a year watching her decline further and further knowing that her end was coming and there was nothing anyone could do. Her parents were lucky and had the ability to afford the best of care for her other parents have not been that lucky. I eventually had to stop. There was just nothing I could do anymore.
End stage liver disease in the undiagnosed alcoholic.
 Paramedic here.
Once had a 4yo that managed to put a key into an outlet. There was a loud nouse and the fuses tripped, but the kid was fine. Just had a big scare. My stomach was one big knot on the drive there. Might have done 50 in a 30 zone... 
One that still makes me think about it, 35yo woman, 4th pregnancy, previous 3 were all c-sections du to anatomy of mom, and she reported her water breaking and contractions about 10mins apart and the incision site hurt a lot. She was told she'd need to have another c-section, and had already agreed, by her OB team and when we got to L&D the nurse/midwife didn't seem to take me seriously when I said 4th pregnancy, contractions now 4mins apart, previous 3 were c-sections and the incision/scar hurts. (That was one of the red flag things I was taught. Pain at c-section scar - more than normal contractions - could mean tearing of the scar tissue/uterus)
I wonder if the pt and baby are alright. 
Terminal cancer in a child, certain birth defects diagnosed in utero.
 As a vet tech- osteosarcoma. 
An owner brings their dog in because it started limping and developed a “knot” on the leg the day before. We take x-rays and find bone cancer. 
Osteosarcoma is also one of those cancers that spreads so fast that in a lot of cases it’s already metastasized elsewhere by the time we find the osteosarcoma, and it’s aggressive with a poor prognosis. 
It’s just me, my fellow tech, and the vet looking at the screen knowing we are about to ruin someone’s day and give them awful news for what they probably thought was a sprain or fracture. 
Oncology PA here. Anytime I have to diagnose a malignancy in someone under the age of 30 a little piece of my soul dies.
Vascular ehlers danlos. Very rare but terrifying.
summary: Medical professionals and healthcare workers share the heartbreaking and devastating diagnoses that have profoundly impacted them throughout their careers. The stories highlight the immense emotional toll of delivering news regarding terminal illnesses, sudden tragedies, and severe conditions to patients and their families. These firsthand accounts demonstrate the heavy psychological burden that medical staff quietly carry in their private lives.
key_points: Healthcare workers shared the most difficult diagnoses they have had to deliver, ranging from advanced cancers to aggressive infections.
Neuromuscular specialists described the dread of recognizing signs of ALS during routine patient testing.
Ultrasound technicians and nurses recounted the deep sorrow of identifying terminally failed pregnancies and infant loss.
Other traumatic examples included fast-moving flesh-eating diseases, severe genetic metabolic disorders, and unexpected pediatric brain tumors.

title: US kindergarten vaccination rates dip as exemptions hit record high
author: Jessica Glenza
content:
A week after Donald Trump made a series of misleading claims about vaccines – including that some injections look “like the size of a soda bottle” – the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released the latest data on national kindergarten vaccination rates.
CDC communications downplayed the changes – a three-sentence announcement said, “overall vaccination rates among kindergarteners remained high” – but medical experts immediately saw cause for concern in the trends.
“There’s been a decrease in immunization rates in all vaccines. There’s a decrease in immunizations in more than half the states, as opposed to the year before. There are at least 280,000 kindergarteners who did not get the [measles, mumps and rubella vaccine],” said Dr Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center and an attending physician in the division of infectious diseases at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (Chop).
Additionally, non-medical exemptions for vaccines for kindergarteners grew by 17% over the last school year – the highest single-year increase ever, from 3.6% to 4.2% nationwide.
Pediatricians, local health officials and vaccine experts, such as Offit, described the latest vaccine data as evidence of how the administration – through almost too many means to enumerate – has sowed confusion about the safety and benefits of vaccines, leading to depressed vaccination rates and parents’ efforts to opt-out.
“If we had a secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) who was an actual secretary of HHS instead of an anti-vaccine activist and science denialist, he would stand up in front of the American public and say, ‘Vaccinate your children.’ – please, vaccinate your children,” he said.
Even so, the picture is not entirely bleak. The overwhelming majority of American parents still vaccinate their children. Data released by the CDC showed that vaccination dropped by only 0.1% between the last two school years, to 92.4% of children vaccinated with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
While there is a high overall rate of vaccination, parents who refuse vaccination are not evenly distributed around the United States. Often, low vaccination rates are found in pockets, such as in Idaho or Ohio. The US is currently experiencing the worst year for measles since 1991, where there have been hundreds of cases in Utah and South Carolina.
“In Cleveland, for example, a couple years ago, our percentage of kindergartners being up-to-date on vaccines was 68%,” said Dr David Margolius, director of the Cleveland Department of Public Health. “This past school year, we’re up to 76%. We are doing the work.”
However, “the federal government is causing more and more confusion, and that’s washing out the effects and the work that all of us are trying to do,” Margolius added.
Vaccines have saved millions of lives globally. Widespread measles vaccination alone is credited with saving 59 million lives between 2000 and 2024, according to the World Health Organization. Prior to widespread US vaccination in the mid-20th century, measles killed roughly 500 people per year.
Still, vaccines have been under attack for decades by well-known activists who have linked vaccines to rising rates of autism. Autism has been linked to some infections, parental age and genetics, but because it is a complex spectrum disorder, experts argue there will be more than one single cause, according to Chop.
The height of recent confusion came directly from the White House. On 10 August, the US president sat and signed an executive order calling for fewer vaccines, flanked by Robert F Kennedy Jr and his new nominee for the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Dr Heidi Overton. He then proceeded to link vaccines to autism (without evidence) and soda bottle-sized doses (a wild falsehood), assertions he said were supported by “gold standard” science (they’re not).
He then signed an executive order that called for the US to reduce the number of vaccines children routinely receive, from 17 diseases to 11, and critically administer the MMR vaccines as three separate doses.
“We have the MMR, which hopefully will be split up. We have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations given at separate times,” said Trump. “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal, and separately it looks like they are not at all lethal,” he said, without any evidence.
Trump clearly stated the potential impact of this: “You should have five separate visits for vaccines, rather than getting them all in the same day.”
Aside from the obvious logistical barriers for parents of newborns, who would suddenly be tasked with medically unnecessary doctor’s visits, there are legal and manufacturing barriers. Drug companies have not produced separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines in decades, and doing so would require companies to reengineer supply lines on some of their least profitable products.
Then legally, the federal government may recommend vaccines, but it’s the states who set policies about the vaccines children must receive before attending public school – requirements that are arguably the most effective way to get children vaccinated.
Indeed, one of the quirks of American public health law is that the constitution delegates the health and welfare of Americans to states. Trump’s symbolic order marks a high point, but certainly not the depth of anti-vaccine advocacy.
The MMR vaccine has been targeted since 1998, when discredited former doctor Andrew Wakefield published studies in The Lancet linking the two. His studies fell apart under scrutiny and are now retracted. Investigative journalist Brian Deer revealed that Wakefield patented a measles vaccine months before his study was released, and Wakefield infamously called for separating the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines.
Kennedy took up the mantle before he became health secretary. He led an anti-vaccine advocacy group called Children’s Health Defense, a non-profit that was one of the world’s most prolific spreaders of false and misleading vaccine claims. His 2023 salary at the nonprofit was $325,056 (while on leave campaigning for president) and $510,515 in 2022, according to nonprofit tax filings. Additionally, Kennedy earned $1.5m for “referral fees” from Wisner Baum and $62,500 from Morgan & Morgan, both law firms leading vaccine injury cases, according to ethics disclosures first published by Politico.
“The first concern with MMR is typically autism,” said Dr Mysheika Roberts, commissioner of the public health department in Columbus, Ohio. Dr Roberts was scheduled to serve on the CDC’s advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP) before being fired by Kennedy in June 2025.
Kennedy has continued his work against vaccines as health secretary, often under the banner of “gold standard” science. He falsely claimed that the MMR vaccine contained “aborted fetal debris”, and in the midst of a measles outbreak in Texas in 2025, recommended vitamin A supplementation, which led to children being hospitalized for liver dysfunction.
Kennedy amended the CDC’s website to assert that, “The claim ‘vaccines do not cause autism’ is not an evidence-based claim because studies have not ruled out the possibility that infant vaccines cause autism.” In fact, studies have examined the claim that vaccines cause autism and, across large population studies in multiple countries, found no evidence for the claim.
He disbanded the CDC’s group of expert advisors on vaccines, and replaced them with a group ideologically aligned with himself. The recommendations of Kennedy’s hand-picked group are now the subject of litigation.
What’s more, changing federal recommendations have made it significantly harder to get certain vaccines, such as for Covid-19. That led a pregnant doctor to sue the HHS because she could not obtain the Covid-19 shot.
“[Kennedy] is waging a war against vaccines because he believes … there is an epidemic of chronic diseases in this country. He believes vaccines are a major cause of that epidemic, and therefore he is going to do everything he can to lessen vaccines.
“He said that when he runs into a parent holding a child on a hiking or walking path, he goes up to them and says, ‘Don’t vaccinate your child,’” said Offit. “That’s who he is – a zealot – and that’s why he ignores the vaccine epidemic data.”
summary: Data from the CDC shows a decrease in US kindergarten vaccination rates and a record 17% increase in non-medical exemptions over the past school year. Medical experts attribute these declining rates to growing confusion and misinformation propagated by federal officials, including the president and the Health and Human Services secretary. Despite these concerning trends and localized outbreaks, the vast majority of American parents still vaccinate their children.
key_points: National kindergarten vaccination rates have dipped, with declines noted across more than half of US states.
Non-medical vaccine exemptions for kindergarteners rose to a record 4.2% nationwide.
Federal leaders have promoted unsubstantiated claims linking vaccines to autism and issued executive orders urging a reduction in routine childhood vaccines.
The US is currently experiencing its worst year for measles cases since 1991, with outbreaks reported in states including Utah and South Carolina.

title: 8 Things Geriatricians Wish More People Did Before They Got Older
author: Jillian Wilson
content:
“Longevity” is the buzzword of the moment on social media. Everyone wants to live longer and healthier. And while some factors aren’t in your control, many habits will greatly impact your longevity and quality of life as you age.
“It really is a lifetime of health that makes you have healthy ageing and good longevity and good healthspan,” said Dr Elizabeth Eckstrom, a professor of medicine in the division of general internal medicine and geriatrics at Oregon Health and Science University School of Medicine.
Even aspects of your early life, such as your childhood education, can affect how you age, according to Dr David Nace, a geriatrician at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center.
That said, “no matter what age you are, you can start now and still have huge benefits from doing things – don’t let anyone think it’s too late to start with lifestyle changes,” Eckstrom noted.
Below, geriatric medicine experts share the habits they wish folks would commit to throughout their lives, whether they’re 22 or 92.
1. Prioritise exercise
Physical activity is paramount for healthy ageing. Dr Nace said it’s specifically important to stay active through midlife, which he defined as ages 35 to 64, though you should prioritise it outside of this timeframe, too.
Getting exercise doesn’t have to mean going to the gym or a workout class (although those are great options). It can mean going for a walk or gardening, if that’s what you prefer, Dr Nace said.
Staying active helps you sleep better, feel better, manage your weight, and reduces the risk of arthritis. “It just has benefits all the way around,” Dr Nace added.
2. Consider trying tai chi.
“When I talk about exercise, I talk mostly about tai chi,” Dr Eckstrom said.
Research shows that doing tai chi reduces the risk of falls in older adults by about 60%. “Falls [are] one of the major reasons that people have disability and death over age 65,” Dr Eckstrom noted.
“But some of our newer work shows that it also improves brain function, so if you do tai chi two to three hours per week on average, it will give you an additional three to six years of healthy brain life. That’s a lot,” she said.
Doing tai chi regularly also lowers blood pressure and cholesterol and reduces pain. “So, everybody should be doing tai chi ... start young, do it your entire life,” Dr Eckstrom said.
![Residents practice tai chi along the Grand Canal in Gucheng County, Hengshui City, north China's Hebei Province, June 5, 2026.](https://img.huffingtonpost.com/asset/6a84e23e2200001b28ad373f.jpeg?ops=scalefit_720_noupscale)
3. Protect your hearing
According to Dr Kenneth Koncilja, a geriatric medicine specialist at Cleveland Clinic, protecting your hearing from damage as you get older is crucial for healthy ageing.
“A lot of people wish they would have had some hearing protection when they were younger to reduce hearing loss when they’re older,” Dr Koncilja said.
Hearing loss also impacts socialisation as people age. “People with better hearing later in life socialise more,” Dr Koncilja added.
There are also cognitive benefits that happen when you protect your hearing. “It’s a modifiable risk factor for dementia – so, something you can do, preventing hearing loss and treating hearing loss and addressing hearing loss, can actually reduce your risk of dementia, which is a big deal,” Dr Koncilja said.
4. Address vision loss
According to Dr Koncilja, it’s also crucial to address any vision loss. “If you can’t really see, you don’t walk as much. If you don’t walk as much, you’re not as active,” Dr Nace said. And, again, staying active is crucial for healthy ageing.
You don’t read as much or go out as much if you can’t see well, either, which makes isolation more common, he said. This is an important way to lower your dementia risk, added Dr Nace.
5. Follow a nutritious diet
What you eat is important all throughout your lifespan, and the best diet to follow is the Mediterranean diet, according to Dr Eckstrom. This is a meal plan that’s high in fruit, veggies, nuts, seeds, whole grains, beans, plant-based proteins and fish.
“There are lots of other fad diets out there, but if you 100% follow the Mediterranean diet for your lifetime, there’s pretty good evidence that you can probably reduce your risk of Alzheimer’s dementia by at least 50% just from diet alone,” she said.
![Healthy aging isn’t totally in your control, but there are specific lifestyle habits that can help you live a long and healthy life.](https://img.huffingtonpost.com/asset/6a84a8fa230000bd5c7c9c54.jpeg?cache=PcwEWHcZSt&ops=scalefit_720_noupscale)
6. Don’t use tobacco products
“Don’t smoke. Don’t vape. No cigars. None of it is better than any of the rest of it,” Dr Nace stressed, noting that these behaviours add up and have a detrimental effect on your health.
Tobacco products are linked to cancer, and smoking is particularly linked to lung cancer.
“I think one of the things most people don’t realise ... there’s also stroke, heart disease and peripheral vascular disease, and one of the things that’s very clear is that vascular disease is related to the onset of dementia,” Dr Nace said.
“If you want to age, don’t smoke. And if you want to age well, don’t smoke. And if you are smoking, get help to quit,” Dr Koncilja added.
7. Limit your alcohol use
Excessive alcohol intake is also bad for ageing. “There’s a lot of arguments back and forth as to what a healthy alcohol intake is,” Dr Nace said, but making sure you limit your alcohol use is important for healthy ageing.
According to the World Health Organisation, “there is no form of alcohol consumption that is risk-free. Even low levels of alcohol consumption carry some risks and can cause harm.”
“The newest evidence reports that we should only be having two alcoholic drinks per week,” Dr Eckstrom said. “It markedly increases your risk of dementia. So, if you drink six drinks per week instead of two drinks per week, your risk of dementia goes up by 16%.”
And the more you drink, the more your dementia risk increases.
“It’s also carcinogenic, and if you drink more than two drinks per week, it increases your risk for cancer,” she noted. It also causes heart disease, liver disease, high blood pressure and many other illnesses.
8. Stay active when you retire
“Don’t retire and just sit. That’s the worst thing in the world,” said Dr Nace.
Staying active when you retire – cognitively, physically and socially – is key, the expert noted.
Your cognition suffers when you’re isolated and not challenging yourself in your day-to-day life. Keeping your mind active is one way to reduce your risk of dementia.
“Staying active, it gives you meaning in your life [and] that has benefits cognitively,” Dr Nace said. “The brain is still resilient and still can learn, and physically I think that also becomes important.”
During retirement, give yourself something to look forward to, whether that is babysitting grandkids, volunteering at a local food pantry, helping out at church or joining a book club with your neighbours.
“So often, I see people who just kind of withdraw, and that’s a recipe for disaster,” Dr Nace said.
summary: Geriatric experts emphasize that adopting healthy lifestyle habits at any age can significantly improve longevity and quality of life. Key recommendations include staying physically active, practicing tai chi, protecting hearing and vision, following a nutritious diet, and avoiding tobacco and excessive alcohol. Additionally, maintaining cognitive, physical, and social activity during retirement is crucial for healthy aging.
key_points: Prioritizing physical activity and considering tai chi can improve brain function and significantly reduce the risk of falls.
Protecting hearing and addressing vision loss help prevent isolation and lower the risk of dementia.
Following the Mediterranean diet and avoiding tobacco products reduce the risk of Alzheimer's dementia, cancer, and heart disease.
Limiting alcohol intake to a maximum of two drinks per week helps mitigate the risks of dementia and cancer.
Staying cognitively, physically, and socially active after retirement prevents isolation and supports overall health.

title: Expert tips to support your puppy’s early development
author: Helen Coffey
content:
Getting a new puppy is a tiny bit like having a new baby. There’s suddenly a new addition to the family – one that needs constant care, aeons of sleep, and is prone to waking its parents in the middle of the night with plaintive cries – around whom everything suddenly revolves.
And, like any new parents, puppy owners are naturally anxious to give their little one the best possible start in life. It can feel a little overwhelming, but a few simple principles can get things on the right track from day one.
Make sure your puppy gets enough sleep
![For their health, puppies’ sleep needs to be undisturbed and good quality](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/20/14/56/GettyImages-2280178423.jpg)
First of all, sleep: it turns out they need an awful lot of it, advises Cat Henstridge, widely known as ‘Cat the Vet’. “Puppies sleep an extraordinary amount; between about 18 and 20 hours a day,” she says. That sleep needs to be undisturbed and good quality for their health – “it’s important for growth and brain development and learning” – whereas if they get overtired, they’re likely to be cranky and start acting out. “A lot of what we perceive as bad behaviour in puppies is often due to the fact that they’re not getting enough sleep,” Cat adds.
Creating good sleep hygiene is key. Cat’s top tips include being respectful of your puppy’s sleep by leaving them alone when they’re slumbering, rather than disturbing them; ensuring they have a designated safe sleeping space they can go to, such as a crate; and learning to recognise when they’re overtired and in need of some more shut-eye.
Another fundamental piece of the puzzle lies in understanding the biological changes that puppies undergo and how to support them.
In the early stages, one issue to be aware of is the immunity gap. When a puppy initially feeds from their mother, they are drinking colostrum. “The mother is essentially sharing her immune system with the baby,” Cat explains. “She gives them immune protection via her milk.”
As the puppies mature, during their first six to eight weeks, that immune protection starts to wane while their own immune development isn’t fully developed yet. “There’s this point where they are more vulnerable, when their immune system is learning about the world and learning how to protect itself,” Cat says. “That’s the immunity gap and that’s what we work really hard to minimise and support during early development.”
Recommended diet for your dog
![“It’s really important that puppies are fed nutrition that’s specifically tailored to their body size and breed,” says Cat Henstridge, AKA Cat the Vet](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/20/10/22/GettyImages-1572226203.jpg)
One option is a diet enriched with colostrum, such as Purina Pro Plan Healthy Start, as it “has been shown to help support gut health and immune development in puppies”.
Some studies suggest colostrum may help support immune responses following vaccination.
More broadly, balanced, robust nutrition can be hugely impactful in supporting a puppy’s immune development — around 70 per cent of all immune cells are located in the gut. “What that means is that’s where a lot of the lymph nodes and lymph tissues, the places where your white blood cells, your body’s defense mechanisms reside,” clarifies Cat. “Having good gut health really does positively impact on good immune health, and the way to have good gut health is to have good nutrition.”
Another crucial function of nutrition is to support puppies’ growth. Medium and large breed dogs have got “an enormous amount of growing to do in that first year,” advises Cat. Some can go from 500g to 50kg within the first 18 months. “We want them to grow slowly and steadily and healthily,” adds Cat, “So it’s really important that puppies are fed nutrition that’s specifically tailored to their body size and breed. Purina Pro Plan, for example, produces specific diets for small and mini, medium, large athletic and large robust dogs.”
Supporting healthy growth for puppies boils down to a diet that’s balanced: good quality animal and plant proteins that are highly digestible and support muscle growth; adequate levels of fat to aid with skin, coat and brain development; carbohydrates for energy. Feeding your puppy adequate fibre is essential for their gut microbiome health, too.
Purina Pro Plan is enriched with omega-3 fatty acids
![“It’s never too early to start doing some recalls to teach them their names, to help them to learn to sit and to stay and to wait when you ask them to,” Cat the Vet says](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/20/10/55/GettyImages-1792762989.jpeg)
Essential healthy fats should also be a priority. “We should definitely be looking for diets like Purina Pro Plan that are enriched with omega-3 fatty acids like DHA and EPA, because they play an important role in brain development and may help support learning,” recommends Cat. She says studies have suggested puppies fed omega-3 enriched diets may show improvements in learning and memory tasks.
Speaking of training, when should it start? Right from the jump, according to Cat. “It’s never too early to start doing some recalls to teach them their names, to help them to learn to sit and to stay and to wait when you ask them to,” she says. “What you’re doing when you first get your puppy is building the bond; you’re building the trust; you’re creating that secure attachment. Your puppy needs to know to trust you and be in a partnership with you – and so really simple training and interactions right from the start are always helpful.”
How to socialise your pet and help them feel secure outdoors
![Before they’ve had their vaccines, a puppy papoose is great for taking your dog out and about](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/20/10/58/_GettyImages-1482354874.jpg)
Finally, socialising your puppy in the right way will have a massive impact on their wellbeing.
It’s all about calm, organised, secure introductions. “The aim of socialising is to normalise the world and help them cope – we don’t want to overwhelm our puppy,” stresses Cat. After a few days of letting them settle in and get to know their new immediate family, gradually introduce different humans – particularly children, if possible, so that they can get used to the fact that kids often behave more erratically than adults.
Cat’s number one tip when introducing pups to the big wide world is to get a puppy papoose for taking them out and about — before they’ve had their vaccines, puppies aren’t allowed to go on the ground outside. “It’s really helpful for them to see the world from a safe space and at a bit of a distance,” she says. “It means that, regardless of the size of your puppy, you can carry them in a way that they feel secure.”
Ultimately, if you support your puppy’s health and well-being through developing a good sleep routine, feeding them a nutritious diet of high-quality puppy food, and building a secure attachment through spending time together, training, and safe socialisation, you can’t go far wrong.
Find out more about pet nutrition and start supporting your pet through all stages of their lives today.
summary: Raising a new puppy successfully relies on establishing key principles for their early development, as advised by veterinarian Cat Henstridge. Essential steps include ensuring they get 18 to 20 hours of undisturbed sleep daily, feeding them a balanced, breed-specific diet tailored to support gut health and growth, and beginning early training and socialization. Proper care during these early stages helps build trust, ensures healthy development, and prevents common behavioral issues.
key_points: Puppies need 18 to 20 hours of undisturbed sleep daily for proper growth, brain development, and learning.
Good nutrition tailored to size and breed is crucial, as about 70 percent of immune cells are located in the gut.
Diets enriched with colostrum and omega-3 fatty acids like DHA and EPA support immune development and brain function.
Early training should begin immediately to build a bond of trust, teaching commands like sit, stay, and recall.
Calm socialization, including using a puppy papoose before vaccinations allow ground walking, helps puppies safely experience the world without becoming overwhelmed.

title: Doctors missed by small baby's 2kg tumour six times, then it spread
author: Alice Giddings
content:
![Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, with their daughter Florence. // A toddler whose belly ballooned was diagnosed with a 2kg tumour after doctors repeatedly told her parents she was constipated. Florence Wilde, two, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma - a rare cancer of the cell - in November 2024. Her parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, both 32, first noticed something was wrong when Florence became repeatedly rundown. The toddler's tummy began to swell so the pair rushed her to Three Villages GP in Stourbridge but doctors ruled out the symptoms as constipation, prescribing the tot laxatives. Photo released 21/08/2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309110805-8583.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
In 2024, parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde were pleading with doctors to do a blood test on their baby girl Florence.
Their one-year old’s belly had ballooned over the course of three weeks, but doctors told them six times over that she was simply constipated.
But Anna and Dom, 32, knew something wasn’t right and were vindicated when their daughter was diagnosed with neuroblastoma in November that year.
Florence’s tumour weighed 2kg, while she weighed just 13kg, meaning it made up nearly 15% of her body weight.
Neuroblastoma is a cancer almost always found in children and it develops from the cells left behind from a baby’s development in the womb. It occurs either in the sympathetic nervous system or closely associated adrenal glands and is usually found in the abdomen.
There are around 100 children diagnosed with it each year in the UK, meaning it’s responsible for about 6% of all childhood cancer diagnoses.
‘Florence was diagnosed a month after her first birthday,’ Anna, a clinical psychologist from Stourbridge, says. ‘There was a period of six weeks beforehand where she was poorly with one thing or another.
![Florence Wilde, in hospital with her father Dom. // A toddler whose belly ballooned was diagnosed with a 2kg tumour after doctors repeatedly told her parents she was constipated. Florence Wilde, two, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma - a rare cancer of the cell - in November 2024. Her parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, both 32, first noticed something was wrong when Florence became repeatedly rundown. The toddler's tummy began to swell so the pair rushed her to Three Villages GP in Stourbridge but doctors ruled out the symptoms as constipation, prescribing the tot laxatives. Photo released 21/08/2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308994328-0530-e1787394474490.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=600) 
‘She picked up infections, she had hand foot and mouth, she had antibiotics but remained off for a while.’
Then her tummy began to swell, so Anna and Dom were back and fourth with their daughter to their local GP.
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
‘We were told she was constipated at the GP,’ Anna explains. ‘For three weeks I had to force-feed her laxatives which was horrendous.’
The young mum says Florence was crying in pain and was unable to sleep on her own because she was in agony. Anna had to cradle her upright at night to help her get some rest.
‘When her stomach hadn’t gone down, doctors gave her more laxatives, but it was getting bigger,’ she says. ‘She wasn’t right and the laxatives weren’t helping so we had to keep pushing the doctors.’
But despite the parents’ growing concerns, doctors dismissed them. ‘On one occasion a GP said she’s fine and “let’s address the elephant in the room, we don’t think it’s cancer”,’ she adds.
They went to the doctor again for a final time, accompanied by Anna’s mother, who pushed for a blood test.
![Florence Wilde, in hospital with her father Dom. // A toddler whose belly ballooned was diagnosed with a 2kg tumour after doctors repeatedly told her parents she was constipated. Florence Wilde, two, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma - a rare cancer of the cell - in November 2024. Her parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, both 32, first noticed something was wrong when Florence became repeatedly rundown. The toddler's tummy began to swell so the pair rushed her to Three Villages GP in Stourbridge but doctors ruled out the symptoms as constipation, prescribing the tot laxatives. Photo released 21/08/2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308994199-ad10-e1787394604609.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=600) 
‘Her bloods were heightened and they referred us to the PAU (paediatric assessment unit) immediately,’ she says. ‘We had another doctor who felt her stomach. As soon as he felt her tummy he said he didn’t think it was poo, there were lumps and bumps.’
Anna says Florence was reassured her symptoms were constipation on at least six occasions in the three weeks before her diagnosis.
‘When the tumour was discovered it was 30cm, which was heart-breaking,’ she recalls. ‘She’s only small so that took up quite a lot of her.’
Florence underwent surgery at Birmingham Children’s Hospital on November 26, 2024 and started emergency chemotherapy the very next day.
Anna adds: ‘She had three months of induction chemotherapy to try and shrink the tumour. They thought the disease was in one place, in her stomach, they assumed it was localised.’
Sadly, further scans in January 2025 revealed Florence had metastatic, or stage 4 cancer, which happens when cells break away from the main tumour. In this case the disease spread to her spine.
![Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, with their daughter Florence. // A toddler whose belly ballooned was diagnosed with a 2kg tumour after doctors repeatedly told her parents she was constipated. Florence Wilde, two, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma - a rare cancer of the cell - in November 2024. Her parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, both 32, first noticed something was wrong when Florence became repeatedly rundown. The toddler's tummy began to swell so the pair rushed her to Three Villages GP in Stourbridge but doctors ruled out the symptoms as constipation, prescribing the tot laxatives. Photo released 21/08/2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308994185-6559-e1787394694436.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=600) 
‘We look back now, how did we think she was constipated because her stomach was massive?’ Anna says.
‘It grew rapidly in a few weeks, that’s why we have so much anger because if someone would have seen her the first time we went to the GP we could’ve caught this sooner.’
She had up to 95% of the tumour removed from her spine in March 2025, before beginning her first rounds of high-dose chemo just three weeks later.
Florence began five cycles of immunotherapy in October that year, before her parents were eventually told the tumour had stopped progressing in April 2026.
