‘All throughout we were told she was doing great,’ Anna says. ‘Every admission she was full of life throughout it, she was just incredible.
‘We’ve met families along the way who have been pushed back from GP’s and doctors more than what Florence’s has.
‘For us, I do think if she was diagnosed sooner it might have not been that large. We sat in that headspace for many months and it was horrifying. There was a lot of anger there.’
The family are now fundraising £100,000 to pay for anti-relapse treatment (DMFO) no longer offered by the NHS, after the treatment was withdrawn by the manufacturer from standard UK access routes, forcing people to pay for it out of their own pocket.
![Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, with their daughter Florence. // A toddler whose belly ballooned was diagnosed with a 2kg tumour after doctors repeatedly told her parents she was constipated. Florence Wilde, two, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma - a rare cancer of the cell - in November 2024. Her parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, both 32, first noticed something was wrong when Florence became repeatedly rundown. The toddler's tummy began to swell so the pair rushed her to Three Villages GP in Stourbridge but doctors ruled out the symptoms as constipation, prescribing the tot laxatives. Photo released 21/08/2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308994181-f341-e1787394768476.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=600) 
‘Florence has finished the gold standard NHS treatment, after that you can either watch and wait to see if the cancer comes back, or other families chose to do a relapse prevention treatment, but they aren’t NHS protocol,’ Anna says.

Subsequent scans revealed the cancer had metastasized to her spine, requiring extensive surgery, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy. Her family is now fundraising £100,000 to pay for anti-relapse treatment (DFMO) after it was withdrawn from standard UK NHS access routes.
key_points: Florence's parents were told six times over three weeks that her swollen belly was simply constipation before a blood test led to a cancer diagnosis.
The 2kg tumour made up nearly 15% of the toddler's total body weight when it was discovered.
Subsequent scans in January 2025 revealed the cancer had spread to her spine, classifying it as stage 4 metastatic neuroblastoma.
The family is raising funds for DFMO anti-relapse treatment because the medication is no longer offered on the NHS following its withdrawal by the manufacturer.

title: Seven simple ways to maintain muscle strength later in life
author: Camilla Foster
content:
As we age, many people notice small changes that make them feel a little weaker or slower.
Lucy Macdonald, a physiotherapist based in Surrey at Restart Physio, says many often don’t realise the cause is sarcopenia.
Here’s exactly what sarcopenia is and tips on how to stay strong later in life.
What is sarcopenia?
“Age-related sarcopenia is the process by which muscles get weaker as you get older,” explains Macdonald.
This condition is caused by a combination of factors, including the natural ageing process, physical inactivity and changes to hormonal levels.
“There are some factors, like hormonal changes, that people can’t do anything about. For example, decreasing levels of testosterone in men and women as they get older can be a factor,” says Macdonald. “However, we are in control of our activity levels.
![Sarcopenia is caused by a combination of factors](https://static.the-independent.com/2025/12/03/14/03092516-6ac8fa45-521a-4cbc-8504-aaa94cfbbdcf.jpg)
“A lot of people will reduce their activity levels, in part just because of general lifestyle but also sometimes because of fear of injury, and actually these things can significantly contribute to muscle wasting as well.”
She highlights that she usually sees sarcopenia in patients who are in two particular phases of life.
“The first one would be people in their late 40s because around that age, people’s lives tend to be very busy,” says Macdonald. “They’ve got busy careers and often have caring responsibilities for kids and older relatives. So, in terms of the amount of time they have to stay active, that’s quite a sort of crunch point.
“Sarcopenia is also very prevalent in the early 60s age range. At this age, people are thinking of retiring which is another turning point as some people will have a really active retirement and some will do considerably less.”
What are some symptoms that might suggest you have sarcopenia?
“Finding it difficult to get out of a chair or to go up and down stairs easily are two key indicators,” says Macdonald. “If you start to notice that you’re struggling a bit to get that power to do these things without using your upper body, I would seek professional advice about this.”
How can sarcopenia impact your daily life?
“Day-to-day things like carrying your shopping or playing with the grandkids might become difficult,” says Macdonald. “So many things involve physical activity, and if you haven’t got the muscle strength to do it you’re going to start to enjoy these activities less.
![Sarcopenia is also very prevalent in the early 60s age range](https://static.the-independent.com/2025/12/03/14/03093242-2cdc0e04-f0e5-45a0-b113-42581d218f53.jpg)
“It could also become painful to do things. Sarcopenia is considered to be a significant contributing factor to joint pain which can really affect people’s quality of life.”
Can you slow down the progression of sarcopenia or prevent it?
“The best thing to do to slow down the progression of sarcopenia or to prevent it is strength work,” says Macdonald. “A physio can give you specific exercises to strengthen your muscles in relation to the things that you want to be able to achieve.
“For example, if you wanted to be able to take your grandchildren to the park, then a physio can help you strengthen the muscles that are involved in that.”
What are your top tips for building and maintaining muscle later in life?
Try sit and stand exercises
“When you’ve just got out of bed in the morning, try sitting on the edge of your bed and standing up and sitting down again in a controlled way, and repeat that 30 times,” says Macdonald. “Sit to stand is basically a squat and you can progress by adding a bit of weight to this exercise or try doing it on a lower surface, such as a sofa.”
Wall press-ups
“Lean as much of your body weight as you can against your hands on a wall, and then just gently bend and straighten your elbows,” recommends Macdonald.
Introduce weights under the guidance of a professional
“Slowly introduce some lifting exercises under the guidance of either a physio or a personal trainer,” recommends Macdonald. “They will help you learn a bit more about your own body and how important strength is, and will also provide some encouragement.”
Increase the weight gradually
“If you suddenly launch into doing weights, you will probably get injured,” warns Macdonald. “By overloading them, you’ll get tears in the muscle, which can be very painful and you’ll end up weaker, rather than stronger. So, you want to start low and increase the weight gradually.”
Join a group
“There are lots of groups out there where you can go and do resistance training and use weights in a group setting,” says Macdonald. “The advantage of doing exercise in a group is that you’re more likely to stick to it.”
Don’t be afraid
“Try not to let fear get in the way of getting strong,” advises Macdonald. “Although fear of injury is very normal, fear often ends up increasing the likelihood of getting injured because if you don’t use it, you lose it.”
Remember that losing strength isn’t inevitable
“Just because it’s harder to be strong as we get older doesn’t mean that it’s not possible,” says Macdonald. “I’ve seen some incredibly strong older people, so there’s full potential to be strong later in life. You have control over it, so getting weaker and weaker as you age is not an inevitable thing.”
summary: Age-related sarcopenia is a condition where muscles get weaker due to factors like the natural aging process, hormonal changes, and physical inactivity. Physiotherapist Lucy Macdonald notes that it is often prevalent in people during their late 40s and early 60s when lifestyles change. However, individuals can manage or prevent muscle wasting by staying active, performing strength exercises, and gradually introducing weights under professional guidance.
key_points: Sarcopenia is caused by a combination of aging, hormonal shifts, and reduced physical activity.
Common indicators include struggling to rise from a chair or walk up and down stairs easily.
Strength work, such as sit-and-stand exercises and wall press-ups, can slow or prevent muscle loss.
Lifting weights should be introduced and increased gradually under professional supervision to avoid injury.
Maintaining strength later in life is controllable and not an inevitable consequence of aging.

title: Heartbroken woman tells boyfriend 'leave me' after being diagnosed with aggressive cancer - AOL
author: Liam McInerney
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![Lydia Whelan](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/8cb5539f-3d7b-4cf9-bc47-02edbc5b22ea.jpg)
A woman revealed the heartbreaking conversations she had with her loved ones after being diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of just 32 — including telling her boyfriend to leave her.
Lydia Whelan and her long-term partner Colm had just been given the green light on a house sale agreement when their lives took an unexpected turn two years ago.
Just one week before the sale was agreed, Lydia, who is from County Kildare, Ireland, was visiting her doctor after spotting a change in her breast.
And on July 30, 2024, Colm was by Lydia’s side at St James’s Hospital in Dublin when a doctor confirmed she had cancer. It was later confirmed to be aggressive and stage two.
In an emotional interview with Dublin Dialogues, Lydia remembered: “I just erupted and my partner erupted and I was like, ‘I knew it.’
![Lydia Whelan](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/29f6d674-5a00-4ce9-97c9-6d124fe35da4.jpg)
“Then very quickly I was like, ‘How am I going to tell my mother?’ It was all like a lot of emotions and feelings kind of came at once and I found myself sitting there… myself and my partner after going ‘sale agreed’ on our home in the middle of all this.
“So that was very daunting.”
Due to her diagnosis, Lydia, a support worker for adults with intellectual disabilities, could not get approval for mortgage protection, and there was a fear that she could lose the house.
And being remarkably honest, she said: “I have said it before to a lot of people, I was more upset about the potential of losing my house than I was of being told I had cancer because I was looking at the future, myself and my partner for 10 years together at that point, this was the next stage for us.”
She added: “I was like, ‘I don’t know how I’m going to cope.’ If we lose our house, I was telling him to leave me. I was like, ‘I’m holding you back.’
![Lydia and Colm](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/17a0df03-3c30-4daa-ae09-33c4f9da88ee.jpg)
“It’s conversations that you don’t expect to have at the age of 32.”
And in another heartbreaking conversation, this time with her parents, she revealed: “I remember going home to my mum and dad and I was still living at home at this point and I just burst out crying. I was like, ‘I don’t want to lose my hair.’”
Thankfully, Lydia’s partner, family and friends offered nothing but love and support, and she said she would not have gotten through her treatment without them.
Lydia is now a cancer survivor after several brutal rounds of chemotherapy and she said the last two years still feels surreal to her.
“There was a lot of questions,” she said. “A lot of hurt, a lot of anger, a lot of why me? Like, how? I was healthy. I was on a fitness journey.”
![Lydia Whelan](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/2aa01d43-88b2-429f-8144-6df50e70343c.jpg)
She added: “It’s been the roughest rollercoaster I could have ever imagined. It’s not something you know how to deal with or are told how to deal with.”
Lydia started her chemotherapy at the end of August 2024 and she gave a devastating insight into how difficult it was.
“It absolutely wipes you, takes away what you see in the mirror,” she said. “I really struggled with that aspect. Still to this day I do. But my friends and my family, the support network I have is amazing.”
Lydia, who also had radiation and surgery, was extremely ill during and towards the end of her chemotherapy and at one point she felt unable to complete another two rounds to take the total to six.
However, while some days she would cry for hours, there were others when she remained positive and looked towards the future. She is now living a beautiful life having completed her treatment.
![Lydia Whelan](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/b2723bfe-bcb5-4995-b875-28c75583e904.jpg)
Her house sale went through after Colm had to draw down the mortgage by himself and this December will mark two years since she and Colm moved in together. Lydia must now wait another four years before she can be named on the mortgage when she will officially be in remission.
She now shares her story to raise awareness about breast cancer and in a message to others, she said: “I continue to drive home about checking yourself every month.
“People have come up to me and said, ‘I’m afraid to check myself because of what I’d find.’
“And it’s wild how that’s someone’s thoughts on it. And I’m like, ‘Yeah, but if I didn’t find it when I found it, I would not be here today. There’s no might. I wouldn’t.’
“My cancer was spreading very very fast. I would not be sitting here today.”
She said she now lives her best life, just as she did before her cancer diagnosis, and says “yes to everything”.
Lydia, now 34, added: “It’s given me a new lease of life. As hard as the journey has been, I now don’t stress about the small things. I take a beat. I would have been a very quite anxious and nervous person.”
She added: “I’m still here, I’m still alive, I’m still breathing. I’m just grateful for every day that now if I do have a bad day, I’m angry at myself for having a bad day.
“But as humans, we’re always hard on ourselves. But no, continue to looking forward to even the small things in life.
“A cup of coffee, fresh air, the sun. Little things that we so easily take for granted."
summary: At age 32, Lydia Whelan was diagnosed with aggressive stage two breast cancer just as she and her partner Colm agreed to buy a house. Overwhelmed by the diagnosis and the fear of losing their new home due to mortgage protection issues, she heartbreakingly told her partner to leave her. Following rigorous chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery with the support of her loved ones, Lydia is now a survivor and shares her story to urge others to regularly check themselves for breast cancer.
key_points: Lydia Whelan was diagnosed with aggressive stage two breast cancer at age 32, just a week after she and her partner Colm agreed to buy a house.
Due to mortgage protection complications, Whelan feared losing the home and initially told her partner to leave her.
She underwent intense treatment, including chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery, supported by her family and partner.
Whelan successfully completed her treatment, and Colm secured the mortgage independently so they could move into their home.
She now shares her story to encourage others to regularly check themselves for breast cancer and appreciates life's smaller moments.

title: The unexpected and visible places STIs will show up on your body
author: Alice Giddings
content:
![the concept of prostate and bladder problem, crotch pain of a young person .](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309142473-4a8c.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
When it comes to sexually transmitted diseases, it’s typically an itching or a burning sensation in your privates that makes you think something’s up.
But, it’s not just our genitals we should be worried about. It turns out there are far more unexpected places on our bodies that symptoms can manifest.
And with 402,000 new STI diagnoses in 2025 alone, it seems some of us may need a refresher course in some of the less obvious signs we might need to go to a sexual health clinic.
‘STIs don’t always follow the textbook pattern people expect,’ superintendent pharmacist at Chemist Click, Abbas Kanani, says.
‘It can affect different parts of the body depending on the type of infection and how it has been transmitted, and it shouldn’t automatically be ruled out as having nothing to do with your sexual health.’
The palms of your hands
A rash on the palms of your hands can actually be a later symptom of syphilis, and it can sometimes spread all over your body. This can develop if the STI has been left untreated.
‘Syphilis is one of those infections that can present in ways people simply would not associate with an STI,’ pharmacist Thorrun Govind tells Metro.
‘Later symptoms can include a rash on the palms of the hands which isn’t usually itchy, but it can be mistaken for a number of more familiar skin conditions like eczema, psoriasis or an allergic reaction.’
![Doctor checking sexually transmitted disease , STD on infected patient skin under magnifying glass](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309142498-dea7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
What’s challenging is this rash can look quite different from person to person. While Thorrun explains you cannot catch syphilis from hand-to-hand touching, you could catch it from touching an infected fluid-filled sore called a chancre.
The soles of your feet
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
The soles can also be affected by the characteristic rash seen during secondary syphilis. Again, the rash may spread across the body and can be subtle enough to go unnoticed.
‘A rash on the feet is easy to put down to something like athlete’s foot or irritation from footwear,’ Abbas explains. ‘But if you notice an unusual rash on both the palms and soles, particularly alongside other unexplained symptoms, it’s worth getting it checked rather than assuming it’s simply a skin problem.’
If you have a rash like this which also coincides with swollen glands, tiredness and unprotected sex, you’ll want to get yourself down to clinic for an STI test.
The eyes
Not even our eyeballs are safe when it comes to symptoms from sexually transmitted diseases.
And, this time it’s gonorrhoea that’s the likely culprit. ‘Gonorrhoea can reach the eye if infectious genital fluid is transferred there by the hands,’ Thorrun explains.
![Close up of a woman showing a red infected eye with conjunctivitis. Health care concept](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309142452-6a76.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
This can cause redness, pain and discharge, and Thorrun adds it can lead to a serious condition called gonococcal conjunctivitis, which requires urgent medical attention to prevent permanent eye damage.
Untreated syphilis can also affect the eyes and cause symptoms such as eye pain, redness and changes in vision.
The throat
Yes, we just gulped, too. But it’s not difficult to realise why a bad throat could be a symptom of an STI.
‘The throat can be exposed to sexually transmitted diseases through oral sex,’ Thorrun explains. ‘Infections such as gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis, herpes and HPV can all affect the throat.’
Superintendent pharmacist Abbas admits that a sore throat is much more likely to be caused by a common respiratory infection than an STI, but says sexual contact can expose the throat to certain infections.’
The joints
This one is much easier to misdiagnose, because some STIs can spread to the joints.
In rare instances, gonorrhoea can spread to the bloodstream and joints, and other STIs can prompt a case of reactive arthritis.
Symptoms can include painful, stiff or swollen joints. ‘Unexplained joint pain isn’t something most people would immediately associate with an STI,’ says Abbas.
‘But, if joint symptoms develop alongside a rash, eye problems, urinary symptoms or other signs of infection, it’s worth seeking medical advice.’
![Close-up of a woman applying topical cream to a cold sore on her lower lip, illustrating personal care, home treatment, skincare routine, minor injury care and medical self-treatment concepts.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309142458-c95d.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
The mouth and lips
‘A painless mouth ulcer or sore is very common and usually has nothing to do with an STI,’ Abbas explains. But, the mouth and lips are a very vulnerable spot for sexually transmitted diseases from oral sex.
‘The risk can be higher if there are cuts, sores or broken skin in or around the mouth, because this can provide an easier route for infection,’ Thorrun adds.
For example, syphilis can cause painless sores in areas including the mouth and lips, meaning an infection can sometimes be present without obvious genital symptoms.
‘A persistent or unusual sore, particularly after sexual contact with a new partner, shouldn’t simply be ignored,’ Abbas says. ‘Syphilis sores can be painless, which means people may not recognise them as a sign of infection.’
The anus and rectum
This might be far less surprising, but it’s worth an honourable mention. It’s not just the penis and the vagina that can be affected downstairs, but the anus and rectum, too.
- 
	![Young woman in bed with her arms by her head](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307896638-cbfc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0px%2C0px%2C2500px%2C1406px&resize=646%2C363)
- Dirty hotel sex made up for this big disappointment after 10 years of marriage
- Iconic '90s chocolate bar with controversial past makes its return to Asda's shelves
- I let my 4-year-old have unlimited screen time - I don't care what the experts say
Gonorrhoea and chlamydia can infect the rectum and can cause symptoms like discharge, soreness, itching, bleeding or pain when passing poo – although many infections also cause no symptoms.
‘People can feel embarrassed talking about symptoms affecting the anus, but they’re important symptoms to mention,’ Abbas says.

- ![Parents can save up to 30% on Kickers school shoes ahead of the new term](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307346057-1e66.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=635&crop=1) Parents can save up to 30% on Kickers school shoes ahead of the new term

‘Some infections in this area cause no noticeable symptoms at all, so testing is particularly important following unprotected anal sex or if you’ve been told a partner has an STI.’

summary: Sexually transmitted infections can manifest in various unexpected parts of the body beyond the genitals. According to health experts, symptoms such as rashes, sores, and inflammation can appear on the hands, feet, eyes, throat, joints, and mouth. Recognizing these less obvious signs is crucial for proper testing and treatment.
key_points: Untreated syphilis can cause a non-itchy rash on the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet.
Gonorrhoea can reach the eyes via the hands, potentially causing gonococcal conjunctivitis.
Oral sex can expose the throat and mouth to infections like gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and syphilis, leading to sore throats or painless sores.
Certain STIs can spread to the bloodstream and joints, resulting in painful, stiff, or swollen joints.

title: 'My OCD is so bad I spend seven hours taking a shower'
author: Ciara Healy
content:
'My OCD is so bad I spend seven hours taking a shower' says South Yorkshire woman
South Yorkshire woman describes debilitating OCD
A woman's OCD is so bad she spends seven hours taking a shower.
It has also caused her to have intrusive thoughts about attacking her family members with a kitchen knife.
Victoria Korlewala, aged 20, first began to have symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder, a mental health condition characterised by intrusive thoughts and compulsions at age 13, when she became obsessed by the idea that she smelled bad.
![Victoria Korlewala, 20](https://www.thestar.co.uk/jpim-static/image/2026/08/22/9/27/i-have-to-hide-1591181.jpg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=640&quality=65)
![placeholder image](https://www.thestar.co.uk/img/placeholder.jpg)
She then became convinced that she was a "bad person", and was unable to look at a kitchen knife without a graphic image of her using it to stab someone forming in her head.
Victoria, from Doncaster, says her OCD is now so debilitating that it takes her up to seven hours to have a shower, as she is convinced her body is contaminated or dirty.
She is only able to go to the toilet once every two days, as her handwashing routine takes so long, and is hoping to have a catheter fitted to alleviate the pain of having to hold in her wee for so long.
For the last two years she has only left the house for hospital appointments.
Victoria, who is hoping to go to university to study biomedical sciences when her symptoms improve, said: "Every time I'd go into the kitchen, I'd see an image of myself attacking my family with a kitchen knife.
"I had to completely avoid looking at the knives.
"I knew I would never do something like that, but the OCD made it seem so real, and as though it was about to happen.
"My showers take up to seven hours, and I can't go to the bathroom regularly as my handwashing routine takes up to 11 hours."
!["My showers take up to seven hours, and I can't go to the bathroom regularly as my handwashing routine takes up to 11 hours."](https://www.thestar.co.uk/jpim-static/image/2026/08/22/9/15/i-have-to-hide-1589316.jpg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=640&quality=65)
![placeholder image](https://www.thestar.co.uk/img/placeholder.jpg)
When the COVID pandemic hit in 2020, Victoria's symptoms began to ease, as she was no longer around people in school, so she wasn't worried that her classmates were talking about her.
However, in 2021, she started obsessively washing her hands, to the point where she would be late for school due to her handwashing routine.
Around this time, Victoria also began to experience morality OCD, where a person becomes convinced they are a bad person.
She then began to experience harm OCD, a subtype where sufferers experience intrusive thoughts about causing harm to themselves or others.
Every time Victoria would walk into the kitchen and see a kitchen knife, her brain would show her a violent image of herself attacking someone with it.
She went to the doctors, and was diagnosed with OCD in July 2021.
"When I was diagnosed, I felt happy that I wasn't going crazy," she said.
Victoria is currently on anti-depressants and anti-psychotics to try and help manage her condition.
In six month's time, Victoria is set to start inpatient Exposure and Response Prevention therapy (ERP), which helps sufferers to face anxiety-inducing situations whilst resisting compulsions, at Springfield Hospital in Tooting, London, which she hopes will alleviate her symptoms.
Victoria shares insights into how her symptoms affect her daily life on her TikTok channel @victoriaocd to raise awareness that OCD isn’t just about “organising or cleaning”.
summary: Victoria Korlewala, a 20-year-old from Doncaster, suffers from severe obsessive-compulsive disorder that causes debilitating symptoms, including showers lasting up to seven hours and distressing intrusive thoughts of harming her family. Diagnosed with OCD in July 2021, she experiences severe contamination fears, handwashing routines, and morality OCD. She is currently managing her condition with medication and anticipates starting inpatient Exposure and Response Prevention therapy at Springfield Hospital.
key_points: Victoria's OCD symptoms cause her to spend up to seven hours taking a shower due to contamination fears.
She experiences harm OCD, involving intrusive thoughts about attacking her family members with kitchen knives.
Her handwashing routine can take up to 11 hours, limiting her ability to use the bathroom regularly.
She was officially diagnosed with OCD in July 2021 and uses her TikTok channel @victoriaocd to raise awareness about the condition.

title: Chronic illness left me the skinniest I've ever been – I've never felt worse
author: Hannah Van De Peer
content:
![At my slimmest, I was malnourished, and it took a massive toll on my mental health (Picture: Hannah Van De Peer)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729878-a387-e1787055438697.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Stepping on the scales for the first time in 10 days, I saw the result I’d been fearing: I’d lost 21 pounds in under two weeks.
It was June 2025, and I was preparing to have my gallbladder removed. Despite the fact that I was in so much pain and had virtually no appetite, my hospital had put me on a strict, two-week diet to shrink my liver, to make it easier for the surgeon to access the gallbladder itself.
In the Ozempic era, rapid weight loss is seen as an overwhelmingly positive thing. But throughout that diet, I was terrified of losing it too quickly, and the impact it might have on my physical and mental wellbeing.
Sure enough, I soon started experiencing constant fatigue, brain fog, fragile emotions – my hairline even receded. My body wasn’t getting the nutrients it needed to function at a basic level, and my brain was paying the price.
Switching diets and restricting food, sadly, has become my new normal.
In the last two years, I’ve been managing symptoms of four chronic illnesses; during which time, I’ve struggled to maintain my weight.
At my slimmest, I was malnourished, and it took a massive toll on my mental health. I felt exhausted, quick to anger (or break down in tears) for seemingly no reason, and I was trying to push myself to function normally despite the brain fog.
I enjoy being a midsize, curvy woman – because fundamentally, that’s what healthiness looks like to me. But, two years on, my weight is still in a constant state of fluctuation, and the tiredness I feel is second-to-none.
My health woes began in June 2024. Unbeknown to me, I was living with gallbladder disease which was progressing to a dangerous level.
![Hannah Van De Peer: 'Chronic illness left me unable to eat - skinnier doesn?t always mean healthier'](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729976-f678-e1787055548648.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
I had just one gallstone,but it was the size of a golfball and was preventing my gallbladder from working properly, which gave me frequent, excruciating pain attacks and had a domino effect on my appetite.
At the time, I took measures to eliminate all saturated fat and spicy food from my diet, as well as cutting down on alcohol.
I’ve never had any desire to stigmatise food for myself – but I developed a phobia of eating socially in case I’d suffer an attack while out and about.
Birthday meals and date nights became anxiety-inducing – and I’d often find myself leaving sooner than I wanted to.
My biggest fear was – and still is – pain, vomiting or diarrhoea coming out of nowhere, which happened on several occasions. I worry about everything from not having easy access to bathrooms, to how long I’ve spent in the bathroom itself.
While preparing to go out for my ex-partner’s birthday dinner last year, I started suffering from terrible stomach cramps and diarrhoea – which has become my new normal – and I spent the entire Uber ride to the restaurant shaking with anxiety.
‘What if my body betrays me?’ I thought. The pain wasn’t just something I could ignore, it was agonising. I managed to get through it, praying no-one would notice I barely touched my meal.
And, of course, I lost a lot of weight.
![Hannah Van De Peer: 'Chronic illness left me unable to eat - skinnier doesn?t always mean healthier'](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729975-cb27-e1787055642714.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
To anyone else, dropping from a size 18 to 12 might seem healthy – I was even praised by a neighbour who said I looked ‘great’ – but I was getting more and more frustrated with how physically weak and tired I was, all the time.
Gallbladder surgery was my light at the end of the tunnel. By the time I had to start my NHS-prescribed pre-op meal plan, I was already limited on food choices because of how much pain and discomfort I was in, and I was looking forward to being able to tuck into a gigantic roast dinner when I was well enough to do so.
Unfortunately, though, my health issues didn’t end there.
Two months post-op, I began experiencing more pain – this time at the very top, midsection of my stomach. Again, these were 10-out-of-10 on the pain scale, and would often result in violent vomiting. Sometimes it would start after a glass of wine; occasionally, it would be triggered by stress or a big, bloaty meal.
![Hannah Van De Peer: 'Chronic illness left me unable to eat - skinnier doesn?t always mean healthier'](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729978-49f3-e1787055398518.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
While my appetite wasn’t necessarily smaller, I was incredibly selective about which food I ‘allowed’ myself to eat. I subscribed to anti-inflammatory diets and would only stick to what I deemed to be ‘safe’ meals.
My symptoms stumped various GPs for months, and I was referred for a gastroscopy – a small camera fed through the throat, into the stomach.
In January 2026, I was diagnosed with stage three gastro-oesophagus reflux disease (GORD) as well as chronic oesophagitis (inflammation in my food pipe), and placed on a lifelong prescription of omeprazole, which decreases stomach acid production.
Even now, I’m in the middle of more abdominal investigations and a potential fourth diagnosis. Food of any type has been causing sudden, intense lower tummy cramps and diarrhoea on a daily basis for months.
![Hannah Van De Peer: 'Chronic illness left me unable to eat - skinnier doesn?t always mean healthier'](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729977-78fb-e1787055884167.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
My diet – if you can call it that – has been pared down to fruit, plain carbohydrates and protein. Fibre, while healthy and important for most, is a major trigger for me; and, without a gallbladder, I need to be careful about how frequently I tuck into a sweet treat nowadays.
I rarely eat takeaways and restaurants are mostly off-limits, because I need to be aware of every single ingredient.
As a foodie who used to feel genuinely ecstatic about trying new meals, it all feels like a bit of a cosmic joke. My chronic digestive illnesses are debilitating, and it can be exhausting trying to plan my days around them.
I feel like I’ve lost a little part of myself – the person who used to love a morning coffee and croissant, as well as a weekly takeaway without a care in the world, is long gone.
- 
	![Young woman in bed with her arms by her head](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307896638-cbfc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0px%2C0px%2C2500px%2C1406px&resize=646%2C363)
- Dirty hotel sex made up for this big disappointment after 10 years of marriage
- I let my 4-year-old have unlimited screen time - I don't care what the experts say
- Iconic '90s chocolate bar with controversial past makes its return to Asda's shelves
Constantly having to keep an eye on my body, in case it decides to freak out, is really fatiguing – and I wish it wasn’t my life.
My weight is still not stable, having recently lost seven pounds in under a month. My confidence now is tied to how physically strong I feel – all I want is to build muscle, not lose fat.
And so I despair when I hear people lauding skinniness as their ultimate goal. Though I appreciate (and feel endless empathy for) those who find Ozempic helpful for existing health issues, it’s hard to not feel frustrated when others treat it as a silver bullet.
- ![Simba's cooling mattresses are now up to 30% off ahead of the bank holiday](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309025740-1e03.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=635&crop=1) Simba's cooling mattresses are now up to 30% off ahead of the bank holiday
- ![The best hosepipe ban-friendly products to protect your garden this summer](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308681605-7c59.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=635&crop=1) The best hosepipe ban-friendly products to protect your garden this summer
- ![Amazon has slashed the price of Cetaphil's bestselling sensitive skin products](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308284045-e781.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=720&crop=1) Amazon has slashed the price of Cetaphil's bestselling sensitive skin products
- ![Parents can save up to 30% on Kickers school shoes ahead of the new term](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307346057-1e66.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=635&crop=1) Parents can save up to 30% on Kickers school shoes ahead of the new term
- ![The back-to-school hack that's helping parents avoid queues and sold-out sizes](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEC_307273147-b677.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=720&crop=1) The back-to-school hack that's helping parents avoid queues and sold-out sizes
Skinniness, often, isn’t actually the pinnacle of health. That certainly hasn’t been true for me.
