summary: Managing multiple chronic digestive illnesses, including gallbladder disease and GORD, has caused the author severe weight loss, malnutrition, and significant mental distress. Despite people praising her rapid weight loss, the author emphasizes that being dangerously thin due to illness is far from healthy. Her condition heavily restricts her diet, social life, and daily routine, leaving her exhausted and constantly managing unpredictable physical symptoms.
key_points: The author suffered severe weight loss and malnutrition due to gallbladder disease and subsequent pre-surgery diets.
She was diagnosed with stage three gastro-oesophagus reflux disease (GORD) and chronic oesophagitis in January 2026.
Chronic illness and food triggers have caused extreme social anxiety regarding eating out and public symptoms.
The author stresses that extreme skinniness resulting from illness is not a sign of health and takes a heavy toll on physical and mental wellbeing.

title: I taught myself to wake up without an alarm in a week. Here's how it fixed my sleep
author: Ally Hirschlag
content:
I taught myself to wake up without an alarm in a week. Here's how it fixed my sleep
![Ally Hirschlag Ally Hirshlag, a woman with red curly hair wearing a black sleep mask, wakes up in bed with her cat beside her. She is pulling off her sleep mask (Credit: Ally Hirschlag)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5pz0f.jpg.webp) Ally Hirschlag
Ally Hirschlag discovers that waking up naturally can be surprisingly easy, if you take care of other sleep essentials.
My reliance on alarms has varied a lot through my life. When I was a teenager, I habitually woke up on school days before my alarm went off. I wasn't exactly jumping out of bed, but my internal alarm clock was reliable enough that I never worried about being late. That partly had to do with my always-on routine, which typically ended at 11pm, when I would crash out.
Then, in college, my sleep routine broke down due to a less structured schedule, and I began depending far more on my alarm. When I later entered the workforce, I switched back, reverting to a largely consistent sleep schedule and easily waking up alarm-free once again.
In my mid-30s, though, I found myself relying more and more on my alarm, and now I'm past 40, sleep doesn't come as readily at night, while groggy mornings have me regularly mainlining caffeine.
So when my editor suggested I test out learning to wake up without an alarm, based on tips from sleep researchers, I eagerly accepted. My circadian rhythm needed a tune-up, and I was ready to put the work in to fix it.
Finding my rhythm
After talking with experts, I decided a week of no alarms would be a reasonable time to try to reprogramme my own internal alarm. It involved a little preparation, however.
The researchers I spoke with all suggested taking a few days to find my true sleep rhythm before starting (more later on how to adjust your circadian rhythm if this ends up not fitting your schedule).
I typically sleep for seven to eight hours, but my bedtime can be anywhere between 11pm and 2am. Occasionally, I'll fall asleep watching TV on the sofa, only to wake up at 2:30am, which makes it a real challenge to get back to sleep.
Thankfully, I happened to be going on a cruise and had ample time to observe when I naturally felt sleepy at night and ready to wake up in the morning. It turned out to be about 11:30pm and 8am – an eight-and-a-half-hour sleep period.
Getting adequate sleep is vital for our bodies and minds to function properly, and adults should generally aim for seven to nine hours (anything below six increases the risk of premature death by 20%). But there's no magic number that suits everyone.
"Eight [hours] is the middle, but some people are fine with seven, while some need nine," says Eti Ben Simon, associate director of the Sleep Innovation Labs at the University of Texas at Dallas. There will be some biological variability, based on your circadian rhythm, she says.
So how could I maintain this during a work week, when higher anxiety – and worrying about managing to sleep eight hours a night – often impacts my sleep quality?
![Ally Hirschlag To support my new sleep routine, researchers suggested I use blackout blinds, but also to open them first thing in the morning to let in the morning light (Credit: Ally Hirschlag)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5pzz1.jpg.webp) Ally Hirschlag
The experts I spoke to say what's important is not just getting enough sleep, but adhering to a consistent schedule. "You want to make sure that you're going to bed at a pretty regular time, and that it's early enough that you'll be able to get that eight [and a half, in my case] hours that you need," says Helen Burgess, co-director of the sleep and circadian research lab at the University of Michigan in the US. "That regular routine will feed back, and often our bodies will start to relax as we get into that routine."
That advice was very reassuring as I was already anxious about potentially waking up too early (something I tend to do when I've an important event the next day).
Light and winding down
My new routine also needed to incorporate natural light, to help sync my internal clock with my sleep schedule. Ideally, these work in tandem, so you're "tired at night and awake during the day", says Simon. Light plays a major role in this partnership by activating the hormones that signal sleep and wakefulness.
"Light is the single biggest regulator of the circadian clock," says Anna Joyce, a chartered psychologist, sleep specialist and researcher at Regent's University London. "It tells melatonin to turn off, and that it's time to be awake." Studies have also shown that bright morning light can have a significant antidepressant effect by providing a healthy dose of serotonin.
I'm quite light-sensitive, so the researchers I spoke to suggested using blackout blinds (which I already had) while sleeping, and I decided to wear my sleep mask for added protection. Then, upon waking, they recommended I immediately open the blinds to let in the morning light, which triggers a surge of cortisol, a hormone that allows us to be alert and ready for action. "That helps tell the clock, 'Okay, this is when I start my day'," says Simon.
Joyce also stressed the importance of having a "predictable wind-down routine" within approximately two hours of when you want to be asleep. Exactly what works here will vary person by person, but dimming the lights is key, as it signals your body to produce melatonin, prepping you for sleep. I planned to get into PJs, brush my teeth and do my skincare regimen as soon as I felt sleepy, so I could simply climb into bed at my designated bedtime.
Simon advised paying attention to my body's temperature. At night, our core temperature drops because we're exerting less energy, and the body releases lingering energy through the hands and feet via vasodilation (widening of blood vessels). This is why it's harder to fall or stay asleep when it's hot. Overheating absolutely disrupts my sleep, so I set our thermostat to drop earlier than usual, at 11pm, and outfitted our bed with thermoregulating bamboo sheets.
Sleep obstacles
My biggest sleep impediment, though, is my smartphone. That's a common complaint, according to the experts I spoke to.
The blue light devices emit may be partly responsible: it's on a similar wavelength to daylight, which can send confusing signals to the brain when it's nighttime. The likely more impactful aspect of smartphones, though, is dopamine scrolling, aka habitually scanning social media feeds to chase small hits of good feelings. Algorithms on these platforms are designed to keep us engaged, so it's not surprising that a recent analysis found that excessive scrolling inhibits sleep.
![Ally Hirschlag During the experiment I aimed to eat meals at a consistent time and finish dinner at least three hours before bed (Credit: Ally Hirschlag)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5q011.jpg.webp) Ally Hirschlag
To overcome this obstacle, I used a physical app-blocking device, scheduling my block from 9pm to 12pm every night of the experiment. I also put my phone into greyscale mode (typically found in your accessibility settings, if you're interested) to make the imagery look duller and less attention worthy.
I restricted myself to one cup of coffee a day in the morning, aimed to eat meals at a consistent time and finish dinner at least three hours before bed (since your metabolism influences your circadian rhythm). Burgess also suggested I avoid alcohol as much as possible. "It will actually help you fall asleep a little bit faster," she says, but "messes up your sleep later on", as it suppresses REM sleep.
Before kicking off the experiment, I noted where it could go awry. We have two cats that like breakfast at 6am. Thankfully, they're mostly programmed to wake my husband up for this (I'm the evening feeder). His gentle early-morning alarm rarely wakes me, but he offered to sleep on the couch whenever he was getting up egregiously early (5am).
And finally, at the recommendation of all the experts I spoke to, I set an emergency alarm 20 minutes later than my desired 8am natural wakeup time, just in case.
A seven-day test
On the first night, I was asleep by midnight, half an hour after my target of 11:30pm, though I woke a few times during the night. That morning, I awoke slightly before 8am but snoozed until 8.15am. I fell asleep around the same time the second night, but it took some coercion – listening to an ASMR (autonomous sensory meridian response) video with my phone turned upside down conked me out. I ended up sleeping until my emergency alarm at 8:20am.
Day three was quite busy, so I fell asleep around 11pm, and woke up naturally at 7:10am. Since I didn't need to be up yet, I lingered a bit in bed, but didn't fall back asleep.
The key thing about sleep is it's not an on and off switch.
Life inevitably threw some hurdles. By night four, I had no trouble falling asleep a bit before midnight. The next morning, however, I was woken up at 6:45am by an offensively early doorbell (I did still manage to fall back asleep for a further hour).
Night five had me asleep by 11:30pm and awake the next morning at 8:12am, despite a brief cat paw to the face at 5:30am. Night six was my birthday, so I had a couple of drinks and was in bed by 12:30am. I woke up with some heartburn at 6am (which I considered karmic punishment for deviating from the experiment), then fell back asleep until 9am.
![Ally Hirschlag I put my phone in greyscale mode in the evening – and locked it in a physical app blocking device from 9pm to stop myself dopamine scrolling (Credit: Ally Hirschlag)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5q026.jpg.webp) Ally Hirschlag
On night seven, a Friday, I fell asleep easily between 11:30pm and 12am, and woke up Saturday morning at 8:05am. It's a rare occasion for me to be up before my husband on a weekend, so I went to get us cortados from around the corner.
My week-long experiment had officially wrapped, but I still woke up comfortably a few minutes after 8am on Sunday, and this continued into the following week with little effort. In the weeks following, I've maintained some of the expert-recommended sleep hygiene routines, like regular mealtimes and less phone use before bed. I've somewhat reverted to alarm wakeups but have had much less of a struggle naturally waking up when I want to – as long as I've had at least eight hours of sleep.
My big takeaways
My internal clock was by no means a German train by the end of the experiment, but it still felt successful overall. I had less trouble waking up naturally around 8am and felt less morning grogginess by day four. What helped the most, I felt, was the regular bedtime routine and limiting screen exposure.
I plan to keep this up as much as I can, even on weekends: it legitimately left me feeling more rested and energised. Eventually, I'd like to shift my wake-up time an hour earlier, though Burgess says that can be a slow process. "The circadian system is slow to shift. I would say start with a half-hour shift in both bedtime and wake time, half an hour earlier each day until you get to where you want to be, and then try to hold it," she suggests.
More like this:
With all that life throws at us, from doorbells to birthdays to stress, consistent, truly restful sleep can be an elusive commodity. While exploring the scientific research for this article, what struck me most was how strained our relationship is with sleep today.
Over-reliance on tech is impacting sleep quality, especially in adolescents, whose developing brains and bodies need sleep more than any other demographic. A 2025 analysis of a survey of 45,000 Norwegian students found that excessive smartphone use was directly correlated with poor sleep.
"We do see a strong link between these mental health disorders and sleep disruptions in young adults, and we also see that if you have any tendency or any risk for mental health disorders, sleep loss can push you over the edge," says Simon. "They need at least nine hours of sleep, about 70% don't even get to seven."
Many adolescents could certainly benefit from a sleep recalibration week. It was worth it for me, though I recognise that finding the time is a luxury not everyone can afford.
Still, incorporating any of these habits into your daily routine could help in finding a more restful night, and an easier wake-up.
If your sleep schedule is off, and you do have some room to try a reset, be patient with yourself. It might take some trial and error to discover your own unique rhythm. "The key thing about sleep is it's not an on and off switch," says Burgess. "It doesn't quite work that way."
--
For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.
summary: An author undertook a week-long experiment to reprogram her circadian rhythm and wake up naturally without an alarm clock, guided by sleep researchers. By establishing a consistent bedtime routine, incorporating natural light exposure, managing room temperature, and limiting evening smartphone use, she successfully reduced morning grogginess and improved her ability to wake up naturally. Following the experiment, she maintained several of these improved sleep hygiene habits to feel more rested and energized.
key_points: Light serves as the primary regulator of the circadian clock, with morning light signaling the body to suppress melatonin and increase alertness.
A consistent bedtime schedule helps the body relax and naturally aligns the internal clock for adequate rest.
Evening smartphone use, including blue light exposure and dopamine scrolling, negatively impacts sleep quality.
Additional sleep hygiene measures such as finishing dinner three hours before bed, keeping the bedroom cool, and setting an emergency backup alarm supported the experiment's success.

title: The three ‘primary drivers’ behind cancer cases in men, according to scientists
author: Storm Newton
content:
Men with heart disease are at a higher risk of developing and dying from cancer, new research suggests.
Researchers identified smoking, obesity and drinking too much alcohol as “primary drivers” behind cases in men, with the link most pronounced in lung and oesophageal cancers.
Experts called for "more to be done" to manage these risks, such as targeted screening interventions.
The study, conducted by researchers at the University of Aberdeen and Keele University, examined how cancer risk and mortality differed between men and women over more than 25 years.
It drew on data from 22,534 people taking part in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer (EPIC)-Norfolk study.
Almost 11,000 either had cardiovascular disease (CVD), an umbrella term for conditions affecting the heart or blood vessels, at the start of the study, or developed it during monitoring.
The study found the lifetime risk of developing cancer among those with CVD was higher in men (17.3 per cent) compared with women (12.8 per cent).
In those without CVD, the risk of cancer was 10.2 per cent for men and 8.2 per cent for women.
![More than eight million people - four million men and four million women - are living with CVD in the UK](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/05/19/16/55/PA-84260452.jpeg)
Dr Tiberiu Pana, specialty registrar in cardiology at NHS Grampian, and honorary early career clinical research fellow at the University of Aberdeen, said: “We found that cancer incidence and death were higher in people with cardiovascular disease than in those without – a relationship we already knew a bit about.
“However, through looking at this large patient group over a very long period of time, we were able to examine it more thoroughly.
“We have identified clear differences between men and women across a range of factors in those with cardiovascular disease and all types of cancer.”
Further analysis of cancers found outside of the reproductive system found that people with heart disease faced higher rates of gastric, oesophageal, lung, bowel and non-melanoma skin cancers. These were also more prominent among men, according to the study.
Men with CVD also had an increased risk of dying from gastric, oesophageal, and lung cancers compared with those without heart disease.
Researchers said this “may be partly driven by common risk factors” between CVD and cancer.
The findings, published in the European Heart Journal, suggest the “primary drivers” of cancer cases and cancer deaths in men with heart disease were smoking, obesity and drinking too much alcohol, they added.
Who is at risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD)?
NHS
There are things that may make it more likely you'll get CVD, including:
- your lifestyle – such as smoking, drinking too much alcohol, being overweight and not being active
- your age – CVD mainly affects people over 50 years old
- your sex – men are more likely to get CVD than women
- your ethnicity – you may be more likely to get CVD if you're from a South Asian, Black African or African Caribbean ethnic background
- having family members with CVD
- having certain conditions, such as diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol
Dr Rosa Thuemmler, of the University of Aberdeen, said: “We found that men had a higher incidence of both getting cancer in the first place and sadly, also in dying from it, and this was particularly true among people with cardiovascular disease.
“Although the pattern was the same across all subtypes of cancer, this was most pronounced in lung and oesophageal cancers.”
According to the British Heart Foundation, more than eight million people – four million men and four million women – are living with CVD in the UK.
Professor Phyo Myint, of the University of Aberdeen, said: “More needs to be done to improve risk management, targeted screening and prevention to address this health inequality.”
Mamas Mamas, professor of cardiology at Keele University, said: “We need to better understand the driver of cancer development in these populations.
“Furthermore, whilst cardio-oncology services have focused mainly on cancer patients preventing the development of cardiovascular diseases, we need better pathways that can identify and prevent cancer development in patients with cardiac conditions.”
Nicola Smith, senior health information manager at Cancer Research UK, said: “Many causes of cancer and heart disease overlap, which may explain why there’s a link between the two, and both of these diseases are more common in people from deprived areas.
“Cancer is slightly more likely to affect men, partly because smoking rates are higher, but more research is needed before we can say that there is a stronger link between cancer and heart disease in men compared to women.
“If anyone is concerned about their risk of cancer or heart disease, there are proven steps they can take to reduce it.
“These include not smoking, keeping a healthy weight, and cutting down on alcohol.”
summary: New research from the University of Aberdeen and Keele University shows that men with heart disease face a higher risk of developing and dying from cancer than women. Researchers identified smoking, obesity, and excessive alcohol consumption as primary drivers behind these cancer cases, with the strongest links seen in lung and oesophageal cancers. Experts are calling for improved risk management, targeted screening, and better healthcare pathways to address these overlapping conditions.
key_points: Men with cardiovascular disease have a higher lifetime risk of developing cancer compared to women.
Smoking, obesity, and excessive alcohol intake were identified as primary drivers for cancer cases in men with heart disease.
The link between heart disease and cancer was most pronounced in lung and oesophageal cancers.
Researchers and health experts are calling for improved risk management, prevention, and targeted screening interventions.

title: What Happens to Your Blood Pressure When You Eat Bananas Every Day
author: Melissa Mitri; M S; RD
content:
Getty Images. EatingWell Design.
- Bananas are rich in potassium, which helps balance sodium for healthy blood pressure.
- They have antioxidants and fiber that support heart health and a healthy gut microbiome.
- People with kidney issues or on certain meds should consult a doctor before eating bananas.
When it comes to lowering blood pressure, we hear a lot about the importance of reducing sodium intake. However, we don’t hear nearly as much about another blood pressure–lowering measure: Increasing potassium. Yet research reveals that adding more potassium to your plate can be an easy (and tasty!) way to keep your blood pressure numbers in check.
Nearly half of adults in the U.S. are living with high blood pressure (aka hypertension).potassium-rich fruits around. Yet, many of us avoid these healthy fruits. Dietitians, like Michelle Routhenstein, M.S., RD, CDCES, say it’s time to bring them back to the table. “Bananas often get a bad rap for their sugar content, but they are known to help lower blood pressure in several ways,” she says.
Keep reading to learn what makes them so great for blood pressure, plus even more blood pressure–friendly fruits to add to your day.
3 Ways Bananas May Impact Blood Pressure
They May Help You Excrete Sodium
Studies show that most Americans consume too much sodium, which is linked to higher blood pressure.offset the negative effects of sodium. How so? “Bananas are rich in potassium, a mineral that helps lower blood pressure by filtering sodium out of the kidneys, restoring fluid balance and relaxing blood vessels,” says Sheri Gaw, RDN, CDCES.
One medium banana contains about 420 milligrams of potassium. So, slice one into your cereal or over a bowl of yogurt. Add sliced bananas to a peanut butter or almond butter sandwich. Or, toss banana chunks into your favorite smoothie. They’re a super-satisfying way to support healthy blood pressure.
They Can Relax Your Blood Vessels
Potassium in bananas helps balance sodium levels in the body, which, in turn, helps relax blood vessel walls.
But it’s not just the potassium in bananas that’s responsible for these benefits. Bananas are also a surprising source of antioxidants, especially catechins, which help your blood vessels dilate.reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in the blood vessel walls, both of which can contribute to high blood pressure, says Routhenstein.
They Help Promote Gut Health
“Emerging research suggests a healthy gut may be linked to lower blood pressure,” says Routhenstein. Turns out, bananas can help with that, too. One medium banana contains 3 grams of gut-friendly fiber. And if you’re OK eating your bananas before they’re fully ripe, they also provide resistant starch, a unique type of fiber that helps feed your good gut bacteria, helping them grow and thrive.
Related Stories
![A man holding a mug and eating from a bowl with a spoon](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/g_AKOZ4uAP5FcogcOOvGqJZYuuk=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/Foods-Men-Should-Eat-Every-Week-for-Better-Blood-Pressure-163333cc1fd64eeba2de05505c5c2b83.jpg>) 
![Person holding a cup of hibiscus tea at a table indoors](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/c9YlQAdPMe31hXsTlqPcgAAeqUc=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/What-Happens-to-Your-Blood-Pressure-When-You-Drink-Hibiscus-Tea-According-to-Dietitians-7146c1406c874d11a0b96fd67e87efb2.jpg>) 
Is It Safe to Eat Bananas Everyday?
Gaw says that for most people, eating a daily banana is generally safe and can be a great way to boost fiber, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants.
Routhenstein agrees and notes eating a banana a day is OK for most healthy adults, and can be beneficial due to its potassium and antioxidant content. However, both experts say that eating lots of bananas may not be ideal for certain people, such as those with diabetes, kidney disorders or who take certain medications.
For example, for those with diabetes, a banana may cause blood sugar to spike, says Gaw. This is especially likely if it’s not paired with a source of protein and fat, such as a tablespoon of peanut butter, a handful of nuts or a slice of cheese, she explains. She adds that those with kidney disorders may need to limit bananas, as kidney disease makes it harder for the kidneys to clear potassium from the body, which can lead to heart and muscle issues.
Routhenstein stresses that people taking medication that may increase blood potassium levels, or who need to restrict their potassium intake, should consult their health care provider to see if bananas are safe for them to eat.
Medications that may raise blood potassium include:
- Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, such as benazepril (Lotensin)
- Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), like losartan (Cozaar)
- Potassium-sparing diuretics, such as amiloride (Midamor) and spironolactone (Aldactone)
- Loop and thiazalide diuretics, like furosemide (Lasix), bumetanide (Bumex), chlorothiazide (Diuril) and metolazone (Zaroxolyn)
Other Blood Pressure–Friendly Fruits to Consider
Bananas are a great choice for healthy blood pressure, but they’re not the only fruits that can help keep your numbers in check. For additional blood pressure–lowering power, try these fruits.
- Pomegranates. Pomegranates are rich in antioxidants called polyphenols, which may help lower blood pressure. While most of the research on pomegranates and blood pressure has been conducted using pomegranate juice, adding some juicy (and fiber-rich!) pomegranate seeds to your day certainly couldn’t hurt.
- Kiwis. Gaw notes kiwis are high in vitamin C and contain compounds like actinidin, which support nitric oxide production. That’s key, as nitric oxide helps blood vessels dilate more effectively to reduce pressure on vessel walls.
- Oranges. These juicy citrus fruits are loaded with vitamin C (nearly an entire day’s worth in one fruit!). They also give you a decent chunk of potassium and fiber. Because they’re sturdy, they don’t bruise easily. So, they’re easy to toss into your backpack or bag for healthy snacking on the go.
- Berries. “Berries are rich in plant compounds, vitamins and minerals which help blood vessels to relax and lower blood pressure,” says Gaw. While all berries are good, wild blueberries may be especially beneficial. One study found that older adults who consumed a daily wild blueberry powder supplement for 12 weeks (equivalent to slightly more than 1 cup of wild blueberries) experienced reductions in systolic blood pressure.
Recipes to Try
![Recipe image of No-Sugar-Added High-Protein Strawberry Shake.](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/dwZdyLl8XT05nsUT287QZ7x3xZ8=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/No-Sugar-Added-High-Protein-StrawberryShake-beauty-37456_preview_maxWidth_4000_maxHeight_4000_ppi_300_quality_100-4e1ba78266934792b1894e8125c1d17a.jpg>) 
![Berry-Almond Smoothie Bowl](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/s0crQRNsbufnDwRYNgXZju-M5oM=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/7881886-c9dffe4276184c12b0bd1812afdbd9f2.jpg>) 
![an image of the Banana Overnight Oats](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/G_YOuz-X0BcRCp-o96-4VSiJBoE=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/EWL-banana-overnight-oats-beauty-148_preview_maxWidth_4000_maxHeight_4000_ppi_300_quality_100-2231fcbf1ed74681a1902a4ebf5bfdf6.jpg>) 
Our Expert Take
A daily banana can be a delicious, satisfying way to support your blood pressure. Bananas are rich in blood pressure–friendly potassium and contain compounds that relax your blood vessels. That’s not all. Their unique fibers may also promote healthy blood pressure by favorably influencing the gut microbiome. If lower blood pressure is a goal, don’t stop with bananas. Pomegranates, kiwis, oranges and berries are also filled with nutrients that can do your blood pressure good. While most healthy people can safely enjoy a banana—or other potassium-rich fruits—every day, speak with your health care provider if you have diabetes, kidney disease or take certain medications, such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics, to find out what’s best for your unique health needs.
summary: Eating a daily banana can help support healthy blood pressure because the fruit is rich in potassium, antioxidants, and fiber. Potassium helps the body excrete excess sodium and relaxes blood vessel walls, while fiber promotes a healthy gut microbiome linked to lower blood pressure. However, individuals with diabetes, kidney disorders, or those taking specific medications should consult a doctor before making bananas a daily habit.
key_points: Bananas are rich in potassium, which helps filter sodium out of the kidneys and restore fluid balance.
Antioxidants in bananas, such as catechins, help reduce oxidative stress and dilate blood vessels.
Bananas contain fiber and resistant starch that support a healthy gut microbiome, which is linked to lower blood pressure.
People with kidney issues, diabetes, or those taking certain medications like ACE inhibitors should consult a doctor before eating bananas daily.

title: I went for an eye test and discovered I had a brain tumour the size of a lemon
author: Alison Bartlett
content:
![Alison Bartlett](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000497959848_17869749891160_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqKrVQ3kpMSBXudFn-LKazWaBaCuyZikPrjFVhkKG8zak.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Alison Bartlett](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000497959848_17869749891160_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqKrVQ3kpMSBXudFn-LKazWaBaCuyZikPrjFVhkKG8zak.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
When I started suffering from intense migraines, I put them down to stress. After all, we were in the midst of the Covid pandemic and my (now) husband, Richard, and I had just discovered that our house purchase had fallen through. We were stuck in limbo, living with his parents while trying to continue to work from home and find somewhere new to live.
But over the following months the migraines became more frequent and I developed a string of strange symptoms, including dizzy head rushes, cloudy vision and unexplained weight gain. Eventually, I booked an appointment with my local optician. I never imagined that less than 24 hours later I’d be in hospital, after an eye scan revealed signs of a brain tumour the size of a lemon.
My migraines wouldn’t go away
Before Covid, Richard and I lived together in London. He worked as a research director for a consultancy firm and I was a graphic designer specialising in print and digital marketing. Our house purchase fell through when the pandemic hit. Fortunately, we were able to move in with Richard’s parents and could continue working remotely, while settling into a new routine.
Then, in June, the migraines started. My dad has suffered from migraines for years and I’d experienced the occasional one myself, but these were unlike anything I’d had before. Every couple of weeks I’d be left unable to work or even hold a conversation. I’d shut myself away in the makeshift bedroom Richard and I shared, lying in the dark with my eyes closed until the pain eased.
Around the same time, I also started gaining weight. Richard’s mother cooked comforting home-cooked meals, often followed by pudding, and with us exercising far less than usual that seemed easy to explain. By the time we eventually moved into our new home, in October, I’d gained around 3st 2lb.
I was emotionally absent
Once we’d settled into our new two-bedroom detached house in Bicester, I expected everything to improve. Instead, the migraines continued. Richard encouraged me to see our GP, but I was reluctant. At the time, the NHS was still under enormous pressure following the pandemic and I convinced myself it wasn’t serious enough to warrant an appointment.
![Alison Bartlett and](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000497959831_17869814938190_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Eventually, however, I went. After a quick consultation, I was diagnosed with migraines, prescribed medication and reassured that the tablets should help. In hindsight, I wish I had pushed for a more thorough examination, but I accepted the prescription and hoped things would improve. Unfortunately, they didn’t.
At the start of 2021, I developed what I called “wobbly leg syndrome”, where my knee would suddenly give way when I stood up. Most mornings I woke with dark patches clouding my vision, and I regularly experienced dizzy head rushes.
The biggest change in me, though, wasn’t physical. Looking back, I now know the tumour was affecting my frontal lobe and changing my personality. I became increasingly withdrawn and apathetic. I stopped caring that I felt ill and had little energy or motivation to cook, exercise or even help around the house.
Richard did everything he could to support me, gently encouraging me to go back to the doctor, but I simply couldn’t bring myself to do it. At the time, I thought I was depressed. It wasn’t until much later that I understood the tumour itself was responsible for so much of how I’d been feeling.
The months after moving into our first home together should have been exciting. We should have been wandering around town choosing furniture and paint colours. Instead, I spent most of that time emotionally absent, while Richard desperately tried to help me find my way back.
The eye test that changed everything
For more than a year, I refused to seek any further medical advice. By August 2022, Richard had reached breaking point. He called my dad, who lives in South Africa, and explained everything that had been happening. My dad immediately contacted a doctor friend, who gave one piece of advice: I needed to see a professional as soon as possible.
Hearing how worried they both were finally persuaded me. A few weeks later, I spoke to a private doctor who referred me to a neurologist. He recommended I have an OCT scan at my local optician before arranging an MRI. The scan creates detailed images of the retina and optic nerve, helping detect problems such as swelling behind the eye.
So, I booked an appointment at my local Specsavers in Bicester. The scan itself took only a couple of minutes. Afterwards, though, the optician called the manager in to see me. “You need to go to John Radcliffe Hospital today or tomorrow at the latest,” she told me. “Both of your optic nerves are swollen.”
Most people would have panicked. Strangely, I barely reacted. By then I was so detached from everything around me that I simply couldn’t process how serious the situation was. The next day, I went to hospital where further tests were carried out before I was referred to St Mary’s Hospital in Paddington for an MRI scan.
![Alison Bartlett eye scan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496741342_17852494861446_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq7t4Eljyiy6iRMFuEKY2dXA1vLvhkMtVb21dMmpQBfEs.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
A frightening diagnosis
The scan took place the following Sunday. Afterwards, Richard and I sensed something wasn’t right. Although the radiographers couldn’t discuss the images, we were told that “something was there” and they arranged an urgent neurology appointment for two days later. I was also prescribed steroids to reduce the swelling while doctors investigated further.
Even then, I struggled to grasp the seriousness of what I was being told. At the appointment, the neurologist confirmed I had a benign brain tumour measuring 6cm across – roughly the size of a lemon. The tumour was pressing against my pituitary gland and affecting my frontal lobe, explaining the migraines, vision problems, weight gain and dramatic changes in my mood and personality.
As frightening as the diagnosis was, it also brought enormous relief. After more than two years, at the age of 42, everything finally made sense. Two days later, I met my neurosurgeon to discuss the operation. Fortunately, years of watching Grey’s Anatomy meant I wasn’t especially squeamish. I was fascinated to learn how the surgeons would carefully access my brain, remove as much of the tumour as possible and reconstruct everything afterwards.
The operation
On the following Tuesday, Richard dropped me off at Charing Cross Hospital ahead of surgery. The next morning, I remember being wheeled into theatre, meeting my neurosurgeon and then drifting off under general anaesthetic.
After 11 hours in theatre, I woke up feeling surprisingly comfortable. Along my scalp I could feel there were around 60 staples holding everything together, but the pain was nowhere near as bad as I’d imagined.
![Alison Bartlett](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496741350_17852494857800_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqv3bZLUcinocdxThoasxukcwZgCewa-xkrckcIXHk6m8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
During the operation, doctors had also performed a lumbar puncture to measure and relieve the pressure of the fluid surrounding my brain. Ironically, that proved more painful than the surgery.
Richard visited as soon as he could and, over the next nine days in hospital, I began feeling better than I had in years. The migraines disappeared. My vision cleared. It genuinely felt as though someone had lifted a weight off my shoulders.
When I was discharged, I walked slowly because my back was still sore from the lumbar puncture, but otherwise I already felt like a different person. Over the following months, I gradually returned to work and regained my strength. As my hormones stabilised and my energy returned, the weight I’d gained naturally disappeared too.
![Alison Bartlett brain scan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496741346_17852494859303_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqUdzhVSO1dBnYosldNXMOeZOZvj214O3LJs23BwERrf4.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Within a year, I was back to my previous weight, but more importantly I felt like my happy self again. Friends and family all commented that the old Alison had returned.
Making the most of every day
Richard and I have our lives back now. He proposed in January 2024 and we got married this June. I jokingly told everyone I was waiting until my scalp had healed and my hair had grown back before walking down the aisle – but it did.
I still have yearly MRI scans because my surgeons couldn’t safely remove every part of the tumour. This is fairly common. Some of the tumour has wrapped itself around important arteries, meaning removing it entirely could have caused further damage.
![Alison Barlett wedding](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496741345_17852494863094_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf-0Jyi0jPPD6Zx1hiwTPhlc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The small amount that remains will continue to grow very slowly. I don’t need medication for it, and have only had the occasional migraine since the operation. One day I may need further treatment, but for now I’m focused on enjoying married life, working hard and making the most of every day.
Looking back, it’s frightening to think how close I came to dismissing the warning signs. If my tumour had continued to grow, I could have gone blind and I presume the surgery would have been even more complicated. If I had refused to seek help, it could have even killed me.
I now know that not every brain tumour is cancerous, but that doesn’t mean it can’t have a huge impact on your health and your life. If something doesn’t feel right, keep asking questions and seeking answers. I dread to think what might have happened if Richard and my father hadn’t encouraged me to get checked again.
As told to Ella Nunn
OCT eye scans are quick, painless, and can catch sight-threatening conditions like glaucoma up to four years earlier, plus warning signs of other health conditions like brain tumours and cancer. Visit specsavers.co.uk or your local optician to find out more.
summary: After suffering from worsening migraines, vision problems, and personality changes for over two years, Alison Bartlett was urged by her family to seek medical help. An OCT scan at her local optician revealed swollen optic nerves, leading to the hospital diagnosis of a benign, lemon-sized brain tumour. Following an 11-hour successful surgery to remove most of the tumour, her symptoms disappeared, and she has since returned to health and married her partner.
key_points: Alison Bartlett developed frequent migraines, weight gain, vision issues, and personality changes that she initially attributed to stress and the Covid pandemic.
An optician's eye scan revealed swollen optic nerves, prompting an urgent hospital visit and an MRI that found a 6cm benign brain tumour.
The tumour was pressing against her pituitary gland and affecting her frontal lobe, explaining her physical and emotional symptoms.
Surgeons successfully removed most of the tumour during an 11-hour operation, instantly relieving her migraines and clearing her vision.
She requires yearly MRI scans because a small portion of the tumour remains wrapped around arteries, but she has since recovered and returned to work.

title: Putting mice into hibernation causes a major loss of synapses
author: Jacek Krywko
content:
Our leading hypothesis for how our memories are stored is that when you learn something, the connections among neurons involved get stronger and physically larger, and that constitutes the memory. The trouble is that these connections significantly change over time—they’re plastic.
“If you compare the arrangement of these connections on day one with the same on day four or five, it’s very, very different,” says Kazumasa Tanaka, a neuroscientist at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University in Japan. To learn how a memory that can last for years can sit on hardware that shifts every few days, Tanaka’s team made the shift a bit more dramatic. In a recent Science study, they induced a hibernation-like state in mice, which basically erased the state of more than half of their synapses. And yet the mice apparently have kept their memories.
Hibernation on demand
Hibernation is a specialty of squirrels, hamsters, and bears, but the neural circuit that triggers it is conserved across mammals, and is present in species that never hibernate in the wild—like mice. In June 2020, a team of researchers led by Takeshi Sakurai, a neuroscientist at the University of Tsukuba and a collaborator on Tanaka’s study, developed a technique to artificially activate this hibernation circuit. This can be done by activating a population called Q neurons in a region of the hypothalamus.
The result is a state dubbed QIH, for Q-neuron-induced hypothermia and hypometabolism.
“With our protocol, we can bring mice’s body temperature down to somewhere around 20° Celsius, and their heart rate and breathing rate decrease significantly as well,” Tanaka explains. Whether that counts as real hibernation depends on which hibernator serves as a reference. Bears in a hibernation state reduce their metabolic demand but don’t change their body temperature, which remains around 36° or 37° Celsius. On the other extreme, some species of squirrels enter super deep hibernation where their body temperature can go very close to freezing. “Artificial hibernation sits somewhere in the middle of that spectrum,” Tanaka says.
summary: Researchers studying how long-term memories persist despite constantly shifting neural connections induced an artificial hibernation-like state in mice. This technique, called QIH, erased more than half of the mice's synapses. Despite this massive loss of synaptic connections, the mice apparently retained their memories.
key_points: Neural connections that store memories change significantly over time.
Researchers induced a hibernation-like state in mice by activating Q neurons in the hypothalamus.
The artificial hibernation state, known as QIH, lowered the mice's body temperature and metabolic rates.
Inducing QIH erased more than half of the mice's synapses, yet they appeared to keep their memories.

title: Salmonella outbreak: How to check if your eggs are safe
author: Ella Pickover
content:
One person has died and hundreds have been taken ill following an outbreak of food poisoning across the country.
According to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the wave of salmonella infections "may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK".
The agency confirmed one fatality associated with the outbreak. Salmonella typically triggers self-limiting gastroenteritis, with common symptoms encompassing diarrhoea, stomach cramps, fever, and vomiting.
However, 38 per cent of those affected in this outbreak required hospital admission, and two individuals suffered potentially life-threatening infections in their bloodstream.
Is it still safe to eat eggs?
The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has told the BBC that vulnerable groups should not consume eggs that are runny or under-cooked while dining out.
It said this includes those under the age of five, over the age of 65, pregnant women and anyone with underlying health conditions.
Vulnerable groups should avoid certain foods containing raw egg that are made fresh, such as mayonnaise or souffle. However, eggs that have been well-cooked are fine to consume when eating out or ordering takeaway.
It comes after the FSA said that there is “no evidence that UK-produced eggs are affected”. The standards agency said that investigations had identified links to imported eggs “mainly used by food service and catering establishments such as restaurants or cafes, as a potential source”.
Jacquelyn McCormick, head of incidents at the FSA, says advice around eating eggs remains the same.
She said: “Eggs which are thoroughly cooked and handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk.”
Is there anything I should check when buying eggs?
The FSA says that infants, young children, pregnant people and older adults are advised to only eat runny or raw eggs if they have a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain egg assurance scheme.
However, people who are severely immunocompromised and require medically supervised diets should follow their doctor's advice.
Anyone handling eggs, eggshells or egg packaging should always wash their hands thoroughly with warm water and soap and dry them properly afterwards.
How many cases have been reported?
Between 11 August 2025 and 1 August this year, 207 cases were identified: 199 in England, six in Scotland, one in Wales, and one in Northern Ireland. London registered the highest total among English regions with 47 confirmed cases, while Yorkshire and the Humber recorded 38.
People affected include babies and people as old as 90, according to the UKHSA.
![The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the salmonella outbreak ‘may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK’](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/03/04/21/05/GettyImages-103647421.jpg)
Hannah Charles, lead epidemiologist for gastrointestinal infections at UKHSA, said: “We’re working with Food Standards Agency and other public health agencies to investigate a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK.”
What are the symptoms of salmonella?
Salmonella generally causes a mild illness, although vulnerable groups with weakened immune systems may experience more severe illness.
Symptoms of food poisoning include:
- feeling sick or being sick
- diarrhoea
- tummy pain
- a high temperature
- feeling generally unwell
The symptoms usually start within a few hours or a few days of eating food that caused the infection.
Ms Charles said: “Anyone who is concerned about symptoms should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance.
“Salmonellosis is often caused by eating or handling contaminated food and can be spread rarely from person-to-person.
“There are simple steps to prevent the spread of salmonella: wash your hands thoroughly after using the bathroom and before preparing and handling food, cook food thoroughly, and if you have any symptoms, avoid handling food for others where possible.”
The news comes as cases of salmonella poisoning after eating contaminated food has hit a decade high in England.
Dr Kimon Andreas Karatzas, professor in food microbiology at Reading University, told The Independent that the cost of living crisis could be behind the rise in cases.
“The cost of living crisis might be potentially driving changes in supply chains. It is possible that the cost of living crisis forces more people to prepare food by themselves, which might increase the chances of cross-contamination,” he said.
He added: “The fact that there is no major increase in salmonellosis infections associated with outbreaks and a concurrent increase in Campylobacter cases [highly associated with cross-contamination at home] might be pointing to this direction.
“A better investigation of the above factors, such as the numbers of salmonellosis infections associated with outbreaks or individual cases, might help us understand what the reason for this salmonellosis increase.”
summary: A national salmonella outbreak has resulted in one death and hundreds of illnesses, with infections potentially linked to imported eggs used primarily in catering establishments. While the UK Health Security Agency reports 207 cases across the UK, the Food Standards Agency confirms there is no evidence that UK-produced eggs are affected. Vulnerable groups are advised to avoid runny or undercooked eggs unless they carry a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain scheme.
key_points: An outbreak of salmonella infections has caused hundreds of illnesses and one fatality across the UK.
Investigations indicate the outbreak may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK, mainly used in restaurants, cafes, and catering establishments.
UK-produced eggs are not affected, and thoroughly cooked eggs present no food safety risk.
Vulnerable groups should avoid runny or undercooked eggs when eating out, unless the eggs bear the British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain scheme.
Common symptoms of salmonella include diarrhoea, stomach cramps, fever, and vomiting.

title: How strength training can overhaul your health in just an hour a week
author: Harry Bullmore
content:
If you could bottle up the benefits of strength training and stock this product on a shelf, it would sell out before you could say “better health and longevity”. As you grow older, the relative benefits only increase.
Yet, despite this activity being free for all to access, relatively few people commit to strength training regularly. Why is that?
“The number one reason why people do not engage in resistance training is because they make the excuse that they don’t have the time,” says Dr Brad Schoenfeld, a professor of exercise science at Lehman College in New York, and one of the world’s leading authorities on muscle growth.
But, he says, you probably don’t need to do as much as you think to make “huge improvements” to your health and fitness: “Just two 20- to 30-minute sessions each week is enough – we’ve done research in our lab which shows this.”
This routine won’t leave you looking like a bodybuilder, Dr Schoenfeld explains. But it will deliver a body that looks good, feels good and handles the rigours of life remarkably well, all in less than one per cent of your week. You will also enjoy better heart health and a significantly reduced risk of a laundry list of chronic diseases. As returns on investment go, it’s largely unmatched.
Below, Dr Schoenfeld reveals how to start strength training at home, and shares the science behind why it is never too late to reap the rewards – even if you are in your 90s.
How to start
For strength training to be effective, there are a few simple criteria you need to meet, according to Dr Schoenfeld.
Firstly, consistency is key. For the minimum effective dose, aim for two weekly workouts on non-consecutive days, every week.
Secondly, once you have fine-tuned your technique using lighter weights, your workouts need to be challenging. If the body is not challenged, it has no reason to change and adapt in the ways we want – more muscle, stronger tissues, myriad better health markers.
“If you’re lifting a weight, and at the end of your set you could do 10 more repetitions with the weight you’re using, you’re not really going to see much in the way of benefits,” says Dr Schoenfeld. “The last few repetitions [of each set] need to be difficult to complete.”
And finally, in each of your sessions, he recommends hitting every major muscle group for a full-body workout. (You can find an example of how to do this with just a pair of dumbbells below.)
If you meet these three conditions, and you give your body the fuel and recovery it needs, “you can produce really large improvements in overall strength, overall health, appearance and other factors too,” Dr Schoenfeld says.
Read more: Scared exercise will injure you? These rules make any routine safe
Why it’s never too late to begin strength training
In 1990, researchers recruited 10 frail residents of a chronic care hospital, each aged 90 or above. They were put through eight weeks of “high-intensity resistance training” – in this case, machine leg extensions.
By the end of the study, two of the 10 subjects no longer used walking sticks to walk, while another regained the ability to rise from his chair without support from his arms. Gait speed, mobility and strength also shot up, while no injuries or adverse impacts on the heart and lungs were reported.
If you start lifting when you’re younger, you can basically maintain your muscle throughout your life
“It’s never too late to start,” says Dr Schoenfeld. “Many people would say the leg extension is one of the least functional exercises – it’s single-joint and uses a machine – but it allowed multiple people to walk without their canes in a very short period of time.”
He caveats this with the message that, the earlier you start strength training, the better.
“This is because there is a progressive loss of muscle over time,” Dr Schoenfeld explains. “Once you get into your thirties and forties, you start to lose about a half per cent of muscle per year if you’re sedentary. This goes up exponentially as you get into your fifties and sixties, and then your seventies and eighties, because you become less and less active.
“But if you start lifting when you’re younger, you can basically maintain your muscle throughout your life.”
![A couple of 20-minute dumbbell workouts each week can transform your health and fitness, according to muscle expert Dr Brad Schoenfeld](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/15/41/AdobeStock_417863469.jpeg)
For many reasons, exercise can be easier to pick up when you are younger. And, due to various biological factors, a 20-year-old might have a higher fitness ceiling than someone in their 50s, 60s, 70s and beyond. But a fit and active person in the latter group will likely trounce a sedentary 20-something on many health and fitness fronts.
“We see over and over in studies on the topic that older individuals see these massive benefits from strength training – again, in a very short period of time,” Dr Schoenfeld says. “If you just stick with it, training on a couple of days a week for a couple of months, you’ll see huge benefits.”
His group conducted a meta-analysis into the effects of strength training on people aged 75 and above. They uncovered significant strength and muscle benefits, which naturally carry over to mobility, functionality and independence.
In other words: strength training is not the fountain of youth, but it’s one of the closest things we have, and it’s more accessible than many would have you believe.

Feel the fear – but do it anyway
The other major obstacle standing between people and regular strength training is trepidation. They fear injury, or believe they are not flexible enough to perform any of the exercises.
But there is a form of strength training that is suitable for everyone. Take the nonagenarians in the study above. Several could not stand up from their chairs unassisted, so squats were out of the question as a leg-strengthening exercise. Instead, they used a leg extension machine to bolster the leg muscles, and significant benefits soon followed.
If you do not have access to a gym, you could simply sit in a chair then use your hands to support you as you stand up again, and repeat this for several repetitions. If this feels challenging to you, it will have the wanted impact on your fitness levels.
“People think that, when you lift, you have to lift really heavy weights,” Dr Schoenfeld explains. “But in research from our lab we’ve consistently seen that moderate to lighter loads can provide very similar benefits.
“Heavy loads do carry risk, and as people get older they tend to have osteoarthritis and other joint-related issues. But whatever load you’re lifting, if you’re challenging your muscles at the end of the set, you will get very good results.”
summary: Strength training offers profound health and longevity benefits, yet many avoid it due to perceived lack of time or fear of injury. According to exercise science expert Dr Brad Schoenfeld, just two 20- to 30-minute sessions per week targeting major muscle groups can yield major improvements in health and fitness. Furthermore, research shows it is never too late to begin, with older adults—including those in their 90s—experiencing rapid and significant gains in strength, mobility, and independence.
key_points: Just two 20- to 30-minute strength training sessions a week are enough to significantly improve health and reduce chronic disease risk.
Effective workouts require consistency (non-consecutive days), challenging effort where the final repetitions are difficult, and full-body engagement.
Studies on individuals aged 90 and above demonstrate that strength training can rapidly improve mobility, gait speed, and independence.
Moderate to lighter loads can provide benefits similar to heavy lifting as long as the muscles are adequately challenged at the end of a set.
